News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: US appeals court halts Trump ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown
News.content:
President Trump has asserted that the new ballroom is needed to "accommodate people for grand parties, State Visits", and has also said that it is "vital for National Security".

The ballroom building would consist of the large entertaining space above ground and also a security complex below ground.

Trump doubled down on the need for the space after an assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April.

Trump has repeatedly touted the ballroom project since he unveiled plans for it in July 2025. It would have been the most substantial structural change to the presidential residence in more than 70 years.

But the project has been mired in legal issues since October, when the Trump administration demolished the East Wing, which was built in 1902 to begin construction. Trump had initially said the project would be "near" the East Wing not that it would be demolished.

Government lawyers have argued the additional security complex and features included in the ballroom project are needed to protect the White House complex from drones, ballistic missiles, biohazards and other threats - changes essential to protecting the president, his family, and staff. Trump said on Friday that construction includes bomb shelters, hospital and medical facilities and top secret military facilities.

But the preservation group that sued to stop construction said there was no basis to "disturb" the White House and argued that having a ballroom isn't a national security emergency.

The three-judge appeals court panel said on Friday that its ruling "has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable", nor does it weigh in on whether the administration may ultimately construct the ballroom.

"What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require," the order said.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation celebrated the ruling, noting that no above-ground construction can take place "unless and until" Congress takes action.

"The White House, a global landmark that symbolizes American identity and the ideals of democracy, belongs to the American people," said Brent Leggs, President and CEO of the National Trust.

"The National Trust for Historic Preservation and its partners are proud to defend this irreplaceable monument on behalf of all Americans."

News.title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
News.content:
AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up.

"We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves.

"I don't want anyone who has the ambition and talent to join our armed forces to be deterred, so it's contingent on us to make sure that we've got our act together," he added.

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

News.title: Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president
News.content:
Gianni Infantino stepped off a plane in Cali and was greeted on the runway by the president of the Colombian Football Federation.

Ramon Jesurun, a close ally of Infantino's, saw it as a chance to show his support, with the two men smiling in a photo opportunity for the federation's Instagram account.

Infantino had not travelled to Colombia for any run-of-the-mill meeting on Friday. He would attend the inauguration of the country's new president Abelardo de la Espriella.

Infantino was accompanied by Alejandro Dominguez, the president of South America's football governing body Conmebol.

This is the life of a Fifa president.

It involves building ties with some of the most powerful people in the world, shown by Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Before the biggest scandal to hit his tenure - the aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise plan - Infantino was an incredibly powerful figure who appeared bulletproof.

Now, after an apology and stated desire to withstand the backlash of his plan to sell a stake in the men's World Cup to private equity firms, Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual.

It may not be that easy.

Uefa's threat to boycott Fifa tournaments still stands. That will be tested with the Fifa Under-20 World Cup set to kick off in Poland in 29 days.

Perhaps emboldened by the support he has received from outside Europe in recent days, Infantino is not going to stand down easily.

But what exactly is the role of the Fifa president?

News.title: Record spells with no rain across parts of central and south-east England
News.content:
As the extremely dry spell continues across much of England and Wales, a number of weather stations have smashed their previous longest periods without rain.

It comes after the driest July for England and Wales, external since Met Office records began 190 years ago.

Already Wales and most of England are in drought, with parts of eastern Scotland in significant water scarcity.

Despite some locations receiving rain this week, not enough fell in drought-hit areas to provide any meaningful relief.

These include Wisley in Surrey, which has notched up 51 consecutive dry days and Coningsby in Lincolnshire with 42 days of no rainfall.

News.title: Six-hour train services between London and Stirling running with no toilets after fault
News.content:
A train operator is running services lasting more than five-and-a-half hours despite having no toilets available on board.

The Lumo trains run on the West Coast Main Line, covering the new 417-mile (671km) route between Stirling and London Euston.

Lumo, which is owned by FirstGroup, first warned about a "fault" with the toilets on a service from Stirling to Crewe on Saturday.

Some services have since been stopping for longer at stations such as Preston to allow passengers to get off and use toilets on platforms.

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Brothers jailed for killing man and injuring his son while racing cars home
News.content:
Following sentencing, Rhys' wife Caroline Jenkins, also known as Carrie, said in a statement she often wondered what difference it would have made to her family's future "if we'd hugged a little tighter and a little longer" when she waved them off that day.

She said, for her son, life "without a dad who was involved in everything you did is a hard adjustment" and it "carried an element of PTSD".

Carrie said Ioan was emotionally and physically scarred by the crash.

"It's impossible to convey the full impact Rhys' death had on us," she said, and there remains a "massive hole left in our lives by his unnecessary death".

Ioan, who broke both arms, and suffered a fractured rib and perforated bowel, said he wished his dad was still here to "watch me grow up and be my dad".

Rhys' youngest son, Gruff, was six when the crash happened.

In his own victim impact statement, he said he was in bed when police arrived to tell his mum what had happened.

After being told his dad had died, he said: "I ran out of the house. I didn't know where I was going. It was the worst feeling of my life."

The court was told Umar Ben Yusaf's car was not directly involved in the crash, but the "competitive" nature of his driving with Abubakr Ben Yusaf contributed significantly.

Judge Timothy Petts said the trauma the Jenkins family had been through in the last 21 months was "difficult for me to summarise".

"You have all been suffering with your own devastating grief but also trying to deal with the practical consequences of Rhys's death and Ioan's injuries.

"It has been an horrendous time for all of you," he told them.

Petts said to Umar and Abubakr Ben Yusaf that he was satisfied they were racing each other.

"Both of you were constantly riding your luck at high speed, completely unnecessarily, and eventually it ran out with appalling consequences.

"Rhys Jenkins never stood a chance because you were so close to him when you lost control. He was driving perfectly properly and did nothing wrong. He had no time to avoid the collision."

Sgt Sara John, from Dyfed-Powys Police's serious collision investigation unit, said: "The sentences passed today cannot undo the tragic loss suffered by Rhys's family."

She added she hoped the outcome "provides them with some closure as they begin to move forward with their lives, which have been changed forever".

"The actions of Abubakr and Umar Yusaf on that day were catastrophic. Their choice to drive in the manner they did shows their utter disregard towards other road users."

News.title: England footballer Toney charged with assault in Soho
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
News.content:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and Pink, has died at the age of 69.

A statement, external released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

News.title: Police make further arrests as Thetford disorder continues
News.content:
More arrests have been made over disorder linked to anti-immigration protests that saw crowds attempt to storm the homes of suspected asylum seekers and a police officer "seriously bitten".

Asylum seekers were removed from properties in Thetford on Thursday for their own safety, Norfolk Police said.

Two men in their 40s were arrested as protests in the market town continued for a third night, and a woman was arrested on Friday in relation to an assault on a police officer, bringing the total number detained to six.

Protesters attempted to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living on Tuesday and Wednesday night, when officers were also "subjected to significant aggression".

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after search at Midlothian beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search was launched over reports of concern for the girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

The force said the girl's family was aware.

News.title: Two firms guilty over man killed by falling window
News.content:
Two companies have been found guilty of health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane.

Mick Ferris, 53, died when glass weighing 130kg fell 300ft (90m) from a penthouse flat at The Corniche tower block on Albert Embankment in central London in October 2018.

St James Group Ltd and specialist contractors Lindner Prater Ltd were convicted at Inner London Crown Court of "failing to discharge a duty" under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. The firms will be sentenced on 24 September.

Foster + Partners, the architecture firm behind The Gherkin, and engineering consultants Wintech Ltd were cleared of the same charges.

During the trial, the court heard the "extraordinary" fact that a window panel had already fallen from the same development in August 2017, and the design was not substantially changed as a result.

Prosecuting, Gordon Menzies said: "It's reasonably practicable for clever people to do a simple thing and design a window that doesn't fall out once every year."

News.title: Data breach investigation into Minnie Merriman's medical records
News.content:
NHS Tayside is investigating an alleged data breach into the medical records of a nine-year-old girl at the centre of a murder probe.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in Arbroath.

Her father has appeared in court charged with her murder.

NHS Tayside said it was "investigating the circumstances" of the alleged breach that happened in a clinical area where staff access patient information.

A spokesperson added: "As a matter of governance, any data protection breach would be recorded and investigated by NHS Tayside and, where appropriate, reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment further on individual staffing matters."

News.title: Trump says White House staff’s lives are in danger after court halts ballroom construction until Congress approves
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

President Donald Trump derided a federal appeals court ruling halting construction of his White House ballroom and demanding he seek congressional approval, insisting it would “severely jeopardize the lives and welfare” of White House staff.

In a lengthy Truth Social post Friday afternoon, the president said two judges on the D.C. Court of Appeals had made a “politically motivated” and “totally wrong” decision and characterized his White House ballroom project as crucial for national security.

“The Circuit Court’s decision, which is totally wrong on the vital subject of STANDING, of which the plaintiff has none, severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working, at the White House — including all future Presidents of the United States, and their families, as well as the lives of all those visiting…” Trump wrote.

In a 2-1 decision, the appellate judges said the president was only a “temporary tenant” of the White House and had unprecedentedly knocked down the East Wing, paid for with American tax dollars, to build a 90,000-square-foot space without consulting Congress.

But Trump disagreed and further characterized his project as a national security matter because the administration is building an underground bunker, complete with a military facility, emergency operation center and more.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has rushed the construction of his White House ballroom, claiming its necessary for national security purposes ( AFP/Getty )

“It is all tied together as one big, expensive, and very complex unit, which is vital for National Security and Military Operations of the United States of America!” Trump wrote.

Though the president is insisting the project should continue, the judge’s ruling allows necessary national security construction to continue as legal challenges play out. It only halts above-ground, non-national security-related construction.

The court’s ruling will take effect for two weeks to give the Trump administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court, which the president said he would do.

Judge Patricia Millet, an Obama appointee, and Judge Brad Garcia, a Biden appointee, ruled in favor of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the group suing the administration to stop construction of the ballroom.

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now,” they wrote.

open image in gallery Last year, the president demolished the historic East Wing of the White House to make room for his new ballroom – sparking outrage from Democrats and members of the public ( Getty )

In doing so, they agreed with a lower court ruling, issued in April, that found Trump overstepped his authority when he demolished the East Wing to make room for the new ballroom.

“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require,” the judges added.

Meanwhile, Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee, said she would have sided with the administration.

The Independent has asked the White House for comment.

Last year, Trump announced he would build the new glamorous ballroom, without using American taxpayer dollars, to serve as an entertaining space for state dinners and events.

open image in gallery Progress on the White House ballroom construction, pictured July 11, shows the administration moved forward with above-ground work while legal challenges played out ( Reuters )

But much like Trump’s other D.C. beautification projects, the cost, scale and public understanding of the project have changed over time.

The cost of the ballroom has surged from its original $200 million estimate to $400 million – with some believing it could cost upwards of $600 million. While Trump has said private donations will pay for the ballroom itself, in June the administration transferred more than $300 million from the Secret Service budget to cover security upgrades to the White House.

The administration has continued building the ballroom as legal challenges play out, arguing the ballroom is essential for national security because they are building an underground bunker containing a military complex, a hospital and an emergency operations center.

As judges have increasingly ruled against the construction of the White House ballroom, the administration has increasingly characterized the project as a pivotal national security or military project.

In Friday’s Truth Social post, the president referred to the project as “the desperately needed Military Center” even though the dispute is over the ballroom.

Andrew Flintoff has stepped down as head coach of the England Lions as the coaching upheaval at the ECB continues.

Flintoff, one of England’s greatest all-rounders, had spent nearly two years in charge of the second-string side after being persuaded into coaching by Rob Key, the ECB’s managing director of men’s cricket.

Well liked by the players, Flintoff had drawn plaudits for his work in developing some of the brightest young talents in England, but is due to take up a new role with the Sydney Thunder in Australia’s Big Bash this winter.

“Unfortunately I’ve made the decision to step away from my role with the Lions. Not only have I enjoyed my time having the opportunity to work with the best young cricketers in the country, but have taken great pride in seeing them develop.

“I’d like to thank the coaches and staff for all their passion, tireless work and support they give everyday. In particular, Ed Barney who I’ve loved working with and was so lucky to have as a performance director, and obviously Rob (Key) for trusting me with one of the most important roles in English cricket.

“I can’t wait to get started with the Thunder later in the year and see where coaching takes me.”

open image in gallery Andrew Flintoff (centre) has proved a popular coach ( PA Wire )

His exit follows the removal of Brendon McCullum as Test head coach, with fellow New Zealander Stephen Fleming appointed. McCullum continues to oversee England’s white-ball teams, while Marcus Trescothick is in interim charge of the Test team for the upcoming Pakistan series.

While no replacement for Flintoff has yet been confirmed, Mike Yardy – the former Sussex and England all-rounder – will step in for the four-day Professional County Club Select XI match against Pakistan, which begins at Beckenham on Wednesday 12 August.

Flintoff’s departure comes just a week after Key had praised his coaching talent highly, and suggested he could well be a contender to be England coach in the future.

"It [the Test vacancy] just came too soon, but he should be someone that goes on to become an outstanding head coach,” Key said of his former teammate. “When you talk about who could be the best person, Andrew Flintoff - in the future, with a bit more experience under him - could do it, and him not being there at times in the Lions gives opportunity for other coaches, and it's for us to choose who comes in to do that.

"I think he's an unsung hero. A lot of these young players that are coming through, you think how hard it is when they've got T10s, T20s, ILT20, SA20. We've got to go to a player and say, 'We want you to come and commit to a red-ball tour of Australia, we want you to come and play 50-over cricket in Abu Dhabi'.

"Having Andrew Flintoff there has made a massive, massive difference in being able to do that, and I think he deserves the respect and the thanks for doing it."

Flintoff, known as “Freddie”, has forged a successful career as a television host and personality since his retirement from playing. He reached a settlement with the BBC after suffering serious injuries following a crash while filming Top Gear in 2022.

News.title: Serial sex offender was free to kill two women because of police blunders
News.content:

A “predatory” serial sex attacker was left free to murder two women because police and court blunders saw him released on bail, allowing him to prey on other victims.

Simon Levy, of Tottenham, north London, was found guilty by a jury at the Old Bailey on Friday for murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months apart last year.

The Metropolitan Police, British Transport Police (BTP), and Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) are all facing serious questions over how Levy was allowed to grope, rape and murder women between February 2023 and August 2025.

The timeline of his escalating crimes reveals a string of errors where officials failed to stop a dangerous predator who was already a registered sex offender.

The 40-year-old fatally suffocated both women in sexually motivated attacks, with Valencia-Trujillo found in a largely abandoned block of flats on the Aylesbury estate in south-east London, and Wilkins behind a car park wall near Tottenham High Road, north London.

He was also convicted of two counts of rape and assault occasioning grievous bodily harm (GBH) with intent, as well as non-fatal suffocation over a brutal sex attack in January 2025, which the victim survived.

The car park was also where Levy carried out the January rape, which left the victim unconscious with a broken collarbone.

Levy was brought into police custody for questioning on 4 September and charged soon after.

open image in gallery Levy had already been sentenced for 11 counts of sexual assault at an earlier trial ( Metropolitan Police )

Members of the victims’ families burst into tears as the verdict was delivered after the jury deliberated for 13 hours.

Prosecutor Will Martin said his desire to sexually assault women was “on the verge of compulsive or pathological”.

Speaking outside the Old Bailey, Detective Chief Inspector Neil John, from Scotland Yard, said: “Simon Levy is a dangerous and predatory offender. His crimes were calculated, cruel and deeply disturbing.

“Throughout the trial, he has shown complete disregard for the victims and victim-survivor, despite being fully aware of the lasting and devastating impact of his actions.”

Flanked by Wilkins’s two sisters and the daughter of Valencia-Trujillo, he appealed for any more victim-survivors of Levy who have yet to come forward to contact the police.

Valencia-Trujillo’s children described her as a “big character” and “full of life”. She became a grandmother in 2024 and was said to be a “much-loved” member of the community with a love of salsa-dancing.

Mother-of-four, Wilkins’ family said she was a much-loved woman and was missed every day by those who knew her.

open image in gallery Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo ( Metropolitan Police )

Jurors heard that Levy was already a registered sex offender. He sexually assaulted two women in 2018 and was jailed in 2021.

He assaulted a prison officer while in jail in 2022, then once released groped a woman on the Tube in October 2023, three more in October the following year, and beat and raped another in January 2025, before he murdered Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025.

He then sexually assaulted six more women on the Tube – one in March, three in April and two in May 2025, before he murdered Wilkins in August last year.

open image in gallery Sheryl Wilkins ( Metropolitan Police )

Jurors saw through his claims that all the contact had somehow been accidental on wobbly or crowded trains, or after he became partially sighted in May 2024.

He would grope the young women he had chosen as victims, with some reacting angrily when they realised what had happened.

One called him a pervert and emptied a can of coke over him, while another shouted at him not to touch her.

He was convicted of 10 counts of sexual assault on the Tube, and an 11th at Brixton prison, by a jury at Inner London Crown Court on 4 February.

An Old Bailey jury reached verdicts after deliberating for 13 hours. Levy, who wore sunglasses in court, made no reaction as the verdicts were delivered.

Levy was arrested by BTP in November 2024 for four sexual assaults on the Tube, for which he has since been separately convicted, but delays in organising an identification parade until the following April left him free to carry out the rape and first murder.

When they took details of his Oyster card, BTP officers did not realise that it had been stolen from a bus driver, meaning Levy had a free travel pass that he used on the day he murdered Valencia-Trujillo.

Following her death, he was released on bail at two magistrates’ court hearings in May and June 2025, with the CPS admitting that it had not opposed bail at the first hearing, and the prosecutor had not given the court all the relevant information for consideration at the second hearing.

There were another three crown court hearings that he failed to attend for various reasons, yet no arrest warrant was requested. Less than two weeks after a hearing on 11 August, he murdered Wilkins.

open image in gallery Simon Levy, 40, was arrested in September ( Metropolitan Police )

open image in gallery Levy was found guilty by a jury at the Old Bailey on Friday ( Metropolitan Police )

His victims spoke of their shock at learning of his other crimes, with one, who cannot be named for legal reasons, telling the court: “After reporting the sexual assaults, it wasn’t long before I learned that my attacker was already known to the police for sexual violence and is a convicted sex offender.

“You could not begin to understand the horror I felt at hearing this.”

An Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) spokesperson said they are investigating the management of Simon Levy from his first conviction in September 2021 up to his arrest in September 2025.

They said: “Our independent investigation began in January following a voluntary conduct referral from the force, relating to alleged failures by two officers in his management following his prison release on licence in February 2023.

“We are examining whether action could or should have been taken to prevent his reoffending, and if all officers involved in his management followed policies, procedures, and training.

“We are also assessing whether any learning, whether individual, force-wide, or nationally or other changes should be implemented in light of the events under investigation.

“At this stage, we have served a gross misconduct notice on a police constable and a misconduct notice on a detective sergeant, which means that the actions of those officers are under investigation.

“The serving of conduct notices does not necessarily mean disciplinary proceedings will follow.”

People can contact the Metropolitan Police’s incident room directly on 07751 700 330 or anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

A QVC host’s on-air slip-up has sent the internet into hysterics.

Toni Brattin, the founder of Toni Brattin Wigs, appeared Wednesday in a baby blue dress on the QVC shopping channel to promote her “Salon Select Wig.”

Showing off the back of the wig, she highlighted its “texture and wave pattern.”

“Again, it looks like you went and got a b****** at your,” Brattin said before slowly correcting herself. “Blowout … at your salon.”

“Oh my god,” she whispered to herself, adding through laughs, “and it looks beautiful.” Her co-host, Terri Conn, quickly took over as Brattin, still back to the camera, continued quietly laughing before slowly sinking down behind the table.

open image in gallery Toni Brattin appeared on the QVC channel to promote her Toni Brattin wigs ( QVC )

The clip then cut to another model standing in a green top, smiling and zhuzhing the wig.

Conn later shared the now-viral clip on Instagram, writing alongside a crying laughing emoji: “The show must go on. Love you, Toni Brattin.”

The official QVC Instagram account commented on the post, praising Brattin for “handling this like a pro. Is there an award for Best Live Blooper Recovery??”

The footage has since been shared on X and viewed more than 11 million times, with thousands of comments expressing amusement at Brattin’s blunder.

“Caught me off guard and I’m still laughing,” one person wrote, while a second declared, “You know it’s a wild moment when even the people on live TV don’t know how to react.”

“She never turned around ever again,” a third quipped, as someone else applauded Brattin’s “freeze right after the wrong word landed” as “pure live TV gold.”

“This is the best thing that happened today,” another chimed in.

open image in gallery Brattin has been in the beauty and wig business for over 30 years ( Getty )

Brattin has been in the beauty and wig business for over 30 years. She regularly appears on the QVC channel to host her dedicated “Toni Brattin Hair Fabulous” segments.

Speaking to TMZ about the hilarious moment, Brattin explained her brief pause, admitting she initially thought producers would switch cameras.

She said that after the broadcast was over, everyone in the studio had a good laugh. Brattin added that QVC approached her the next morning, reassuring her and thanking her for her professionalism.

Instead of shying away from her gaffe, Brattin is leaning into it, recently sharing an Instagram video of Jimmy Fallon’s reaction on The Tonight Show.

After playing the clip, the late-night host mimicked Brattin, facing away from the camera. “By the way, the wigs are totally sold out,” Fallon joked. “Note to all the married men out there, the wig is only available on your birthday.”

“Jimmy Fallon makes it even funnier,” Brattin wrote.

Andrew Flintoff has stepped down from his role as England Lions head coach.

The former England captain had been in charge for almost two years after he got back involved in cricket in 2024 following a car crash on BBC show Top Gear.

Flintoff has since held multiple roles within the England and Wales Cricket Board set-up, but with a coaching stint on the horizon with Big Bash League franchise Sydney Thunder, the 48-year-old has left the organisation.

open image in gallery Flintoff, seen here (centre) with ECB managing director Rob Key (left) and Jofra Archer, will coach in Australia later this year (Jacob King/PA) ( PA Archive )

“Unfortunately I’ve made the decision to step away from my role with the Lions. Not only have I enjoyed my time having the opportunity to work with the best young cricketers in the country, but have taken great pride in seeing them develop,” Flintoff said.

“I’d like to thank the coaches and staff for all their passion, tireless work and support they give every day. In particular, Ed Barney who I’ve loved working with and was so lucky to have as a performance director, and obviously Rob (Key) for trusting me with one of the most important roles in English cricket.

“I can’t wait to get started with the Thunder later in the year and see where coaching takes me.”

Flintoff has been England Lions head coach for 23 months, but spent time with England’s senior white-ball teams and was part of the backroom staff at the 2024 T20 World Cup.

The former Lancashire all-rounder also coached The Hundred franchise Northern Superchargers for two seasons and will continue his journey this winter with Sydney Thunder.

Flintoff was set to miss the end of England Lions’ tour of South Africa due to his maiden BBL job, but that issue is no longer a problem for the ECB.

open image in gallery Andrew Flintoff coached the Northern Superchargers in The Hundred (Richard Sellers/PA) ( PA Archive )

Ed Barney, ECB men’s performance director, said: “Fred has helped to transform the Lions environment into a programme that has had a major impact on young players.

“By creating an environment that both supports and pushes excellence at all times he has helped bring forward a new generation of young players.

“Coaches have also flourished alongside him, whether early in their coaching journey or with decades of experience, and he has consistently maximised the expertise around the group. We wish him the best in the next stage of his coaching career and look forward to a time he returns to the English game.”

Mike Yardy will coach Professional County Club Select XI in a four-day match with Pakistan, which begins at Beckenham on Wednesday.

First-look images have been unveiled for the Call The Midwife Christmas special, Sisters In Arms, following the completion of filming.

The three-part episode serves as a prequel, set in Poplar in September 1939 during the outbreak of the Second World War.

The pictures feature new cast members Julie Hesmondhalgh, Helena Wilson, Ellie McKay, Liv Andrusier, and Lizzie Back, seen in their uniforms for the first time.

Heidi Thomas, writer and showrunner, said: “Call The Midwife has a long and noble history of filming Christmas specials during heatwaves, and this year we welcomed the snow-machine back to the Nonnatus House set like an old friend.

open image in gallery (Left to right) Ellie Mckay as Olive Dobbs, Liv Andrusier as Marianne Siegler and Lizzie Back as Sybil Maxted ( BBC )

“But I was surprised how many new emotions Call The Midwife: Sisters In Arms sparked. In particular, the evacuation of Poplar’s children, and the fear that they may not make it home for Christmas had us all in tears.”

Call The Midwife, which follows the group of nurse midwives working in east London through the decades, began in January 2012 and has had 15 series, with each featuring a Christmas special.

A synopsis for the special from the BBC reads: “Sister Monica Joan is in her prime, Sister Julienne and Sister Evangelina are young and zealous, and Nonnatus House is the beating heart of Poplar.

“Together with Sister Alice, and local GP Dr Kit, the nuns dedicate their lives to mothers, babies and those in need. But there is no gas and air, no penicillin, no cure for TB, and no welfare state.

open image in gallery Julie Hesmondhalgh (left) as Sister Alice and Helena Wilson as Sister Julienne ( BBC )

“Then war is declared – and life gets even harder. The three young secular midwives who complete the team – Sybil, Olive and Marianne – receive a baptism of fire as the blackout and the Blitz take hold.

“While bombs rain from the sky, women give birth underground, families are shattered, children run wild, and whole streets are reduced to rubble. But courage, compassion and resilience triumph as the community unites in its efforts to survive.”

An exact broadcast date has yet to be announced but the special will be aired during the festive period.

Previous series of Call The Midwife are available on BBC iPlayer.

America’s Next Top Model winner Adrianne Curry has offered forgiveness to Perez Hilton amid his current hospitalization.

Hilton’s TikTok followers reported a concerning Tuesday night livestream that appeared to show the celebrity blogger self-harming to police, who “safely recovered” him from his house in Miami and transported him to his local hospital. He is continuing to receive medical attention, according to updates shared by his family.

Many celebrities have spoken out in the aftermath of the terrifying video, including Curry, who became the first-ever winner of America’s Next Top Model in 2003. But that win also subjected her to public scrutiny and an intense feud with Hilton amid his rise to fame as a celebrity blogger.

“For years he targeted me and harassed me. He drew wieners that were erect all over near my face,” Curry said of Hilton in a video shared to X.

“He bullied me and got the public to bully me. And this is during his peak years.”

Curry acknowledged that Hilton’s livestream was “disgusting” and “crazy” before sharing her desire for “him to see me saying that his life has value and that I wish him peace and I don’t want anything bad to happen to him. Because I think sometimes that’s what it takes — not your friends rallying around you, but people who should hate you saying ‘Hey, your life has value. Don’t do this.’”

She said that’s what used to help her when she was in “dark places.”

“I’d like for him to see [that] I forgive you,” she continued. “I don’t think you should be hurting yourself, and I hope you get f***ing better.

“I feel like it took a lot for me to forgive someone who never asked for it, and I think in times where people are down, you have to come out the better person. It’d be really, really, really easy for me to kick him when he’s down.”

Curry’s comments come as Hilton reportedly remains hospitalized following the TikTok livestream.

Adrianne Curry has offered Perez Hilton forgiveness after his TikTok incident ( X/@adriannecurry/Getty )

In an update shared Thursday, Hilton’s family said that his three young children, as well as his niece and sister, were in the Miami home “just minutes before the public livestream incident.”

“When it became clear that Perez was experiencing a severe mental health crisis and harming himself, they immediately fled to protect the children from witnessing any further trauma,” the family wrote on Hilton’s website.

“Our highest priority right now is helping the children begin to heal from what they experienced. An important part of that process is allowing them to safely return home and begin rebuilding a sense of security and normalcy,” the family continued.

“For the children’s safety, privacy, and well-being, we respectfully ask members of the media, paparazzi, content creators, and the public to leave the area surrounding the family’s home and not return. Please allow his children the privacy and space they need during this unimaginably difficult time.”

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you

When the Supreme Court tells a president that his executive order conflicts with more than a century of constitutional interpretation, the ordinary response is to stop.

But Donald Trump doesn’t fancy himself ordinary in any way.

In a hastily arranged Thursday Oval Office appearance, the president announced he was — for a second time — attempting to restrict birthright citizenship by executive fiat while repeating his complaint that a 6-3 Supreme Court decision striking down his previous attempt to do so had been “very unfair.”

“We had a very unfortunate decision in the Supreme Court concerning birthright. It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision. So we're making adjustments because it's very unfair,” he said.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller then told reporters that the new orders would use Trump’s “authority as commander-in-chief” to “expand the definitions of people who are ineligible for birthright citizenship.”

“That includes, for example, alien enemies of the United States, members of foreign terrorist organizations, and large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments. And so, with taking this action, it ensures that large numbers of people who wrongly would be getting birthright citizenship will no longer be eligible for those benefits,” said Miller, who added that Trump was also issuing an order to prohibit what he called “birth tourism.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump looks on as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller speaks on new executive orders about birthright citizenship - despite a Supreme Court ruling ( AFP/Getty )

On the surface, these latest actions represent a dramatically narrower carve-out than the one Trump claimed for himself in the executive order he signed within hours of his second inauguration, which withheld citizenship from any child born in the U.S. unless at least one parent was already a citizen or permanent resident.

That rule was broad enough to cover the roughly 150,000 babies a year born to undocumented or temporary-visa parents, according to the plaintiffs who sued to block it — and broad enough that multiple federal appeals courts called it unconstitutional well before the justices got their turn.

But at no point did Trump or the White House mention that the new orders are a fraction of the size of the one the courts killed. Instead, a fact sheet distributed to reporters late Thursday declared that the administration "continues to guard against" citizenship fraud "after the Supreme Court's decision.

Then it pivots into a section headlined "Putting Americans First" that reads less like legal reasoning than a campaign flyer: three million deportations, 88 denaturalization cases filed against people it says obtained citizenship fraudulently, 1.4 million people cut from public benefits, visa processing paused for "75 high-risk countries," and a drive to purge alleged noncitizens from state voter rolls.

None of that reads like an administration confident enough in its legal position to let the ruling speak for itself. It reads like a White House that needs a citizenship-and-borders headline heading into a midterm election year, and would rather announce two narrower orders under a "continuing to protect" banner than let a Supreme Court defeat sit there for voters to notice unadorned.

That's because immigration remains one of the only lanes where this White House still likes its odds. The tariffs got struck down by the same court. The war in Iran polls badly. Even parts of his own base have grumbled about the price tag on his Washington makeover.

But birth tourism is the kind of narrow, easy-to-caricature target — foreign nationals allegedly gaming a visa to secure a passport for their newborn — that plays well on cable news regardless of how few people it actually affects, which may explain why a policy retreat got relaunched this week as a two-order offensive rather than absorbed quietly.

open image in gallery The Supreme Court ended Trump’s last attempt to end birthright citizenship ( AFP via Getty Images )

But ironically, Trump’s latest citizenship gambit appears to be a play lifted from the playbook of his successor-turned-predecessor, former president Joe Biden.

When the Supreme Court struck down Biden’s roughly $400 billion student loan forgiveness plan in June 2023, his administration didn't drop the subject either.

It pivoted to new executive actions to create what was called the SAVE income-driven repayment plan, then to a second attempt at mass cancellation through Higher Education Act administrative rulemaking — both promptly sued by Republican-led states, both left tangled in injunctions through much of 2024 that stranded millions of borrowers in limbo over debt they'd been told was already on its way to forgiveness.

Biden's team never described the SAVE plan as a workaround for a policy the justices had just killed. But that is functionally what it was, in much the same way Trump's new orders are functionally a retreat dressed up as round two.

Both presidents arrived at the same discovery: voters rarely parse the fine print of an injunction or a 14th Amendment exception, and a fight that still looks like it's being fought can do more for a political coalition than a policy that quietly complies with an unambiguous court decision.

Whether either strategy delivers anything more than headlines remains to be seen. What's already clear is that both the man who wanted to end birthright citizenship and the man who wanted to cancel student debt found it easier to keep signing new paper than admit to their most fervent supporters that neither plan was legal in the first place.

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”

News.title: The underground lab where ‘princess mosquitoes’ are treated like royalty
News.content:
Beneath the grand Art Deco headquarters of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine lies a vast labyrinth inhabited by weird and wonderful creatures.

In this maze of subterranean labs, store rooms and corridors live colonies of disease-bearing insects and arachnids from all over the world, from bed bugs, sand flies and microscopic dust mites to the so-called kissing bugs that spread Chagas disease – a sinister condition that can cause its victims to drop dead of heart failure without warning, albeit decades after the first (silent) infection.

Behind a series of doors, contained in stacks of mesh boxes, you can even find the flies that spread trachoma, the Dickensian eye disease that is still a leading cause of blindness around the world. But be warned: entering the room is not for the faint of heart – the flies feed on human excrement and the smell is impossible to forget.

There are also many varieties of mosquito, including several species of the Anopheles genus that spread malaria, Culex and Aedes mosquitoes that are also vectors for human and animal diseases, and even Toxorhynchites, perhaps better known as the elephant mosquito, a friendly giant which doesn’t bite people but preys on other mosquitoes.

These animals have been studied intensely since the insectaries were established in the building’s vaults in the 1960s, underpinning many breakthroughs in the control, surveillance, and understanding of vector-borne diseases in the developing world.

LSHTM researchers are now looking closer to home. They have established the UK’s first laboratory colony of Aedes vexans mosquitoes, a species native to the British isles, to study whether they could harbour diseases like West Nile virus, Rift Valley fever, Zika or Japanese encephalitis.

SunSport brings you all the information you need.

Carabao Cup first round ties go straight to penalties if the score is level after 90 minutes.

Sports.title: I took on Harry Kane to see how I’d stack up against a professional footballer – I beat England star in key test

My first two attempts clocked in slower than him, at 31.1kph and then 30.2kph, before I finally pulled it together and got the better of him with my third sprint, at 32.3kph – I was buzzing with that.

CANFIELD 1-0 KANE

A professional like the England number nine would be looking to measure up at around 40cm in my next test, a standing vertical jump, with the top five percent of Prem stars clocking in at over 48cm.

Sports.title: Newcastle’s £25.7m keeper Hornicek was wrestling carp while negotiating deal and vows to bring ‘sexy’ back to St James’
Sports.content:

Fellow Czech goalie Pavel Srnicek achieved legendary status as part of Kevin Keegan’s Entertainers.

In fact, he was even wrestling a carp as he fell hook, line and sinker for Newcastle during his very first phone call with Toon’s sporting director Ross Wilson.

Hornicek said: “It’s a funny story. I was fishing for two days in Portugal, because my girlfriend and daughter went to the Czech Republic for one of her exams. So, I was there alone and was like, ‘Okay, let’s go fishing’ to get my mind off of everything that was happening.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“Then my agent called me and said, ‘Hey, there will be a call from Newcastle,’ so I picked it up and I was fishing at that moment.

“For 30 minutes of call everything goes smoothly, and then from nowhere, I got a [makes swishing sound] hit on my rod. Then, for another 20 minutes, I was fighting the carp as they kept talking to me. It was a funny moment.”



The North East’s three big rivers – Tyne, Wear and Tees – are famed for their salmon, trout and pike. Though you will not find the recent arrival hunting the predators down river banks. He much prefers to kick back by a lake.

He revealed: “Pike fishing is too much! You are reeling in and you need to find the fish. This is too demanding for me as a footballer.

Dream Team bosses can wait for the starting line-ups before confirming their team, a useful bonus exclusive to GW1, and if Gyokeres is selected to start against the Sky Blues then his ownership may increase sharply in the hour or so before kick-off.

Sports.title: Liverpool prepare blockbuster offer for PSG star Bradley Barcola - but there's a catch
Sports.content:
Liverpool prepare blockbuster offer for PSG star Bradley Barcola - but there's a catch

Bradley Barcola is Liverpool's top transfer target this summer and the Reds are now ready to move forward with trying to sign the Paris Saint-Germain winger

View 2 Images Bradley Barcola is Liverpool's top transfer target (Image: Getty Images)

Liverpool are ready to make their opening offer for Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola, but their bid will be rejected by the French giants.

‌



Barcola has emerged as Liverpool's number one transfer target this summer, with new manager Andoni Iraola desperate to strengthen in wide areas. The France international has entered the final two years of his current contract with PSG, who have softened their stance on a deal.

‌



The reigning Champions League champions had initially been firm in their stance that the 23-year-old was not for sale at any price. But, having lined up potential replacements, a deal can now be done - if their asking price is met.

‌



Liverpool have found it slow going in the transfer window this summer, with a £35million deal for Osasuna winger Victor Munoz the only significant piece of business done, as the £55m arrival of Jeremy Jacquet was sealed in January.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Liverpool weigh up hijacking £60m Arsenal transfer to appease desperate Andoni Iraola READ MORE :

But the Reds are now ready to step up negotiations with PSG for Barcola, according to L'Equipe. They will submit an official offer in the region of €115million (£98m) in the expectation that it will be rejected.

‌



PSG don't want to lose Barcola, who has contributed heavily to their success under Luis Enrique's management. Yet they are also unwilling to keep a player against his will, so have slapped a €150 million (£128.5m) price tag on their star player.

Their resolve has likely be strengthened by the £120m fee RB Leipzig got from Real Madrid for Yan Diomande - a player four years younger and with far less experience than Barcola.

Barcola has 39 goals in 152 appearances for the club since joining from Lyon three years ago. He has combined well with Ousmane Dembele and Desire Doue under Enrique's management, but is keen to join Liverpool.

‌



View 2 Images Andoni Iraola is desperate for a new winger (Image: Michael Miller/ISI Photos, ISI Photos via Getty Images)

Barcola has already agreed personal terms with Liverpool and it seems likely that a deal can be done. Liverpool sporting director Richard Hughes is leading discussions, with Luis Campos representing PSG and agent Moussa Sissoko speaking on behalf of Barcola.

L'Equipe says that Liverpool are not actively pursuing any alternative to Barcola, which is a measure of their determination to land the Frenchman. Iraola spoke publicly about the need for a winger, even after Munoz was signed.

‌



"There are obvious situations that we know where we need to sign players," he said last month. "A winger, for example – we definitely need to sign a winger.

"But there are other situations that we will have to analyse what the market gives you, what’s the cost, how we also see the players we have. We have some tricky positions where we have injured players that we trust but is still not the ideal situation. So, it will depend on a lot of things."
