Sports.title: Manchester City reject Barcelona’s opening £38.5m bid for Rodri as talks continue
Sports.content:
Manchester City have rejected an offer of £38.5m (€45m) from Barcelona for Rodri and want at least £60m before allowing Spain’s World Cup-winning captain to depart.

Barcelona have emerged as Rodri’s preferred destination after talks with Real Madrid broke down this week. It is understood that the 30-year-old, who is now in the final year of his contract at City, has agreed personal terms with the Spanish champions after indicating that he would like to return to his homeland following the departure of Pep Guardiola.

Rodri moved to the Etihad in 2019 from Atlético Madrid and has turned down the offer of a lucrative extension. Yet City are believed to be adamant that he will not be allowed to leave for less than their asking price. Barcelona are continuing negotiations in the hope of reaching a compromise.

Rodri, who won the World Cup Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player last month, spoke to Barça’s manager, Hansi Flick, and sporting director, Deco, about a potential move on Wednesday.

The Spanish champions will be without Frenkie de Jong for several months after the Netherlands midfielder sustained a knee injury and have targeted Rodri as a replacement. He has had minor surgery on his back and will miss most of City’s pre-season programme.

City have signed Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m and remain in negotiations with Lille over a deal for Ayyoub Bouaddi. The Morocco midfielder could cost up to £80m but they could be tempted to bring in a more experienced replacement for Rodri should he depart, with Chelsea’s Enzo Fernández among those thought to be under consideration. The 25-year-old is also wanted by Real, whose manager, José Mourinho is said to not to have the news of being gazumped by their great rivals well. Reports in Spain have claimed that the 63-year-old is unhappy after making the signing of a central midfielder his priority on returning for a second stint at the Santiago Bernabéu.

Real have already brought in the winger Yan Diomande for £115m and Marc Cucurella, Bernardo Silva, Ibrahima Konaté, Denzel Dumfries and Carlos Espí, so they may have to balance the books by selling either Aurélien Tchouaméni and Eduardo Camavinga if they want to pursue Argentinian Fernández.

Crystal Palace have confirmed the signing of Takehiro Tomiyasu after a successful trial period. The former Arsenal defender has been training with Palace during pre-season and has done enough to earn an initial 12-month deal with the option of extending that by another two years. Tomiyasu becomes new manager Pierre Sage’s second signing of the summer after the arrival of Óscar Mingueza on a free transfer. Palace are expected to complete a deal for the USA youth international Zavier Gozo from Real Salt Lake in MLS.

Sports.title: Tottenham and Atlético in talks over Romero with Van de Ven set to sign new deal
Sports.content:
Tottenham are in talks with Atlético Madrid over the sale of Cristian Romero after categorically rejecting Arsenal’s approach for the Argentina defender and are expected to agree a new five-year deal with Micky van de Ven.

Romero has made no secret of his desire to leave Spurs despite signing a new four-year contract at the start of last season and had looked set to join Inter for a fee of around £35m. But Atlético are long-term suitors of the 28-year-old and are thought to be his preferred destination, with Diego Simeone’s side understood to be prepared to match Inter’s bid.

Reports in Spain on Friday suggested that personal terms have already been agreed with Romero, although his move may have to wait for Atlético to free up space in their squad before they can complete the transfer. Nahuel Molina, Romero’s Argentina teammate, is expected to join Roma while Aston Villa are hoping to sign Matteo Ruggeri.

Arsenal had also made their interest known as they search for a replacement for William Saliba, with the Frenchman out for an extended period due to a back issue. However, Tottenham – who have signed defenders Jan Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi this summer – insisted that they did not want to sell to another Premier League club, least of all their north London rivals. Arsenal are also interested in Villa’s Ezri Konsa.

It is understood that Van de Ven had been considering his future in north London at the start of the summer after Tottenham narrowly avoided relegation last season. But the impact of the new manager, Roberto De Zerbi, has persuaded the Netherlands international to commit his future to the club after talks with his representatives.

Tottenham have already spent more than £200m on six new players this summer and are still in the market for a new attacker. Last week, De Zerbi said that they had “completed 60% of our project in the transfer market”.

Sports.title: Afcon’s biennial switch cost African governing body deal worth more than $1bn
Sports.content:
A deal worth at least $1bn in secured income over eight years was abandoned by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) because the governing body decided to switch the Africa Cup of Nations from a biennial to a four-yearly event, the Guardian can reveal.

On 5 July 2025, the eve of the delayed Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco, the Caf president, Patrice Motsepe, told the Guardian in Rabat, after a prolonged discussion of the bidding process at an executive committee meeting, that a decision on a winning bid would be made “in due course”.

“We announced in Addis Ababa this $1bn partnership that we are looking at over the next eight years. There is a lot of good progress that has been made,” he said.

On 23 July, four days after the World Cup final in New York, Caf opened a fresh tender for the marketing and commercial rights of the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) tournaments, with bidders given until 24 August to hand in their bid books.

The tender is in complete contrast to the 2025 bidding round, in which the entirety of Caf’s competition portfolio was bundled for sale.

Luxolo September, Caf’s head of communications, confirmed that the change in Afcon frequency is wholly responsible for the abandonment of the 2025 bidding round that was on the verge of completion.

“As foreshadowed by the president in his comments last year, following the receipt and evaluation of bids and presentations from the bidders, in the second half of 2025, Caf entered into detailed discussions with shortlisted bidders regarding the precise terms and conditions of their proposals.

“However, at its meeting on 20 December 2025, the Caf executive committee took a unanimous decision – in the interest of African football – to move the Afcon to a four-year cycle, bringing the competition into alignment with the international match calendar,” September said. “This was a significant decision for African football. That executive committee decision materially changed the scope of the commercial rights available for tender, with the result that the 2025 ITT (Invitation To Tender) process could no longer proceed in its existing form.”

View image in fullscreen Patrice Motsepe (left) said in 2025 that ‘good progress’ was being made over a $1bn deal for Caf. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

It has been seven years since Caf has had a long-term deal to secure its financial future. The 2016-2028 billion-dollar “minimum guarantee” revenue contract that it signed with the French company Lagardère during the tenure of Issa Hayatou, the late Cameroonian president of Caf, was the first of its kind for the organisation.

“The Memorandum of Understanding with Lagardère was agreed by a team I led with Hicham [El Amrani, then Caf general secretary] in May 2015, in Zurich,” Suketu Patel, then chair of Caf’s finance committee, said in 2019.

“On that same day, we met with Infront. Their indicative offer on the table was a $450m minimum guarantee for eight years, as opposed to the $1bn, for 12 years, from Lagardère.

“If you look at our earlier contract of 2009, we had a minimum guarantee of $150m, but our income for the period was actually around $350m. We anticipated that the 12-year contract would have yielded about $1.3bn.

“I can tell you that whilst President Hayatou and I had differences on political matters, we never had one on the management of Caf finances. He did not interfere with the processes established for good governance.”

But that agreement was unilaterally terminated in December 2019 during the tenure of Ahmad Ahmad, Hayatou’s successor as Caf president.

A protracted legal dispute at the International Chamber of Commerce led to Caf, just over a year into the presidency of Motsepe, paying Lagardère a final settlement of $50m, as compensation for the breach of contract, just before the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

“There is no way that any sponsor will be prepared to pay the same amount of money for a deal in which you would normally have four Afcons over an eight-year period, when you will now only have two. That is certainly a no-brainer,” said a former FA president with expertise in financial matters.

Sports.title: Newcastle did NOT want to sell £75m Bruno Guimaraes - but 'very emotional' captain asked to leave for Arsenal, reveals transfer chief
Sports.content:
Newcastle did NOT want to sell £75m Bruno Guimaraes - but 'very emotional' captain asked to leave for Arsenal, reveals transfer chief

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Newcastle sporting director Ross Wilson says the club 'didn't want to sell' captain Bruno Guimaraes.

The 28-year-old midfielder is set to leave the Magpies and join Arsenal for a fee of £75million, although confirmation of the move has not been officially announced yet.

Guimaraes' seemingly impending departure comes following a tough summer for Newcastle, who have already seen Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali exit during the transfer window while head coach Eddie Howe resigned last week, with Matthias Jaissle officially appointed as his replacement on Wednesday.

Speaking to reporters at Newcastle's pre-season training camp in Spain, Wilson said: 'We didn't want to sell Bruno. It wasn't in the plan to sell Bruno. None of us — or ownership — wanted to sell Bruno.

'He's our captain, he was very, very important to us and the debate over his price — it's a world-record fee for a player of his age.

'What we had to weigh up was, very respectfully from Bruno with his behaviour towards us, very emotionally as well, effectively told us he wanted to leave and move on.

Newcastle sporting director Ross Wilson has said the club 'didn't want to sell' captain Bruno Guimaraes (pictured)

'That doesn't mean he can go but it certainly plays a part in what our thinking is when we hit a certain range of number. But there's no point in saying it was part of our strategy and was in our thinking this summer — it wasn't.

'But we have got to be flexible and react to things that happen. It might have been in our plan to sign one player but we didn't get him so we move on to another. We can only be honest about that.'

Sports.title: Revealed: Defiant David Sullivan believes he is being 'bullied' into staying away from West Ham stadium as owner, 77 - who is accused of sexual misconduct - prepares to face crowd after explosive Panorama allegations
Sports.content:
Revealed: Defiant David Sullivan believes he is being 'bullied' into staying away from West Ham stadium as owner, 77 - who is accused of sexual misconduct - prepares to face crowd after explosive Panorama allegations

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

David Sullivan plans to defy advice to stay away from West Ham’s first home game of the season because the club’s co-owner, accused of multiple counts of sexual misconduct, feels he is being ‘bullied’ into missing it, Daily Mail Sport understands.

The 77-year-old, the club’s largest shareholder, resigned as co-chair in June ahead of the airing of a BBC Panorama and Times investigation in which seven women accused Sullivan of predatory behaviour, which he strongly denies.

The operators of the London Stadium recommended to West Ham that Sullivan not attend the match against Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup on Saturday over fears of potential fan unrest while the club’s fan advisory board said his presence would cause ‘offence and upset’.

That feeling is shared by insiders who believed the 77-year-old’s resignation would signal a fresh start for the club, with many staggered that Sullivan plans to be there. One staff member told Daily Mail Sport they had planned to attend the Portsmouth game but would now stay away due to the ‘circus’ and added that the club ‘cannot be serious about wanting to do well if this is what is planned for the season ahead.’

Sullivan is understood not to have made a final decision but sources close to the co-owner told Daily Mail Sport that he’s worried about the state of the team and lack of transfer activity heading into their first season in the Championship in 14 years and feels he needs to watch the game live. They also said Sullivan feels he’s being ‘bullied' by 'keyboard warriors’ into staying away.

Sullivan was accused in June of preying on a string of women, some in their teens, during his time as a newspaper chief stretching back to the 1980s as seven women came forward to give detailed accounts of predatory behaviour they had experienced, including pressuring them for sex or oral sex by suggesting it would help their careers. Sullivan described the allegations as ‘factually incorrect and entirely false’.

David Sullivan believes he is being 'bullied' into staying away from West Ham amid allegations of sexual misconduct

Sources close to Sullivan also claimed he’s received numerous messages from fans urging him to attend despite his presence at matches last season sparking continued protests from spectators against his ownership, including marches, boycotts, sit-ins, black balloons and thousands of fans brandishing red cards.

The Panorama investigation revealed that Sullivan had been banned from contact with West Ham women’s and youth teams for the past three years.

London Stadium’s operator has asked to be made aware of any planned Sullivan visits so it can implement its own safety measures. West Ham are said to have told the operator that it does not consider there to be an ongoing safeguarding risk associated with Sullivan attending the stadium.

Until recently, it appeared as though Sullivan’s grip on West Ham was loosening when it was announced in June that Vanessa Gold, daughter of former co-owner David, had agreed to sell part of their stake in the club to fellow shareholder Daniel Kretinsky. The move that would have seen the Czech billionaire overtake Sullivan as leading shareholder.

Last week, however, a new announcement confirmed that Gold had accepted a new offer from a consortium led by former Newcastle co-owner Amanda Staveley for her shares. Staveley agreed to buy a 25.1 per cent stake for £150million, which values the club at around £600million, and would still leave Sullivan as the leading stakeholder.

Staveley, though, has reportedly also made an offer to Sullivan, who is believed to be open to selling his stake in the club but values it at much more.

Sports.title: Inside Jake Paul's plot to overthrow the UFC: How influencer plans to get the upper hand on Dana White... and extend an olive branch to Ronda Rousey
Sports.content:
Jake Paul has never been shy about declaring war on the establishment.

He has spent years accusing Dana White of underpaying fighters, publicly challenged the UFC president on everything from athlete welfare to revenue sharing and repeatedly insisted there is room for a genuine rival in mixed martial arts.

Now, he believes he finally has one.

This week, Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) completed a landmark merger with the Professional Fighters League (PFL), creating a combat sports company that combines boxing, MMA and entertainment under one banner.

The PFL name will gradually disappear over the coming months before being retired completely in January 2027, when the organization officially becomes MVP MMA. The combined company boasts almost 400 athletes worldwide, blending PFL's roster with MVP's rapidly growing boxing stable.

It is the biggest structural shake-up in MMA since the UFC cemented its dominance more than a decade ago.

Jake Paul (pictured above) has never been shy about declaring war on the establishment

He has spent years accusing Dana White of underpaying fighters, publicly challenged the UFC president on everything from athlete welfare to revenue sharing

Nobody inside MVP is pretending Dana White's empire is about to crumble overnight. But behind the scenes, the ambition is crystal clear.

'We know we're not going to overtake the UFC in the near future,' MVP co-founder Nakisa Bidarian said. 'This is a long term plan and over time we can close in on their position and create a Nike-versus-Adidas dynamic, or a Pepsi-versus-Coke dynamic, over the next seven to 10 years.

'We started this company five years ago and have been pioneers in boxing and in changing the way people consume content. We delivered the first live professional sporting event on Netflix.

'When we decided to enter MMA, we always said that if it proved successful, we would do more. Now, we the advantage of world-class infrastructure, elite fighters and the leadership of John Martin as CEO of the overall platform. We are not here to mess around.'

The merger instantly transforms MVP from a boxing promoter into a genuine multi-sport combat sports company.

Former PFL chief executive John Martin now oversees the wider business as CEO, while Jake Paul and Bidarian remain on the board, with Bidarian continuing to lead MVP Boxing alongside the promotion's blockbuster events.

Yet while the structure has changed, the philosophy has not.

From day one, Jake Paul has built his business around one message: fighters deserve more money. That message now sits at the heart of MVP's long-term strategy.

Daily Mail Sport sat down with Nakisa Bidarian to talk about how he and Paul are looking to reshape the economics of MMA

'The focus has always been to give at least 50 per cent of revenue back to the athletes,' Bidarian explained. 'If you look at traditional stick-and-ball sports that operate with those kinds of revenue-sharing models, they've created enormous enterprise value.

'When athletes receive a fair share, they're more invested, more committed, the product improves, and there's greater alignment across the sport.'

The comments represent another direct challenge to the UFC's long-standing business model, where fighter pay has remained one of the sport's most fiercely debated issues.

But simply paying athletes more is only one part of the plan. MVP believes it can also create stars in a way its rivals cannot.

'It's about branding, storytelling, exposure, engagement and producing content 24/7,' Bidarian said. 'It's about presenting our athletes for what they are - some of the best fighters in the world.

'Nobody does that better than MVP and Jake Paul. Our first MVP MMA event was a tremendous success and this merger turbocharges our ability to build on that momentum.'

The next battle will be fought in free agency.

MVP knows it cannot approach contracted UFC fighters, but once those deals expire, the landscape changes.

Bidarian believes PFL star Dakota Ditcheva has what it takes to become a global super star

'In MMA, just like in boxing, if a fighter is under contract you can't interfere with that,' Bidarian said. 'You have to wait until they become free agents.

'For example, the 155-pound champion Usman, who fought on Friday night, has just completed the final fight of his contract. I'm sure the UFC will try to re-sign him.

'But whenever a fighter comes out of contract with the UFC, of course we'll take a look. If they're the right fit for us, and we're the right fit for them, we'd love to make that partnership happen.'

The ambition stretches well beyond signing one or two marquee names.

'Our goal is to become the Pepsi to their Coke, the Adidas to their Nike, and eventually make this a genuine two-horse race,' Bidarian said. 'Sometimes we'll be ahead, sometimes they'll be ahead.

'But make no mistake, there's a real opportunity for a fighter-first platform. Very quickly, we're going to establish ourselves as the leading alternative.

'And in seven to 10 years' time, MVP will be the culturally relevant, empowerment-driven brand that Gen Z, Gen Alpha and even Gen Beta are focused on.'

One major advantage MVP believes it holds is flexibility.

Former UFC heavyweight champion Francis Ngannou remains central to the company's plans

Unlike publicly listed companies, Bidarian insists remaining privately owned allows the organization to pursue aggressive deals without shareholders dictating every financial decision.

'We intend to remain a private company for the foreseeable future because it provides us with a level of financial flexibility that public companies simply cannot match,' he said.

'In many ways, I would love for the UFC to announce tomorrow that they were increasing fighter pay to 50 per cent of revenue. But they can't. Doing so would significantly impact their margins, lower their enterprise value and ultimately affect the wealth of their owners.

'We have the freedom to be more aggressive in how we structure agreements and attract the best talent in the world.'

The roster itself is expected to evolve rapidly. Former UFC heavyweight champion Francis Ngannou remains central to the company's plans.

'That's absolutely what we want,' Bidarian said. 'Francis and I have spoken several times. He's excited to get back competing. He already has a relationship with the PFL, so it's just a case of making sure everyone is aligned on how we move forward. But yes, absolutely, Francis Ngannou is going to be part of what we're building.'

Women's MMA will also become a cornerstone of the new promotion.

Bidarian revealed he has already spoken to former UFC superstar Ronda Rousey about the future of the sport.

MVP already enjoys a close relationship with Matchroom through their recent boxing alliance, and Bidarian believes the partnership could eventually stretch beyond the squared circle

'Ronda Rousey is the most dominant female combat sports star in history in terms of popularity,' he said. 'She'd be more than welcome to be involved in MVP MMA in whatever role she wants. I spoke to her yesterday and listened to her thoughts on what we need to do.'

He also believes the promotion already possesses its next crossover superstar.

'Women's MMA will be a major focus for us. We have Dakota Ditcheva, who I believe is the most marketable female MMA fighter in the world.

'She's still young, undefeated, an outstanding striker and has enormous potential. We're excited to build around that.'

There may even be opportunities for crossover with boxing.

MVP already enjoys a close relationship with Matchroom through their recent boxing alliance, and Bidarian believes the partnership could eventually stretch beyond the squared circle and into their 'talent agency'.

'Listen, if Matchroom's talent from their talent agency become free agents, of course we'll have those discussions. We have a great working relationship with Eddie and Matchroom.

'The two MMA athletes they announced - Tom Aspinall and Ian Machado Garry - are both under UFC contracts, so there are no discussions to be had there for the moment but should they become available that's different.

Bidarian revealed he has already spoken to former UFC superstar Ronda Rousey (winning her contest with Gina Carano above) about the future of the sport

'I do think there's a huge long-term opportunity for Matchroom and MVP as combined entities. That's not today, and probably not three years from now. But when you think about Eddie's position in men's boxing, what we've built in women's boxing, and what we're going to build in MMA, I think there's a very clear path to what's possible over the next five to 10 years.'

For now, the UFC remains comfortably on top.

Dana White has already dismissed the merger between MVP and PFL, joking that it combines 'two organizations that struggle to sell tickets', while TKO president Mark Shapiro has taken a more measured stance, welcoming legitimate competition.

But inside MVP, nobody is looking for a quick knockout.

Instead, Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidarian are preparing for a long fight – one they believe could eventually reshape the economics of MMA.

They are not promising to replace the UFC.

They are trying to become something the sport has never truly had before: a genuine alternative.

Sports.title: Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT
Sports.content:
Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT

Unlock more of the best of our football coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

The most preposterous man in football is staggering on, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself, so perhaps that’s why the biggest hypocrites of another dark week for football appear to have got away with it.

On Sunday, Real Madrid decided to weigh in on the Gianni Infantino scandal, instructing their media people to put out a sanctimonious statement welcoming the scrapping of the egghead’s plans to sell off a slice of the World Cup, and thanking UEFA for fulfilling their ‘duty’ to ‘protect football’.

You really could not make some of this stuff up. Yes, that moralising really did come from the same Real Madrid whose avarice stank football out when they led the contemptible group of 12 clubs who attempted the European Super League breakaway coup, a few years back.

Infantino’s intellectual and moral decrepitude may have been there for us all to see in his email offering nations a small cash consideration if they back his plans to raise $20billion, but have we forgotten the European club men with whiteboards and coloured marker pens, explaining their own despicable little earner in 2021?

Real’s executives back then were just as atrocious as Infantino is now – worse, in fact, given that the FIFA scheme was not actually a breakaway proposal designed to leave the have-nots behind – while the money men they indirectly inveighed against on Sunday are the one and the same suits from JPMorgan Chase, hired by them to advise on the Super League.

Given that the US finance house were forced to apologise for their part in that episode, you might have fancied they’d learned their lesson about how ferocious the backlash to a sell-out like this would be. No. They just couldn’t resist getting their snouts in the football trough again.

Gianni Infantino is somehow staggering on as FIFA President, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself

But many of his critics do not have a leg to stand on. These are clubs that tried to form the breakaway European Super League - and only buckled after immense fan pressure (pictured)

So, please let’s get this right. The new flank in football's civil war is not between the idealists and the profiteers, but between competing profiteers fighting over who gets to cash in on the game.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin, are currently casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions, protectors of the meritocracy, guardians of the fans against billionaire opportunists. Yet this is the self-same organisation which expanded the Champions League into a sprawling competition with 64 extra fixtures in 2024, to create greater TV income and more sponsorship revenue.

The self-same organisation which has been engaged in a pitched battle for territory with FIFA. That fight has spawned the Nations League and the expanded Club World Cup, with each governing body viewing the other’s new tournament with deep suspicion. UEFA’s objection is not to football becoming more commercial but to someone else collecting the commercial rewards.

Our own Premier League claim a moral high ground for themselves, too, proclaiming to be the world's greatest and most unpredictable domestic competition, while generating more money than any such league in history. Yet it is driven by the same monopolistic greed, behaving as though sharing a fraction of the wealth with the rest of the football pyramid would be an act of unconscionable sacrifice.

Don’t let it be forgotten that its biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020. Or that the Premier League held talks with CVC Capital Partners, one of the world's largest private equity firms, about selling a stake in future broadcasting and commercial revenues, at the same time.

That came to nothing, either, but here was an elite equally willing to explore new ways of extracting financial value from our game. The people’s game.

Whenever the redistribution of Premier League wealth is discussed, we witness the language and narrative suddenly change and those overseeing the competition which has negotiated television contracts worth billions begin to fret about the pennies.

It was clear when a White Paper on football governance was published a few years back that a greater flow of money down from the Premier League would be egregiously hard to extract.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin (right), are casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions. Yet they expanded and distorted the Champions League to generate more revenue

It shouldn't be forgotten that the Premier League's biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020

The gilded elite division continued to maintain the fallacy that they were helping the rest, when 70 per cent of the money they sent down below was Championship parachute money. An insurance policy for the division’s own members laughably dressed up as ‘solidarity payments’.

It has taken Government intervention to force a more equitable share of the Premier League’s wealth throughout the game, in the shape of the Independent Football Regulator, with its ‘backstop’ power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

Faced with such a prospect, the Premier League have finally just voted for an additional £1.5billion from those in the gilded cage, to be shared with the EFL’s clubs, though even that is not allocated yet. The cash, to be funded by a two per cent lift in the transfer levy on all top-flight deals, will clearly need to be crowbarred from clubs swimming in wealth, given the opposition led by Manchester City’s petro-dollar billionaire owners – another of the merry little European Super League band.

We understand other members of the so-called ‘Big Six’ are also unhappy that they may now find themselves coughing up more than less elevated Premier League clubs. It’s been left to the more moderately wealthy members of the division, who faced down the big clubs over the Super League, to challenge them again.

If there was one positive to come out of the Super League scandal, it was the way it cut the grasping, spiritually remote 'Big Six' down to size. 'It's like emerging from a slightly abusive relationship,' the owner of one of the smaller Premier League clubs told me at the time.

This weekend, the FA Cup begins its beautiful seasonal arc once more, carrying the customary thrill and sense of pride among all who will compete in its extra preliminary round. North Ferriby, at home to St Helens, Northwich Victoria, playing away to Beverley Town, and Nelson, entertaining Stockport Georgians, are just three of those taking part who know what a precarious financial reality and existential threat look and feel like.

For all the weekend’s 438 competing clubs, reaching the first round proper – six ties away, in November – would be monumental, with £47,750 prize money for those who win at that stage.

But any who progress that far will also experience the chill of strictures forced down from the top of the game. This will be the second season with no replays from the first round proper onwards – a diminishment the FA said was necessary because of increasing pressure on the calendar, particularly following UEFA's expansion of their club competitions.

The early rounds of the FA Cup still bring with them a sense of thrill and pride - though replays with England's top clubs are now sadly a thing of the past

Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go

Critics, especially in the EFL and non-League, have argued that a vital source of income is being removed from smaller clubs, who can no longer earn lucrative replay gates against bigger opponents.

But those little people are shouting in the dark. The abolition of replays, fourth-round matches spread over five days and the scheduling of the 2027 final before the Premier League campaign finishes, rather than as the climax to the season, belong to the story of the competition’s devaluation and diminishment. The Cup has been crushed into virtual irrelevance by football's high and mighty.

As of last night, Infantino’s brazen conceit and vanity were keeping him in a job which any intelligent and self-respecting industry would by now have forced him from. He is no doubt banking on the relentless news cycle moving on and UEFA’s threat to boycott FIFA’s competition receding into the distance.

Qualification games for the 2030 World Cup are just a year away and Infantino can safely calculate that national associations will not want to take the financial hit that a boycott would carry. It seems significant, and concerning, that a mere 11 national associations, including England and Wales, have voiced opposition to him remaining in post.

Yet for all the sound and fury, there is something deeply unsettling and incomplete about some of this moralising. Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go. He is the most despicable emblem of a game which is slowly devouring itself, but by no means the only one.

Sports.title: Chelsea's new £47m speed king Marco Palestra opens up on why he snubbed Inter Milan, how he went from the 'slowest' player to Italy's fastest - and his dream of following Gianfranco Zola's Stamford Bridge legacy
Sports.content:
Chelsea's new £47m speed king Marco Palestra opens up on why he snubbed Inter Milan, how he went from the 'slowest' player to Italy's fastest - and his dream of following Gianfranco Zola's Stamford Bridge legacy

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The Italian connection at Chelsea is alive after their £47million acquisition of Marco Palestra, and as sit down in the bar area of his Sydney hotel, Gianfranco Zola’s name naturally crops up.

Zola went from Chelsea to Cagliari once upon a time, whereas it is the opposite for Palestra. The 21-year-old spent last season on loan with Cagliari from Atalanta, was named Serie A Defender of the Year, won the Frecciarossa Speed Award, appeared for Italy's national team, and turned down an opportunity to sign for Italian champions Inter Milan to join Chelsea.

‘This connection,’ Palestra says, smiling. ‘I didn’t call him, but I know Zola played at Cagliari and at Chelsea. He’s a legend. Maybe I can do what he did at Chelsea.’

You would like to become a legend, too? ‘Maybe, maybe, I hope,’ he says. ‘I know some Italian players came to Chelsea.

'I spoke with Davide Zappacosta after I joined Chelsea. I played with him at Atalanta. He’s a top guy. I have a good relationship with Zappa. He always talked good things from Chelsea. I know a lot of Italian players played here. I want to be the next top one.’

Zola, Gianluca Vialli, Roberto Di Matteo, Jorginho, Carlo Cudicini – Chelsea have had a few. While a confident boy, Palestra did begin our 30-minute conversation by apologising for his English and asking us to speak slowly, yet he only slips into Italian once. That is while trying to explain what his parents’ professions are. Office workers, he tells us in his native language.

Highly-rated right-back Marco Palestra is hoping for a successful debut season at Chelsea

The Blues signed Palestra for £47m from Atalanta this summer after his loan spell at Cagliari

Many Italians have prospered at Stamford Bridge, from Gianfranco Zola (left) to Jorginho (right)

FIVE ITALIANS WHO THRIVED AT CHELSEA GIANFRANCO ZOLA – The ultimate Italian icon who lifted multiple trophies, his magic seeing him score 80 goals as he was voted the club's greatest ever player in a fan poll in 2003. GIANLUCA VIALLI – An idol who played and managed Chelsea, secured silverware, and handed John Terry his debut. His passing at the age of 58 in 2023 prompted an outpouring of grief. ROBERTO DI MATTEO – Di Matteo flew to Hong Kong last week to act as an ambassador on Chelsea’s tour. Played for the club, then was manager for their 2012 Champions League triumph. CARLO CUDICINI – More than 200 appearances in goal for Chelsea, and he’s still at the club now, working within their loan department after a career spent stopping strikers from scoring. JORGINHO – The Chelsea midfield metronome who won the Champions League, Europa League and more during his five years, finishing third for the Ballon d’Or in 2021.

Returning to English, Palestra adds on his mother and father: ‘They don’t follow football too much. Now, yes, because of me, but before me, no. I played football when I was young, at school and at home. At home, I broke a lot of things, so my family was difficult when I was a little kid! But they always say to me, “If you’re happy, we’re happy”. When I was younger, it was a passion, an obsession, every day football. My grandfather played in Inter’s academy, but only him.’

The mention of Inter is intriguing, because Palestra could have signed for Serie A's title winners this summer instead. He hails from Milan, was briefly in Inter’s academy, and is an Italy international, so why choose Chelsea and the Premier League? Xabi Alonso helped him reach that decision.

‘He likes me,’ Palestra tells us about the phone call he received from Alonso. ‘He likes my flexibility because I can play on the right, left, lower, higher. There were some clubs that wanted me but Chelsea, from the first moment they wanted me, I agreed, because they’re one of the biggest clubs in the world. They play in the Premier League, which is the best in the world. I’m excited.’

Chelsea lost 1-0 to Juventus in a pre-season friendly on Wednesday, and face AC Milan in another tomorrow, both giving Palestra an opportunity to catch up with fellow Italians.

On his national team, who missed out on making the 2026 World Cup, Palestra adds: ‘Italy is not in the best moment of its life and it’s a good thing I came to the Premier League because it’s the best in the world. I can prove myself more. We can help Italy get to the World Cup, and to win something.'

Palestra can be used as a full back or a wing back on either side, making Alonso’s first summer signing a Swiss Army Knife. Chelsea captain Reece James texted him after he signed, and the 26-year-old Englishman visited their training ground the day he landed back from the World Cup.

‘He wrote to me when I joined Chelsea, a beautiful message, how happy he is that I joined, and I said hi to him when he came to Cobham one day after the World Cup,’ Palestra says. ‘I know he is a good guy, a good captain, so I can’t wait to play with him. I’m very happy.’

He has also found a nice Italian restaurant close to Chelsea’s training ground – Grappelli Cobham – as he continues: ‘It was one of the first questions I asked! English food is not bad, but for me, Italian food is a little bit better.’

We do not blame him. Indulging in too many toad in the holes might only slow him down. His name translated from Italian to English means ‘Mark Gymnasium’ and it is rather fitting.

A versatile defender, Palestra can be used as either a full back or a wing back on either side

Palestra featured as Chelsea lost 1-0 to Juventus in a pre-season friendly on Wednesday

As well as being named Italy’s best defender, Palestra was Serie A’s fastest footballer last season, as he explains: ‘When I was young, like 15, I remember I was the slowest one in the team, but after maybe one or two years, I grew physically and I changed position.

‘Before, I played in midfield, but I changed position to left back or at the back, and I understood that I am quick. When I was young, I’m the slowest. It’s crazy.’

Is he officially the fastest at Chelsea now? ‘I don’t know, I need to race all of my team-mates! At the start of last season, I couldn’t imagine I would win Serie A Defender of the Year. It’s a big honour to be the best defender but I know it is only the start. I need to improve every day.’

We have been impressed by Palestra in this pre-season, including when he performed the ‘elastico' skill with his left foot in one friendly. Cristiano Ronaldo was his favourite footballer growing up, and we get the sense Chelsea’s fans will like this attack-minded defender.

Asked if he can become the Premier League’s best defender, Palestra answers: ‘I hope! Maybe it’s difficult, but I said the same at the start of the last season. I will try to do my best.

‘It’s crazy because when I was young, always my aim was to play at this level. It’s a dream. The first thing I want is to win for Chelsea, always the team. If after the season, I also win the Defender of the Year, then I am happy, but I prefer to win something for Chelsea and nothing for me.’

Sports.title: Man City reject £40m bid from Barcelona for Rodri as Catalans look to pip bitter rivals Real Madrid to land Spain captain in bitter blow to Jose Mourinho's title hopes
Sports.content:
Manchester City will demand upwards of £60million if Barcelona are to complete a sensational move for Rodri this summer.

Spain’s World Cup-winning captain has agreed terms with the Catalans ahead of the new season and is seeking a fresh challenge.

Barca instigated talks between the clubs and are understood to have had a derisory bid of nearly £40m rejected.

City have a history of allowing unhappy players to leave should the club’s valuation be met - and are standing firm in talks.

Rodri had been in negotiations with Real Madrid but communicated to them earlier in the week that Barca represented his preferred destination and has agreed personal terms.

While they are working on a transfer worth more than £80m for Lille teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi, City sources indicated that they are ready to land an experienced replacement for Rodri were he to depart.

Barcelona have begun talks with Manchester City over a move for Spain's World Cup winning captain Rodri

Man City are set to demand upwards of £60m if Barcelona are to seal the sensational move

The 2024 Ballon d’Or winner had remained coy over his future while away on international duty but is believed to have been open to a return to Spain once Pep Guardiola’s reign came to an end.

Guardiola had suggested last season that Rodri would not return to his best until the World Cup, as he battled various injury problems after the devastating ACL injury sustained two years ago.

Rodri underwent back surgery, revealed by Daily Mail Sport, immediately after lifting the World Cup.

City have kept an offer of a new contract on the table for the 30-year-old, whose deal expires next summer, and he is scheduled to link up with Enzo Maresca’s squad next week.

Sports.title: Revealed: Man United made another enquiry for Newcastle and England defender Lewis Hall - as Michael Carrick looks to strengthen left back options
Sports.content:
Revealed: Man United made another enquiry for Newcastle and England defender Lewis Hall - as Michael Carrick looks to strengthen left back options

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester United made a fresh enquiry for Newcastle United left back Lewis Hall at the end of last month but were told he is not for sale.

As reported, Hall has been on United's radar this summer as it is clear they need to strengthen that position with Luke Shaw, now 31, in the final year of his contract while youngster Harry Amass has been told he may be best leaving for first team football.

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise with Matthias Jaissle now in place.

The club want to add players to ensure they are competitive, having already lost the likes of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, while Bruno Guimaraes is on the verge of signing for Arsenal.

They will do all they can to keep hold of Hall, who is now seen as one of their biggest assets after joining from Chelsea in 2023.

United, meanwhile, feel they are light in the position. Shaw started all 38 Premier League matches last season, though there is no obvious back-up, with Patrick Dorgu viewed as a winger by Michael Carrick.

Manchester United moved to sign Lewis Hall (right) last month but were told he is not for sale

United have signed the likes of Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow this window, but aren't done yet.

Newcastle, meanwhile, want to strengthen at left back themselves and also want a right back with Tino Livramento likely to move on soon.

They are among the clubs who have checked on 19-year-old Jorge Salinas at Racing Santander along with Aston Villa. But Newcastle see Salinas as one for the future rather than ready to go now.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
