World.title: Fingers crossed for ganja
World.content:
Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the Cannabis Licensing Authority, speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THERE is no indication when Jamaica could see its first cannabis company registered on the local stock market, but key players in the sector are hopeful it will happen soon.

As global powers equivocate with the classification of the weed, leaders at Jamaica’s Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) are keeping their fingers crossed that the tight hold on the plant will be relaxed to allow the medical and commercial industry to grow.

During this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange the top brass of the CLA pointed to the recent indication by the United States (US) that cannabis could be moved from a Schedule I drug to Schedule III.

That announcement earlier this year was welcomed by players in the industry; however, months later it is not clear where cannabis will sit on the US drug scheduling list as US lawmakers continue debate on the matter.

According to CLA Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake, “rescheduling of ganja would answer a lot of questions” in relation to access to the banking system and eligibility for grants for farmers and businesses in the industry.

As it relates to Jamaica possibly seeing its first regulated marijuana company hit the stock market, chair of the CLA Dr Nadeen Spence said, “We have to keep our fingers crossed” that marijuana will in fact be reclassified to reflect a Schedule III status.

It would, she argued, “translate into something that reassures the banking sector that ganja is not as risky as it currently is”.

Although uncertainty looms over ganja’s position on the list, Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the CLA, said there nevertheless needs to be an appreciation for the progress being achieved by the entity.

“Wherever we are now, it is a metamorphosis, a giant leap. In the 1970s, if you were caught with even a small amount it was a mandatory prison sentence. Some of our prominent people in society have had trouble. There was a lot of persecution and prosecution. Where we are now is really a massive step. I am making the point to say, who knows. Let’s keep going and we might very well see it there one day,” said Melbourne.

The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) describes Schedule I drugs as substances or chemicals with no currently accepted medical use and have a high potential for abuse, such as heroin and ecstasy.

Schedule III drugs are substances or chemicals with a moderate to low potential for physical and psychological dependence. The DEA states that drugs listed under Schedule III are considered to have less potential to be abused than Schedule I and II drugs.

The US Department of Justice has already officially reclassified cannabis as less dangerous, marking a major shift in that country’s drug policy.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche changed the classifications of products containing marijuana that are covered by the Food and Drug Administration or that have received a state medical marijuana licence.

They will move cannabis from a Schedule I narcotic like heroin to a Schedule III drug — on par with Tylenol with codeine.

Marijuana remains illegal at the federal level. Despite the federal ban, most US states have legalised the medical or recreational use of marijuana, and many have shops where it can be purchased legally.

World.title: Come Alive delivers!
World.content:
H.U.M.B.L.E (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

The East Lawns of King’s House became more than a venue on Saturday night. For several hours it was transformed by a sea of worshippers into a space of praise.

It was the perfect start to the month in which Jamaica celebrates its 64th year of Independence as hundreds gathered for the second staging of the Come Alive Gospel concert.

Dubbed a national call to worship, it became evident from the very first note that this was no ordinary musical showcase. It was an invitation — one that patrons answered with lifted hands, tear-filled eyes, and hearts fully surrendered to praise.

Christian worship, often confined to church walls, spilled freely across the grounds as saints gave their whole beings to the moment, proving that praise can command the same passion and intensity as any secular spectacle.

Yet, unlike the fleeting excitement of entertainment, what unfolded at King’s House was rooted in something deeper — an encounter with the divine.

The group H.U.M.B.L.E opened the main event with a spirited rendition of the Jamaican National Anthem, their harmonies echoing across the venue before they returned with a medley of old-time gospel favourites that ignited a revival spirit which lingered for the remainder of the programme.

That spirit only intensified when Petra Kaye took the stage. With a commanding voice that carried effortlessly across the lawns, the singer brought a fervency reminiscent of the “old-time religion” of generations past. Songs such as Crown Him, I Can Recommend My God, and the beloved Sovereign God Medley became more than performances. Attendees sang along with conviction, their praises rising heavenward like incense.

Johnmark Wiggan followed with a deeply personal set, sharing snippets of a testimony marked by trials that, by his own admission, should have destroyed him had it not been for the hand of God. As he delivered songs including Still Deh Yah, Because You Are Good, Run Me Dung, and Testimony, an intimate atmosphere settled over the audience. Eyes closed, hands lifted, and voices trembling with emotion, patrons appeared to journey back to defining moments in their Christian walk, as if remembering prayers answered, valleys crossed, and the faithfulness of God through every season.

The praise continued with Jermaine Edwards, whose set list included Peace In My Soul, Not Forget, Naa Bow, and Make You Smile. By the time he closed with his hit single Beautiful Day, the East Lawns had erupted into celebration.

Joy radiated from faces of attendance across the venue and, for a while, worries seemed to dissolve beneath the weight of worship.

Then came the evening’s international headliner, Michael W Smith.

Making a grand entrance, the singer’s band set the tone with a dramatic prelude before the legendary worship leader greeted the crowd.

“Jamaica, it’s so good to be here,” he said to great applause.

“We have a set list, but we might not stick to it,” he added, signalling that while plans had been made, the direction of the evening ultimately belonged to God.

Without hesitation, Smith launched into crowd favourites Open The Eyes of My Heart and Draw Me Close To You. The response was immediate. Worshippers surrendered themselves to the music.

Pausing between songs, Smith reflected on the immeasurable love of God; a love, he reminded the audience, that surpasses human understanding despite the Creator’s infinite power. He then transitioned into

Arms Around the Sun, a moving reminder of God’s unwavering affection for humanity.

Reflecting on his time in Jamaica, the singer shared that beyond the island’s beauty, it was the warmth and spirit of its people that had touched him most.

“Honestly, I love the people. I love your country, and I bless your country with all the promises of God,” he said before delivering favourites such as The Air I Breathe, Lord, I Give You My Heart, Above All, and There Is None Like You.

“Here is my prayer for Jamaica — at least one of them,” he said before leading the audience into

Let It Rain.

His set also included stirring renditions of Waymaker, Agnus Dei (Worthy Is The Lamb), Goodness of God, and Awesome God.

Had the curtains closed at that very moment, patrons would likely have left fulfilled, their faces glowing from an evening already overflowing with worship. But Come Alive still had one final offering.

Papa San emerged to deafening cheers, lifting the energy to even greater heights.

From the opening notes of Glory God, the veteran deejay had the audience captivated.

Songs like Hell Bruk Loose and Step Pan Di Enemy transformed the East Lawns into a grand dance floor as patrons abandoned their seats, dancing and rejoicing with uninhibited praise.

“I haven’t been here in a while ennu, so mek we go down memory lane likkle bit,” he told the crowd before launching into a nostalgic rendition of

Pop Style.

But amid the excitement, his message remained clear: “Worship should be a part of your life. Sing about what Jesus did for you,” he encouraged before performing Smile Again, a testimony of redemption and restoration.

Long after the final song faded, the message of the evening remained.

According to Eric Hosin, chairman of the Come Alive Collective, the success of the event was possible only because of God’s grace.

“We’re happy and giving God thanks and all the praises because this was only because of his goodness and his mercy,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“People seemed to have enjoyed themselves. Papa San closing was just something else, and we’re giving God thanks. We saw worship taking place with Michael W Smith, Jermaine Edwards, Johnmark Wiggan, Petra Kaye, and H.U.M.B.L.E, who started out with that lovely rendition of the national anthem. It was an amazing night.”

He added: “It was a national call to worship. We answered a call from the Lord, where He said He was seeking true worshippers. Persons even came with their tambourines for worship and we thank the Lord.”

World.title: FLOW’S US$25-M REBUILD
World.content:
Flow Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million on the Hurricane Melissa rebuild efforts. .

FLOW Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million ($3.90 billion) restoring its network after Hurricane Melissa, including US$12 million ($1.87 billion) during the second quarter as it continued reconnecting fixed-line customers in western Jamaica.

Balan Nair, chief executive officer of Liberty Latin America Limited (LILA), disclosed the expenditure during the company’s earnings call on Thursday, while discussing recovery work in Jamaica.

“The actual business operations itself is improving, and we are getting very close to getting back to full strength. As a matter of fact, our mobile business has improved coming out of this, and our market share has improved coming out of this. Our ARPU (average revenue per user) has improved coming out of this,” Nair said of the recovery effort.

Liberty’s Caribbean segment added 11,000 postpaid subscribers during the second quarter ended June 30, with 6,000 subscribers coming from the Jamaican market. Revenue from Jamaica was down US$3.1 million or three per cent to US$101.6 million ($15.86 billion) for the second quarter. Liberty’s quarterly filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission noted that Hurricane Melissa had a negative impact of US$8 million on revenue.

“We continue to see negative headwinds from Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica, the effect is clearly diminishing,” Nair said.

However, the recovery in Jamaica continues to be impacted by the pace of infrastructure restoration in western Jamaica. LILA noted that approximately 38,000 RGUs (revenue generating units) in the Jamaican market remained offline at the end of the quarter. This comprised 19,000 broadband internet units, 15,000 fixed-line telephony and 4,000 video subscribers.

“I think there are some homes that we will not rebuild back to, and it’s just gone. For the most part, we think we can get back to a pretty high level of penetration,” Nair noted as the company brought 48,000 RGUs back online during the first six months of 2026.

Liberty’s Jamaican operation, led by Flow Jamaica, reported a US$5.2 million or two per cent reduction in six-month revenue to US$204.8 million.

The hurricane had a US$20 million negative impact to Liberty’s revenue and a US$22 million impact on its operating income before depreciation and amortisation.

Nair credited the recovery trajectory to the work of the company’s teams in Jamaica and Miami, including the managers overseeing its Jamaica operations.

Despite the headwinds it experienced from Hurricane Melissa, Flow Jamaica continues to expand its offerings to the Jamaican market. Flow launched the 5G network on June 11 providing coverage to approximately 70 per cent of Jamaica’s population. This service is available to residential and enterprise postpaid subscribers.

Flow also launched the ‘Unbeatable’ Network campaign as it pushes fixed mobile convergence which bundles fixed and mobile services. The fixed broadband service is backed by the ability to switch from home Wi-Fi to the mobile network during power outages. Mobile connectivity is, in turn, supported by satellite through Flow’s Starlink DTC partnership.

“The Unbeatable campaign is now live in Jamaica and Cayman and coming soon to other Liberty Caribbean markets, as well as being deployed across the broader LLA group. In the Caribbean, it encompasses the unique concept of an always-on network, both in fixed and mobile,” Nair said during his presentation.

The Category 5 hurricane and the recent El Niño phenomenon prompted analyst Matthew Harrigan to ask about the availability of parametric insurance in the Caribbean.

LILA Chief Financial Officer Chris Noyes said the company had parametric insurance coverage for the hurricane season.

Parametric insurance has helped Jamaica rebuild and recover from the last two major hurricanes, with a US$81-million payment from weather derivatives received in 2025.

“I think we are one of the key global issuers of the parametric. We were able to do it even with the event we had in Jamaica, with a very cost-effective cover similar to prior years,” Noyes told Harrigan.

Nair said the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) website has become a permanent monitoring tool for his team since July.

He added that LILA’s leadership team would visit NOAA’s headquarters in Boulder, Colorado, to meet climatologists and hurricane experts.

LILA’s consolidated revenue increased one per cent to US$1.10 billion for the second quarter, US$10 million above analysts’ estimates.

Due to lower impairment and restructuring charges, LILA reported an operating profit of US$181.2 million compared to an operating loss of US$333 million. LILA’s adjusted OIBDA grew five per cent to US$436 million.

With a 34 per cent reduction in non-operating expenses to US$157.2 million, LILA reported a profit before tax of US$24 million versus a loss before tax of US$570.8 million.

However, higher taxes resulted in LILA reporting a consolidated net loss of US$10.6 million, with a US$24-million loss attributable to shareholders.

LILA’s consolidated revenue for the six-month period edged up to US$2.19 billion, while the company reported an operating profit of US$326.4 million, compared with an operating loss of US$204.9 million.

The net loss attributable to shareholders improved to US$46.7 million from US$559.7 million.

LILA’s asset base stood at US$12.23 billion, including US$3.78 billion in property and equipment and US$714.1 million in cash. Total liabilities stood at US$11.23 billion, while equity attributable to shareholders was US$528.1 million.

LILA’s Class C shares traded at US$8.54 on Thursday, while its Class A shares traded at US$8.66. The company has repurchased US$60 million of its common shares and has US$140 million remaining under its share-repurchase programme.

“As we look to [the] rest of 2026, we intend to build upon our H1 operational progress and lap the October 2025 Jamaica hurricane, all of which should set us up for a strong fourth quarter and positive momentum leading into 2027,” Nair said.

World.title: Ready to strike
World.content:
Marria Crossfield (left) competes in the first round of the women’s 400m hurdles on Thursday’s second day of the World Athletics Under 20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. She ran a personal best 58.22 seconds to qualify for the semi-final. Emily Montaño of Colombia completed the race in 1.01.43. (Photo: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA ­— Jamaica’s Marria Crossfield and Shevaughn Thomas both ran personal best times to qualify for Saturday’s semi-finals in the women’s 400m hurdles in Thursday’s first round at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field, Eugene, Oregon.

Both women and Jahvanie Tyrell and Robert Miller in the men’s event all made progress while the mixed 4x100m relay team also advanced to today’s first ever final in the event that was added this year.

Meanwhile, today Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas will start their 200m qualification, while the first two rounds of the sprint hurdles for men and women will also be contested.

Joel Morgan and Kevongaye Fowler will contest the semi-finals of the men’s and women’s 800m, respectively.

Yesterday, Crossfield, who was fourth in her first-round heat in 58.22 seconds, was lowering her lifetime best for the 10th time this season, after starting the year with a 1:01.59 time at the Youngster Goldsmith meet at the National Stadium on the first weekend of February.

She lowered the 58.59 seconds time she ran at the Jamaica Athletics Administrative National Junior Championships in June to get into the semis.

Thomas was second in her semi-final heat in 58.36 seconds, lowering the 58.41 seconds she had run last year at the Carifta Games.

Tyrell was a surprise winner in his first-round heat, getting off to a fast start, and clocked 51.02 seconds, while Miller was second in his heat in 51.27 seconds.

The mixed 4x100m of Justin Stewart, Natrece East, Detarje Morgan and Renecia Edwards established a new national Under-20 of 42.08 seconds finishing third in their semi-final race.

Morgan told the Jamaica Observer they were pleased to be part of Jamaica’s track and field history, being the first to contest the event.

“It’s an extraordinary feeling. Jamaica have a great legacy, and we continue to fulfil that during our time running for Jamaica in Under-20s,” Morgan said. “We furthermore will be representing Jamaica sooner or later in the senior level so this is a good start for us.”

For the final he admitted they would have some work to do to get on the podium as they were sixth-best on the day. “We just have to fix it going into the finals and hope for a medal that we can take back home,” he said.

Also today, Sashana Johnson will accompany Shanoya Douglas in the first round of the women’s 200m, while Nathaniel Martin joins Card in the first round of the men’s race.

Tianna Marshall and Akeelah Bell are down to contest the 100m hurdles, while Marquies Page and Taj-Oneil Gordon will run in the 110m hurdles.

World.title: Geely EX5: New EV horizons
World.content:
The Geely EX5 brings some never-yet-seen features to the market. (Photo: Rory Daley)

The electric vehicle (EV) market has blossomed into maturity, with a wide range of options to suit the needs of the masses. With that variety comes competition, and then the need to stand out from the crowd. The Geely EX5 embraces its electric architecture to bring a brand new sense of what is considered premium to the everyday SUV.

EXTERIOR

Like most modern SUVs, the EX5 doesn’t try to reinvent the wheel. This is a very conservative end of the automotive market, and anything too outlandish may scare prospects. LED lighting all around, check. Flush door handles, check. Aero-efficient wheels, check. Black plastic trim over the wheel arches, all there. The EX5 has the EV and SUV design cues to ensure a visual connection to what the buyers expect these days.

That said, the EX5 is a clean modern design, as dictated by its all-electric needs. There’s a hint of sci-fi to it, as if someone ran a current SUV through a time machine — this time forward, not retro.

INTERIOR

This is where things get interesting. Without a traditional internal combustion engine layout, EVs are able to take full advantage of this relatively free engineering direction. For the EX5, it’s space. The Geely feels expansive inside as it maximises the area between its wheelbase for occupant comfort, storage, and features. This can be best experienced in the passenger seat, which can be electronically folded near flat for total relaxation. Just a button press will stretch the lower section of the passenger seat to that of lounge chair proportions. And if that isn’t enough for the passenger prince or princess, then the headrest can be removed to fold completely flat against the base of the rear seat, extending the first-class experience. Look up into the panoramic sunroof and things approach heavenly. At night, standard ambient lighting retains the relaxed vibe of the EX5.

For the rest of the cabin, fit and finish, plus material quality is up to par as soft-touch materials cover every contact surface. The convenience technology is abundant. Most major functions are automatic or powered, accessed from the 15.4-inch touchscreen running Geely’s Flyme Auto infotainment system, or via the voice assistant. Interior noise is low, allowing the 12-speaker surround system to reach its full potential. Wireless charging and smartphone connectivity add even more functionality to the EX5.

Families will appreciate the number of storage solutions and their size.

ON THE ROAD

The front wheels of the EX5 are motivated by a single 215bhp electric motor fed by a 60.22kWh battery. Torque is rated at 236lb/ft. It can fast-charge up to 160kWh. It can be fully charged from 10 per cent using AC power in just over six hours, whereas DC fast-charging can restore up to 80 per cent of the battery in 20 minutes. Maximum range is 267 miles. The Geely EX5 delivers its power in a very linear fashion, rather than outright speed. This makes it handle the urban slog with ease, never really upsetting occupants, but having that instant torque to exploit holes in the city traffic.

From the 10.2-inch instrument cluster, drivers have a plethora of driving assist systems that ease vehicle operation and aid in safety. The suspension matches the overall theme of the vehicle — comfort, absorbing road imperfections without transferring them to passengers. This also helps on longer journeys that may take the EX5 on to the less than perfect country roads.

VERDICT

The Geely EX5 is aimed directly at the family looking for an EV SUV as it’s bursting at the frame with the essentials buyers in this segment are looking for — space, technology, and safety, further adding premium features not usually found in many class rivals, including the unique first-class front seating arrangement. That said, comfort and ease of use are the primary characteristics of the EX5, with enough range to eliminate operational anxiety.

World.title: Market Bag: ‘Auntie Bev’ shares old-time market wisdom as prices fluctuate
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — As Jamaica celebrates Independence Day, this week’s episode of Market Bag takes a nostalgic trip through Coronation Market, where veteran shopper Beverley Thomas Edwards shares decades of experience and the tricks and trades she uses to get the best value for her money.

From choosing produce with brighter colours and firmer textures to selecting clean, quality items, “Auntie Bev” shares tips on comparing prices and shopping wisely to make the most of every dollar.

Meanwhile, prices at Coronation Market continue to fluctuate, with sweet peppers selling for $400 per pound; ginger at $450 per pound; onions at $200 per pound; tomatoes at $200 per pound; Scotch bonnet peppers at $400 per pound; lettuce at $600 per pound; carrots at $300 per pound; and yam at $500 per pound.

Ripe bananas remain one of the more expensive commodities at the market, selling for $1,000 per hand, while plantains are priced at $900 for three.

In the latest feature, Auntie Bev and host Carlysia Ramdeen explore how market culture has evolved over the years, from informal setups of the past to the more organised stalls shoppers see today.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Italy says it won’t take orders from Spain on border checks
World.content:
Earlier in the day, the Spanish government had threatened to take “proportional measures” if Rome did not stop its reintroduced border checks and temporary suspension of the Schengen Agreement by Aug. 9.

In its statement, Rome said it would keep these controls in place “at least until August 15 and, in any case, until security and terrorism risks to Italy can be completely ruled out,” adding that a new “migratory wave” is expected in Ceuta on that date.

“Only when it is certain that there will be no security or terrorism risks for Italy, that there will be no new wave and that there are no irregular migrants heading toward European territory will it be possible to reconsider what has already been decided,” said the document.

World.title: EU adds 5 people to Russia sanctions list after latest deadly attacks on Ukraine
World.content:
Russia this week carried out one of its deadliest barrages on Kyiv, killing 17.

The EU has added five individuals to its Russia sanctions list. The move was driven by Moscow’s “intensified strikes deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure” in Ukraine, according to a press release.

The press release does not refer to a specific attack, but earlier this week Russia carried out one of its deadliest barrages on the Ukrainian capital, killing 17. In July, a similar attack in Kyiv killed 12.

Among those included in the new sanctions is Ramil Badgutdinov — the head of a company that helps produce the Iskander-M ballistic missiles — and Aleksandr Dyukarev, head of the KrasMash plant that produces Sarmat ballistic missiles. Russia has not yet used Sarmat missiles in Ukraine, but Moscow has been testing them.

World.title: Madrid threatens retaliation if Italy keeps border controls on travelers from Spain
World.content:
In addition to slamming Rome for imposing border controls that inconvenienced thousands of passengers by creating legal uncertainty in the middle of the summer holiday season, Madrid also took Italy to task for criticizing Spain’s handling of migrants while failing to protect its own borders.

Even though “Italy is the EU member state that has recorded the highest number of irregular crossings in recent years, with figures that have at times been twice those of Spain … Spain has never introduced controls on travelers from Italy,” the Spanish government said.

Madrid has now given the Italian government two days to either lift the border controls or face reciprocal measures that aim to “protect the interests and dignity” of Spanish citizens.

“Governments should work to promote understanding between countries and serve the general interests of their populations, rather than create divisions and pointless conflicts driven by domestic electoral considerations,” the statement said.

“We trust that Europeanism, common sense and good faith will prevail.”

World.title: Musk says French Greens’ presidential candidate should be ‘shut down’
World.content:
“I’d rather be accused of defending democracy than of trying to buy it.”

Musk, who is a former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, has regularly weighed in on European politics and thrown his support behind far-right candidates and parties — and France is no exception.

In July, Musk said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was “France’s last hope,” but her National Rally party was quick to downplay his backing to avoid being associated with the controversial owner of Tesla and SpaceX.

Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon also slammed Musk’s attacks against Tondelier on Thursday, before accusing the French government of not doing enough to fight foreign interference.

“The French presidential election is an open bar for all the manipulators in the world,” he wrote — a criticism Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot promptly rejected.

Earlier this week, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government was boosting efforts to detect and punish foreign interference in the upcoming 2027 election, while presidential candidates Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe, as well as likely candidate Raphaël Glucksmann shared they had been victims of Russian disinformation campaigns.

World.title: Week Ender: Verhofstadt on “Trumpism”, plus summer must-reads
World.content:
It’s August in Brussels, which means it’s vacation time.

Whether you’re heading off to the beach or holding down the fort in town, this episode is brimming with book recommendations from our newsroom and from you, our listeners. Whatever your genre preference, from true crime thrillers to deep political dives, we’ve got your summer holiday covered.

But this installment is not just a book chat.

We’re also tackling the rise of populism and the crises facing liberal democracies around the world. That’s the topic of “Defeating Trumpism,” a new book by former Belgian Prime Minister and European Parliament Member Guy Verhofstadt. World.title: L’Europe veut sortir de sa dépendance à Palantir
World.content:
"Soyons honnêtes, le produit de Palantir est très bon et addictif, c’est un peu comme le sucre dans le Coca", reconnaît le député MoDem Philippe Latombe, défenseur français de la souveraineté numérique. "Palantir est capable de traiter d’énormes quantités de données avec une grande précision et, grâce à son expérience, l’entreprise a eu le temps d’améliorer ses algorithmes auprès de nombreux clients et de les adapter à de nombreux cas d’utilisation."

Pourtant, la volonté de se libérer de Palantir gagne tout le continent : de Madrid, où le gouvernement de Pedro Sánchez a ordonné aux entreprises publiques d’exclure Palantir des futurs marchés publics, jusqu’aux services de renseignement intérieurs français (DGSI), qui ont préféré l’entreprise française ChapsVision à Palantir. Au Royaume-Uni, le prochain test pourrait avoir lieu en février 2027, lorsque le nouveau gouvernement travailliste d’Andy Burnham devra décider s’il met fin au contrat de 330 millions de livres sterling conclu avec Palantir pour la plateforme fédérée de données de la Sécurité sociale (NHS).

La décision prise le mois dernier par les services de renseignement français et allemands d’opter pour ChapsVision a porté un double coup dur à la direction de Palantir. Le PDG du géant américain, Alex Karp, est toutefois resté sûr de lui après ce revirement soudain, affirmant qu’il ne s’inquiétait pas de la concurrence européenne. "Nous avons un exemple de ce qui ne fonctionne pas", a-t-il ironisé la semaine dernière sur Fox Business. "Ça s'appelle l'Europe."

Alex Karp, PDG de Palantir, est l'invité de l'émission « The Claman Countdown » aux studios de Fox Business Network. | John Lamparski/Getty Images

Olivier Dellenbach, fondateur et PDG de ChapsVision, concède à POLITICO que son entreprise avait tiré profit de ce qu’il qualifie de "rejet viscéral de Palantir" en Europe.

Il refuse toutefois que ChapsVision soit réduit à une simple alternative anti-Palantir. La souveraineté numérique, affirme-t-il, restera une formule creuse si les gouvernements ne la transforment pas en politique industrielle. "Il faut plus de commandes publiques", estime Olivier Dellenbach.

La Belgique, l'Allemagne, le Luxembourg, la Roumanie, les Pays-Bas et le Canada ont déjà manifesté leur intérêt pour le système d'IA "Artemis" de l'armée française, selon Patrick Moreau, l'un des architectes de cette solution développée par l'entreprise française d'aérospatiale et de défense Thales.

World.title: France will test crisis response with 2027 blackout drill
World.content:
Its purpose will be to determine how the country would respond to a paralyzing electricity outage of the kind that hit Spain and Portugal in April 2025, or a major cyberattack targeting the power grid as Poland experienced last year — an act of sabotage Brussels has attributed to Russian intelligence services.

The simulation will test “the country's ability to respond," said one person familiar with preparations for the exercise, adding that it is intended to assess the time needed to restore power and the country’s ability to ensure the continuity of essential services.

The exercise was formally confirmed during an interministerial committee on national resilience on July 8. A detailed announcement should come before the end of the year.

The meeting notes outline other priorities, such as making sure the French state maintains access to goods considered "essential to ensuring the continuity of the state and the protection of the population."

These include “emergency blankets, generators, medicines, telecommunications equipment, equipment for law enforcement, as well as rare and critical raw materials.”

Stress test

Crisis preparedness has turned into a political issue in France as record-breaking heat and wildfires are forcing the country to reckon with its ability to respond to emergencies.

World.title: Trump to appeal ballroom construction halt to Supreme Court
World.content:
A US Court of Appeals upheld a ruling that saying Trump cannot build a White House ballroom without congressional approval. The president vowed to appeal what he called an "unjust decision."

US President Donald Trump was ordered on Friday to halt construction of a ballroom on the site of the demolished East Wing.

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which had sued Trump over the matter last year.

It was a major setback for Trump, who has touted the project, saying the White House needed a large ballroom to host events.

The court's ruling has been placed on hold for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal the ruling to the US Supreme Court.

Trump confirmed the move, saying his team will be "immediately appealing" to the Supreme Court.

The US president blasted the decision as a "horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful ruling."

"The Circuit Court also refused to acknowledge that the desperately needed, and totally secure Ballroom, which is being built ahead of schedule and under budget, is a Gift from President Trump and Great Patriots of the United States of America," Trump added in a social media post.

What did the court say?

Judges Patricia Millett and Brad Garcia, both appointed by Democratic presidents, said the ‌order does not permanently bar construction of the ballroom, but rather it merely halts above-ground work during the lawsuit and until the White House secures approval from Congress.

"Each President is a temporary tenant, not the ‌owner, of the White House" ⁠and ⁠cannot fundamentally reshape it without congressional approval, the court said.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the panel's majority wrote. "Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's House — to fit a particular ‌President's desires."

Additionally, the court scolded "the bold assertion that the Executive can act with utter lawlessness, destroying treasured national landmarks and harming the interests of individuals."

The East Wing demolition is the biggest structural change to the White House in over 70 years Image: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

Court rejects 'national security' argument

Work on the 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom began last year with the swift demolition of the White House's entire historic East Wing. It is the biggest structural change to the White House in over 70 years.

White House lawyers argued that the ballroom includes critical security features to guard against a range of threats, such as drones, ballistic missiles and biohazards.

"These upgrades, alterations, and improvements are essential to protecting the President, his family, and his staff, as well as the White House itself, and the entire project flows from them," government attorneys told the court.

But the justices in the majority shot down the argument, saying that national security arguments "are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card."

World.title: Ceuta: Spain warns Italy it will reciprocate entry checks
World.content:
Spain has told Italy it will impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday threatened to impose reciprocal entry checks on travelers from Italy, unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifts the measures it has implemented by Sunday.

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week.

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Spain say about possible checks on travelers from Italy?

Spain called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population."

Madrid had objected to the move on several grounds, saying it was based on "spurious arguments."

It said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years.

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS

What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain?

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

World.title: How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?
World.content:
Iran says a shipping accord with Oman is in its final stages, but analysts warn sanctions, security concerns and rival US-Iran goals could limit its impact.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said this week that an agreement with Oman, which lies on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, is in the "final stage" of review and drafting — provided that no external party interfered in the process.

The two Persian Gulf states have agreed on the geographical coordinates of a navigation route through the strait, Baghaei was quoted as saying by state news agency IRNA on Wednesday evening.

Baghaei told journalists that even if an understanding was reached, it would not mean that the strait had become safe for all passing vessels.

"The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," he said.

What the agreement could look like

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi also said an agreement on new shipping arrangements was nearing completion, IRNA reported.

Gharibabadi stressed that the proposed arrangement would not amount to a full reopening of the strait, but would instead establish a new model for maritime traffic.

According to IRNA, Gharibabadi said the route would be temporary and could remain open for between two and four months.

Shipowners hope Strait of Hormuz will reopen soon To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tehran said that any reopening of the strait must be accompanied by an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports.

Reports cited by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said Iran was planning to block US and Israeli ships from the waterway as part of a deal with Oman.

Iran also argued that vessels passing through the strait should pay fees for safe passage. Oman did not support unilateral Iranian control of the waterway.

Obstacles and skepticism

A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to give Tehran control over ships entering the Persian Gulf ​through the Strait ⁠of Hormuz is not easily workable because of US sanctions and restrictive insurance clauses ⁠on payments, according to industry sources cited by Reuters on Friday.

However, analysts cautioned that any deal on the reopening of the strait should be viewed as a tactical pause rather than a durable settlement.

Security analyst Shukriya Bradost told DW such a pause could benefit Washington more than Tehran.

"The United States could use the period to improve coordination with its regional partners, review its military strategy and prepare stronger options," she said.

"Iran, meanwhile, would continue facing economic pressure, internal divisions and growing political and security costs."

"If this period becomes merely a pause in tensions and Tehran fails to secure a tangible strategic gain, the passage of time may benefit the United States more than any other party," Bradost added.

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other analysts pointed to fundamental disagreements over the future governance of the waterway.

Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, said Tehran and Washington are pursuing different objectives.

"Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki told DW. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled."

Competing views of Iran's role in Hormuz

Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, said both Tehran and Washington could potentially present a deal as a tactical success.

From Iran's perspective, he said any understanding could be presented as an achievement.

"The regime has not collapsed, its missile capabilities remain intact, enriched uranium has not left the country, and for the first time since the war, Iran has reinforced its leverage over the inbound shipping lane of the strait," he told DW.

Salavati added that Tehran could claim domestically that it has preserved the strategic leverage of the Strait of Hormuz.

He said the United States could also portray the situation as a success in the form of "relief from the pressure of soaring energy prices, an opportunity to replenish weapons stockpiles while easing pressure on defence production, and the ability to declare an end to the active phase of the war."

Salavati suggested that Tehran is unlikely to regard any arrangement as the end of the broader confrontation.

Trump has faced pressure from members of his own party in Congress to bring the conflict to a close before November's midterm elections.

Oman has not publicly commented on the reported agreement, which Iran says was negotiated without US involvement.

World.title: Berlin clubs struggle as drink sales dry up and costs rise
World.content:
Berlin's clubs are still drawing crowds, but shorter nights, fewer alcohol sales and rising costs have changed their business model. Door fees, rather than bar takings, are increasingly their real financial lifeline.

Berlin's world-famous club scene has remained in high demand, but venues are increasingly struggling to turn packed dancefloors into sustainable businesses.

A major survey released on Friday found that club revenue has shifted dramatically away from drinks and toward admission fees.

What's happened to Berlin's clubs?

The shift reflects changing nightlife habits since 2017, when around 60% of revenue came from food and drink sales and just 21% from entry fees.

Today, ticket sales account for 59% of revenue, while food and drink generate just 20%.

"People are planning their club nights more consciously, staying for shorter periods, and drinking less,” according to the report, the first comprehensive study of the sector since 2019.

Some 73% of respondents said alcohol consumption was falling, while 60% reported rising demand for non-alcoholic drinks and 57% said guests were staying for shorter periods.

At the same time, costs are rising.

Staff costs were cited as a major burden by 64% of respondents, operating costs by 62%, customers' declining purchasing power by 60%, and rents and leases by 54%.

Some 85% of the clubs polled said financial pressure was already changing their event programs.

Is running a Berlin club lucrative?

Demand remains strong, with 83% of clubs and event organizers reporting occupancy rates of at least 50% and around a third exceeding 75%.

But fewer venues are making enough money to cover their costs.

Club closures in Berlin: The end of an era? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2017, 79% were at least breaking even. By 2025, that figure had dropped to 61%.

Some 39% ended the year in the red, compared with 21% in 2017.

The number of smaller operators has also risen sharply. Some 45% now generate less than €100,000 ($115,595) in annual revenue, compared with 16% in 2017.

Long-term insecurity remains another major problem. Only 8% of operators own their venues, while 31% have rental or lease agreements lasting less than five years.

How are clubs adapting?

Some 23% of respondents said they were considering closing their business within the next 12 months. Since 2020, at least 24 club and cultural venues have closed, but around 25 new ones have opened.

Many venues have already adapted to the pressure.

Some 67% have increased drink prices, 47% have raised admission charges and 39% have expanded private rentals.

The Club Commission is calling for publicly owned buildings to be opened up for nightlife, more reliable long-term funding, formal recognition of clubs as cultural venues and better working conditions.

World.title: Eco wins: Hungary goes solar, marmots go viral and Rome gets an upgrade
World.content:
From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.

Hungary's former leader Viktor Orban called European Union climate policy a "utopian fantasy" and effectively banned wind turbines. And yet the country has quietly become Europe's solar leader, with 25% of its electricity now being being generated from the renewable energy source, ahead of sunnier countries like Spain, and Greece.

The boom was driven not by climate concern but by self-sufficiency politics and cheap subsidies. Now a 450-megawatt park, just east of Budapest, is due online by September 2026. It's set to power around 106,000 households.



Marmot researchers find a new way to fund their science

When US federal funding dried up, researchers from UCLA and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory got creative. They launched OnlyMarms: a free platform posting videos of yellow-bellied marmots eating, digging and scampering in the wild, where fans can donate to support the science.

The team has tracked individually marked marmots in Colorado since 1962, building six decades of data on family lives, social behavior and responses to environmental change — and say studying marmot hibernation could even hold clues about human aging.

Rome's 'big snake' gets a cooler future

Corviale, a kilometer-long brutalist housing complex outside Rome nicknamed "the big snake," was completed in the 1980s and has since fallen into decay. With summers in some parts of Italy's now averaging around 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), life inside has become tough for its more than 4,000 residents.

But upgrades are coming: a new library doubling as a cooling shelter, more trees and energy efficiency improvements, all aimed at helping Corviale stay cool as temperatures keep rising.

Senegalese designer turns discarded textiles into sustainable fashion

Berlin-based designer Mame Khady Badji transforms discarded clothing into bold garments inspired by her Senegalese heritage, combining traditional Ndiakhass techniques with contemporary streetwear. Her creations have drawn musicians, performers and creatives — and recently appeared at Berlin Fashion Week 2026.

After moving to Germany in 2017, Badji built her label with support from Berlin's textile community. Now she's pursuing an ambitious goal: proving that recycled fashion can be both culturally rooted and commercially viable.

World.title: Thailand: Several killed in school shooting north of Bangkok
World.content:
The shooting incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi, just north of the capital city of Bangkok. Several people were killed in the attack.

Several people were killed and others injured in a shooting at a high school in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, north of the capital city of Bangkok, local authorities said.

Students, teachers and other workers were evacuated from school as authorities deployed police officers, rescue workers and emergency doctors to the scene.

Boy accused of killing grandparents before school shooting

According to the police, the suspected gunman, who is a 14-year-old student at the school, is thought to have first fatally shot his grandparents with his grandfather's handgun. The suspect lived with his grandparents, and police found them dead behind a locked door as they began to investigate the shooting.

Authorities later revised down the total death toll. Having initially said that the suspect killed six people, including students, at the school, police later said he killed two teachers and three other adults who were staff at the school.

Officials said the suspect then took his own life at the site, in the Nonthaburi province bordering Bangkok.

A nearby hospital later said more than 20 people were wounded, with 10 of them in a critical condition Image: Peerapon Boonyakiat/ZUMA/IMAGO

Bangyai Hospital, about 5 kilometers (roughly 3 miles) from the school, said 23 people were wounded, of whom 10 were in critical condition, with most suffering gunshot wounds. Earlier reports gave conflicting casualty numbers.

Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul expressed his condolences and stated that he had instructed relevant officials to assist those affected.

"It's such a terrible incident. It should never have happened," he told reporters.

Later, Anutin said that the teenage suspect in the deadly school shooting was "under stress" and there was preliminary evidence of him planning the attack ahead of time. The prime minister also told reporters that he would discuss gun control with the country's police chief.

Students, teachers and other staff members had to hurriedly leave the site Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

Students express shock

The incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi.

"I didn't think it was a gun at first," an 18-year-old student told Reuters, adding that he initially thought it could be firecrackers. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. ​Then it started again."

"I was afraid that I would die, and I was scared that I wouldn't be able to pursue my dreams," said Pawarisa Maylissa, a grade 12 student who hopes to attend medical school. "I heard many gunshots very loudly because it seemed the suspect was on the floor directly above us. I could even hear bullets hitting the floor."

According to district authorities, the Debsirin Nonthaburi School had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers in the 2025 academic year.

Belongings left behind by evacuated students at Debsirin Nonthaburi School, following the shooting incident at the school Image: Peerapon Boonyakiat/ZUMA/IMAGO

School shootings in Thailand

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. It is estimated that around 10 million firearms are in circulation, or about one for every seven people.

In February, a 17-year-old stole a gun from the police and opened fire at a public high school in southern Thailand. The two-hour attack resulted in one death and two injuries.

In October 2023, a 14-year-old opened fire at Bangkok's popular Siam Paragon shopping mall, killing two people and wounding five others. Police said the shooter used a modified pistol, originally designed to fire blanks, that had likely been bought online.

World.title: What should Europe do about its drying rivers?
World.content:
The Rhine and Danube have reached historic lows. Dwindling water levels are affecting shipping, agriculture and ecosystems — and raising concerns about the future of drinking water supplies.

Following an intense heat wave in June and severe wildfires in southern France and Spain, Europe's summer of climate-fueled crises continues with rivers across the continent running low.

Parts of the vital Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, threatening freight transport, the wider economy, and agriculture, with farmers warning of increased prices due to poor harvests amid the drought.

Along the Danube, cargo and cruise ships can no longer pass in some places. In Hungary, Romania and Croatia, sunken ships and cars have reemerged as riverbeds dry out.

In German cities, including Cologne and Düsseldorf, people can now walk across parts of the Rhine where strong currents normally flow. River levels could fall even more dramatically in the coming days.

The water crisis is being intensified by global warming driven by the burning of coal, oil and gas. Low water levels are also taking a growing toll on ecosystems — and could eventually drive up the cost of clean drinking water.

The impact on nature

Parched fields, millions of hectares of lost harvests and exposed riverbeds are among the most obvious consequences of the drought. But underwater ecosystems are suffering too.

As water levels fall, rivers become warmer and contain less dissolved oxygen, increasing the risk of fish die-offs, explained Jeanette Völker, a scientist with Germany's federal environment agency, the UBA.

"Especially along the Rhine, you can see how the gravel banks are drying up. These are habitats for mussels and invertebrates, which in turn serve as food for fish. This puts enormous stress on these ecosystems. Mussels cannot move away quickly enough and die off," Völker told DW.

Drought, intense sunshine, and high nutrient loads from agricultural fertilizers also encourage algal blooms harmful to fish.

These effects were seen in 2022 on the Oder River in eastern Germany. High temperatures, low water levels and elevated salinity allowed a toxic invasive algae to spread. Around 1,000 metric tons of fish died along parts of the German-Polish border river.

Experts do not expect a repeat of the Oder disaster on the Rhine this summer because oxygen levels remain sufficiently high. But the danger to the wider freshwater ecosystem remains.

As the Danube retreats, long-submerged wreckage is resurfacing — a sign of how far the river has fallen Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

What dwindling rivers mean for drinking water costs

The Rhine and the Danube are fed by numerous tributaries that are also running low. These tributaries are crucial because their lush, reed-filled banks act as natural filters, allowing water to slowly pass through layers of soil that help remove pollutants before water reaches underground wells.

"Much of our drinking water is what's known as 'riverbank filtration,'" said Hagen Koch, a researcher specializing in climate adaptation and resilience at Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

In other words, Germany's drinking water comes from those wells. But drought is weakening this process. Pollutant concentrations are increasing because roughly the same volume of wastewater — largely from industry and sewage works — is discharged into rivers even as water levels fall.

"If the ecosystem is damaged — that is, the animals and plants that contribute to water purification — this results in significant additional costs. Additional treatment is needed to supply clean drinking water to millions of people," Koch told DW.

German industry groups estimate water supply costs could rise by up to 30% as a result of climate change. By 2035, additional investments of up to €14 billion could be needed for improved water treatment systems, as well as deeper mains and upgraded reservoirs designed to keep water temperatures low and limit microbial growth.

The situation has drawn attention to a broader debate over water use. While households pay for the water they consume, several industries — including mining and agriculture — are exempt from water abstraction fees in many German states.

To conserve water, authorities in some German cities are currently severely restricting withdrawal from streams and rivers by private individuals. In Cologne, residents who violate the ban face fines of up to €50,000 ($58,000).

Low water levels hitting the economy

Low water levels in Germany's rivers are already taking a significant toll on the economy. Some vessels are carrying just a fifth of their usual cargo, delaying production and driving up prices. Germany's steel, chemical and petroleum industries have been hit particularly hard.

Energy supplies are also under pressure. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has urged households and businesses to conserve electricity. He warned the country could face an unprecedented energy crisis after low water levels in the Danube forced the shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant.

Rewetted peatlands like this one are the kind of restoration experts say could help rivers retain water Image: Robert B. Fishman/picture alliance

Romania blasts rocks as Europe searches for solutions

Politicians are exploring emergency measures in response to the situation. In Romania, the military blasted apart a rock formation in a branch of the Danube to secure the cooling water supply for the Cernavoda nuclear power plant and avoid a shutdown.

Germany's transport minister brought together representatives from industry, ports and inland shipping on August 6 to consider short- and long-term solutions to the crisis. One proposal under discussion was deepening parts of the Rhine's navigation channel so shipping can continue despite low water levels.

Critics warn that further dredging and deepening of shipping channels would accelerate water runoff, lower groundwater levels, and cause floodplains to dry out more quickly, ultimately do little to solve the problem in the long-term.

Exposed riverbed now stretches beneath Düsseldorf's bridges, where the Rhine once ran deep Image: Kai Kitschenberg/Funke Foto Services/IMAGO

Instead, they're calling for the expanded use of low-water vessels, as well as a shift from freight transport to rail. Koch supports the development of ships with shallower drafts, but notes such changes require significant time and investment.

For Jeanette Völker, the solution lies in restoring parts of Europe's heavily modified rivers. Reconnecting floodplains, protecting wetlands and restoring peatlands would help landscapes retain more water and improve resilience during future droughts.

Reservoirs and dams may also play a role where they are environmentally acceptable. But experts warn adaptation alone will not be enough. Without climate protection and a rapid reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, any investments are little more than a drop in a fast-flowing river.

World.title: Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing seeks legitimacy in Thailand
World.content:
Bangkok rolled out the red carpet for the Myanmar leader, but experts say the former junta chief still faces major obstacles in his bid for regional acceptance.

Myanmar's junta chief turned president Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a two-day visit to Thailand on Friday.

His first visit to the neighboring nation as civilian leader was aimed at recasting himself as the leader of a civilian government after years of diplomatic isolation, experts told DW.

His reception on landing in Bangkok on Thursday had all the pomp and circumstance befitting a visiting head of state — red carpet, honor guard, blaring national anthems and smiling photo ops with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

"Naypyidaw equates engagement with acceptance," said Moe Thuzar, head of the Myanmar Studies Program at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, referring to Myanmar's capital.

"Min Aung Hlaing is seeking to leverage Naypyidaw's space in bilateral relations with neighbours' specific interests to secure greater acceptance of his administration from external partners."

Min Aung Hlaing has pledged to pursue peace and improve ties with the 11-member ASEAN bloc Image: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

Since the retired general seized power in a 2021 coup that toppled a democratically elected government, a brutal civil war between the military and armed resistance groups has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced well over 3 million.

Western countries have imposed several rounds of sanctions on Min Aung Hlaing's regime over alleged war crimes and other human rights abuses, charges the government rejects.

In 2024, the then-chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing himself for crimes against humanity committed against Rohingya Muslims.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which traditionally emphasizes non-interference in another member's domestic affairs, has barred him or his foreign minister from attending its leaders' summits.

Hoping to break out of its growing isolation, Myanmar held staggered elections in December and January that were widely criticized by the United Nations and Western governments as a sham designed to legitimize continued military rule.

The military-aligned Union Solidarity and Development Party won more than 80% of seats, paving the way for parliament to elect Min Aung Hlaing president in April.

What is Thailand's role in Myanmar's reengagement?

Myanmar's government rejects criticism of the electoral process, saying the elections were part of a transition to civilian rule and a return of power to the people.

Since becoming president, Hlaing has paid official visits to India, China, Laos and now Thailand, as Bangkok pushed for peace efforts in Myanmar's civil war and its reengagement with ASEAN.

"For Min Aung Hlaing, visiting Thailand is also [about] finding legitimacy in the ASEAN region, because Thailand is a … founder of ASEAN and has [a] big voice in ASEAN," said Wai Yan Phyo Naing, a visiting scholar at Taiwan's Academia Sinica who studies Myanmar.

"He can show the [other] ASEAN members that Thailand is treating me like this, Laos already treated me like this. So, do you want to [act] based on the realistic point of view, or are you still wanting to argue I'm not the legitimate leader of Myanmar?" he said.

Moe Thuzar and Wai Yan Phyo Naing both agree that the bloc, which did not officially endorse Myanmar's last elections, like most countries, was not likely to let Min Aung Hlaing back to its leaders' summits any time soon.

Human Rights Watch's Elaine Pearson on Myanmar election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

ASEAN still insists that Myanmar first make meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that they all agreed to a few months after the coup, a plan Hlaing has dismissed repeatedly, most recently last week.

Still, Min Aung Hlaing may be hoping that his official trips abroad as newly installed president

help convince ASEAN to accept his government "on its own terms," Moe Thuzar added.

Either way, she said, Min Aung Hlaing will use his trip to Thailand to build on the bilateral relationship between the neighbors, which share a 2,400 kilometer (1,490-mile) land border.

The visit included a business forum on Thursday for Thai and Myanmar firms.

"The focus on trade and economic deals reflects Naypyidaw's and Bangkok's interest in prioritising economic engagement and addressing concerns related to border trade," said Moe Thuzar.

The economics of legitimacy

Thailand is among Myanmar's top trade partners and foreign investors, including in energy projects vital to both. A Thai firm operates two of Myanmar's main gas fields, which supply much of Thailand's natural gas.

David Mathieson, an independent Myanmar analyst based in Thailand, says convincing those investors to stay, or new ones to come in, helps shore up support for Hlaing among a key constituency.

Regardless of the ex-general's official title, he said, "he's a military dictator, and to be a dictator you need a certain level of cooperation, and cooperation comes from economic elites."

"He's appealing to an incredibly cynical international system that's like, hey, you did this. None of us buy it, but it's good enough for us. You dressed up for the party, well done, and [it's] business as usual," Mathieson said.

"Does that help the 54 million people of Myanmar? No, it doesn't. It helps him and it helps the system that props him up."
