World.title: Platform for foreign workers coming to Romania up and running, authorities say
World.content:
Romania’s Interior Ministry announced on Thursday, August 6, that the platform WorkinRomania.gov.ro is now up and running, simplifying the process of hiring foreign workers.

The platform aims to make it easier for immigrant workers to enter the domestic labor market. Among its benefits is the facilitation of the relationship between the employer and the future employee.

The platform helps both Romanian employers looking for a workforce and aids the state in managing more efficiently the employment of new workers coming from other states. “Less bureaucracy, shorter deadlines and the possibility to track each application in real time,” the Ministry noted, cited by Agerpres.

The services of this platform include: permanent access to one’s own electronic file; the possibility to track each stage of the procedure; automatic notifications regarding requests for additional documents or the adopted solutions; reduction of waiting times; increased transparency of the entire administrative process. The platform also connects future employees with the Trade Register, the Employee Records Register, as well as with IT systems for the checks provided by law.

The platform also centralizes the actions of several Romanian state institutions.

The General Inspectorate for Immigration within the Ministry of Internal Affairs handles the procedures within its competence regarding the regime of foreigners and the right of residence for employment purposes; it analyzes and resolves applications regarding the granting and extension of residence

The right of residence for employment purposes, issues the specific documents and participates in the electronic exchange of data necessary for substantiating administrative decisions.

The National Agency for Employment operationally administers the module intended for the registration and authorization of employers and agencies for the placement of foreigners and configures the workflows related to these procedures;

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, through the national visa system and the eViza platform, participates in the workflows regarding the granting of long-stay visas for employment;

The National Agency for Fiscal Administration provides the information necessary for the fiscal checks provided by law;

The Ministry of Education and Research, through the National Center for the Recognition and Equivalence of Diplomas, contributes to the verification of qualifications and diplomas, in the cases provided by legislation.

The platform offers useful information for employers, placement agencies and foreign workers, available also in English. Interested persons can find on WorkinRomania.gov.ro all the information they need for creating and validating an account on the platform, the registration and authorization conditions, the necessary documents and the method of using the electronic services available on the platform.

At the same time, users have a support chat service, available both in text and voice format, which provides assistance and guidance in the use of electronic services, in Romanian and other languages.

In terms of security, the program is included in the Ministry’s Services Hub, specially designed to keep personal data safe at the level of each county.

Although Romania set an official quota of around 90,000 newly admitted foreign workers for 2026, employer demand significantly exceeds that ceiling. In some years, requests have reportedly been more than double the approved quota. Still, filling vacancies is only part of the challenge. A large share of newly arrived workers subsequently seek opportunities in other EU member states, where wages, working conditions, and social benefits are often more attractive.

World.title: Thriller starring Nicolas Cage to open this year's horror and fantastic film fest in Biertan
World.content:
The Full Moon Horror and Fantastic Film Festival, presented by the Transilvania International Film Festival, returns to Biertan for its 11th edition, bringing three days and three nights of premieres, cult films and open-air screenings.

The festival opens with the Romanian premiere of The Carpenter’s Son, starring Nicolas Cage. Another highlight of this year’s edition will be the cine-concert Trenul Fantomă, featuring live music by Dubase, preceded by an acoustic performance by Ana Coman and her guitar as part of Full Moon Unplugged.

At Bastion Open Air, the programme kicks off on Friday, August 14, with Nightborn, the new film by Finnish director Hanna Bergholm, known to horror audiences for Hatching. Selected for the competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, the film follows a couple who move into an isolated house in the Finnish woods, where the arrival of their first child awakens a disturbing presence. The evening continues with The Rocky Horror Picture Show, the horror musical that has become one of cinema’s great cult phenomena. The story behind the film will also be explored from behind the scenes in the documentary Strange Journey: The Story of Rocky Horror, screening on Saturday at Cinema Ion Hobana.

On Saturday, Bastion Open Air will screen Her Private Hell, the new film by director Nicolas Winding Refn, as well as the original Dutch version of the thriller The Vanishing. The programme also includes the 1993 American remake, also directed by George Sluizer, giving audiences an opportunity to compare the two versions.

On Sunday, Carrie returns to the Bastion screen. Directed by Brian De Palma and based on Stephen King’s novel, the classic marks 50 years since its release.

On Friday, August 14, Méliès Open Air will host the Romanian premiere of The Carpenter’s Son. Directed by Lotfy Nathan, the supernatural thriller stars Nicolas Cage as Joseph, alongside FKA twigs as Mary and Noah Jupe as their teenage son.

On Saturday, August 15, audiences are invited to the cine-concert Trenul Fantomă. Made in 1933 by Jean Mihail, the first Romanian-language talking film tells the story of travelers forced to spend the night at a railway station believed to be haunted. The film will be screened with live music performed by Dubase.

The Méliès programme concludes on Sunday, August 16, with The Virgin of the Quarry Lake, directed by Laura Casabé. Inspired by the prose of writer Mariana Enríquez, the film blends adolescence, jealousy and black magic against the backdrop of Argentina’s 2001 crisis.

The selection continues at Cinema Karloff and Cinema Ion Hobana, with titles including The Turkish Coffee Table, Gaua, Species, Roqia, Veins, The Uncertainty Principle, Feels Like Home, Anemoneciacs and Transylvania Tapes.

The program also includes Romanian short films, the documentary Strange Journey: The Story of Rocky Horror, and repeat screenings of The Carpenter’s Son, Nightborn and Her Private Hell.

The festival takes place between August 14 and August 16.

World.title: Romania’s Banca Transilvania extends EUR 71.4 mln loan for Entek Elektrik PV park
World.content:
The largest bank in Romania, Banca Transilvania, announced that it will finance the development of the Eco Sun Niculești photovoltaic park, Entek Elektrik’s first investment in local green energy production, with EUR 71.4 million.

It is one of the largest bilateral financings granted to a photovoltaic project under development in the country. Once completed, the park, located in Dâmbovița County, will have an installed capacity of approximately 205 MW. The total value of the project is estimated at EUR 100 million.

“Projects of this scale contribute to strengthening energy independence and modernizing the Romanian economy. We are pleased to support Entek Elektrik’s first investment in renewable energy production in Romania and to continue the solid partnership that we have built together,” said Cosmin Călin, Deputy General Manager Large Corporate, Banca Transilvania.

The investment in the Eco Sun Niculești project is made through Entek Elektrik Üretimi A.Ş., the renewable energy company of the Koç Group, and its main shareholder is Türkiye Petrol Refinerileri A.Ş. (Tüpraş), the largest industrial company in Turkey and the seventh largest refinery operator in Europe.

In Turkey, Entek owns an energy capacity portfolio of 550 MW. The company aims to further expand its renewable energy portfolio and seeks to become one of the leading green energy producers in Turkey.

World.title: Albanian Court Puts Turkish Activist in Custody After Extradition Demand
World.content:
Protesters rally with pictures of victims of the 2013 Gezi Park protests in Istanbul, April 2022. Photo: EPA-EFE/SEDAT SUNA.

The Tirana Court on Friday ordered a custody remand for Julide Yazici, who is wanted for extradition by Turkey to serve a prison sentence for aiding a terrorist organisation – charges that she claims are motivated by her political activism.

Yazici was arrested on August 4 at Tirana Airport while travelling from France to Albania after it was discovered that she was wanted for extradition to Turkey.

The judge granted the prosecution’s custody request despite Yazici’s lawyer’s arguments that his client “holds political asylum status in France and poses no danger”, and could be placed under house arrest instead.

The lawyer, Artan Shllaku, said that the decision will be appealed.

Shllaku added that Yazici, who teaches at an elementary school in France, had visited Albania a year earlier to see relatives and had encountered no issues.

Yazici is wanted by Turkish authorities to serve the remainder of a four-year prison sentence – three years, five months and 22 days – for providing logistical support to and participating in a terrorist organisation.

According to a decision by the French National Court of Asylum dated November 2020, a document obtained by BIRN, Yazici was involved in political activism in Turkey and participated in the Gezi Park mass protests in 2013 against the administration led by Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

She actively supported the former People’s Democratic Party, HDP, a left-wing political group that supported Turkey’s Kurdish minority, and which later became the DEM Party.

The French court decision granting asylum to Yazici stated that she was arrested in January 2016 “for having allowed a young woman she did not know, who had been introduced to her by a friend, to stay in her student room”.

The French court decision in the document that Yazici had “a well-founded fear … of being persecuted if she returns to her country due to her political activism”.

Yazici is not the first Turkish national to be arrested in Albania for extradition in controversial circumstances in recent years. Teachers and others linked to the movement previously led by the now-deceased cleric Fethullah Gulen, which is classified as a terrorist organisation by the authorities under Erdogan, have also been detained and then deported in line with Ankara’s demands.

World.title: Secrecy Surrounds Croatia’s Arrest of Alleged Serbian State-Linked Hacker
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH.

The Croatian and Serbian authorities are remaining tight-lipped over the arrest last week of a Serbian businessman named as Georgije V., 33, on suspicion of hacking into the computer systems of various Croatian state institutions and public agencies.

The Serbian man is reportedly suspected of hacking into the Croatian Interior Ministry, the Central Register of Pension-Insured Persons, the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, the Croatian Regulatory Agency for Network Activities, the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute, the Croatian Tax Administration and the Croatian Automobile Club.

Tomo Medved, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, was asked about the case on Friday but declined to provide details.

“I would like to commend the entire security and intelligence system for its responsible and vigilant monitoring and protection of the interests of the Republic of Croatia. Given the ongoing proceedings, I cannot comment further than that,” Medved told journalists.

Croatian daily Jutarnji list has reported that the arrest took place on July 28, when Georgije V. was on holiday in Croatia. He had arrived with his wife, two children and mother at a tourist resort on the Adriatic coast a few days earlier.

Following his arrest, police searched his electronic devices, vehicle and accommodation under court orders. They seized items and digital data allegedly linking him to criminal acts, including two mobile phones and a laptop containing a large amount of data.

The court ordered one month of pre-trial detention, despite the man offering 20,000 euros in bail money and his family home in Novi Sad as collateral.

Croatia’s Chief State Attorney, Ivan Turudic, initially sparked public interest on Monday when he made a comment about a case related to national security. It was then reported by Jutarnji list that Turudic was referring to the arrest of an alleged hacker linked to Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA.

It is not known whether the suspect’s alleged access to the computer systems of various institutions and agencies endangered Croatia’s national security in any way, or what he did with any data he may have obtained.

Nera Gajdarov Beg, the suspect’s lawyer, told Jutarnji list that the court’s custody order is being contested.

“An appeal has been filed against the decision to order pretrial detention because we believe that not all legal requirements for such a decision have been met. At this point, I cannot provide details of the defence because the proceedings are in the investigation phase, which is secret,” Gajdarov Beg said.

The Serbian authorities have not commented on the arrest so far. However, Serbian media have reported that Georgije V. is the owner of an active Novi Sad-based company specialising in computer programming and cybersecurity.

World.title: Croatian Serb Leader Deplores Hate Speech at Operation Storm Commemoration
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Milorad Pupovac, president of the Independent Democratic Serb Party, SDSS, and MP, on Friday said that slogans and chants heard on the streets of Knin on August 5, the day marking the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, represented a “serious attack on constitutional values and democracy”.

Pupovac, leader of the main party representing Serbs in Croatia, argued that “hatred and incitement to crime are incompatible with true patriotism”.

At a press conference, he showed a compilation of recordings from Knin, the town that was the headquarters of a rebel Serbian statelet crushed by the Croatian Army’s Operation Storm in 1995.

They included sports fans and army veterans singing songs glorifying the Ustasha – the army of the Independent State of Croatia, NDH, a World War II fascist puppet state operating under the patronage of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

The recordings also showed people chanting: “We Croats do not drink wine, only the blood of Chetniks [Serbian nationalists] from Knin”; “The battle is fought, it is fought, the Ustasha flag is flying”, as well as insults directed at St Sava, the patron saint of the Serbian Orthodox Church.

“Those who have been trying to pass this off as an act of patriotism for years are actually seriously violating the true values of patriotism. In peacetime, the greatest patriotic virtue is constitutional patriotism,” Pupovac said.

He added that such behaviour was a “vicious attack on democracy”.

The SNV cited articles of the Croatian Constitution that it believes were violated by the shouting of the Ustasha salute “For the Homeland, Ready” and other glorifications of the NDH. The violations came after, not during, the official anniversary celebrations, it said.

Every year, Knin hosts a commemoration of Operation Storm, which liberated about 18 per cent of Croatia’s territory from rebel Serb forces and was followed by the flight of around 200,000 Serbs from Croatia. Some of them later returned.

SDSS leader Pupovac also criticised the Croatian judicial authorities, questioning why the State Attorney’s Office often does not react to hate speech and incitement to violence, appealing for an end to what he called a policy of appeasement.

He warned that failure to condemn such phenomena represents a direct threat to the Serb community in Croatia, and to all citizens who advocate for a state governed by the rule of law.

World.title: Week in Review: The Electoral Merry-Go-Round
World.content:
Last week, a no-confidence motion in the Serbian government was held in the country’s parliament. A boisterous discussion ensued between ruling and opposition MPs, but the motion failed – as expected.

Its real significance was not so much the outcome as the fact that the holding the vote, tabled at the beginning of the year, cleared an important obstacle to calling early parliamentary elections.

President Aleksandar Vucic has fuelled speculation that polls are imminent. Our analysis takes a look a look at what will determine when they happen – and whether they will happen at all.

World.title: One Year in the Palace: How Nawrocki Made the Polish Presidency His Own
World.content:
Nawrocki vetoes again and again

At home, he has repeatedly used his veto to frustrate the government. In his first year, Nawrocki vetoed 41 bills, more than any other Polish president since the fall of Communism. Among the most consequential were legislation linked to Poland’s access to nearly 44 billion euros under the EU’s SAFE defence program, bills concerning the justice system and public finances, two laws expanding rights for unmarried couples and, three times, legislation regulating the crypto-assets market.

The conflict, however, extends beyond legislation. Forty four ambassadorial nominations remain unsigned amid a long-running dispute between the palace and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski. Poland still has no fully accredited ambassador in Washington, one of its most important diplomatic postings; Bogdan Klich continues to run the embassy as chargé d’affaires.

But Nawrocki has also been unusually active in proposing legislation of his own. In a year, he submitted 22 bills; if he continues at this pace, he is on course to breaking another record by the end of his term. His predecessor Andrzej Duda by comparison submitted 32 during the entire first five years of his presidency.

“I want, in fact, to change the model of the presidency,” Nawrocki told the crowd on Thursday. “The president is not only there to review the law and deal with bills that come from parliament. The president is also there to come forward with legislative initiatives and carry your voice and your demands.”

That ambition goes beyond the number of bills. Poland is a parliamentary democracy in which the government runs most day-to-day policy, while the president has important but more limited powers, including the veto and a role in foreign and defence affairs. Nawrocki has repeatedly floated constitutional change and has been pushing the Presidential Palace towards something closer to a parallel centre of power. His ministers regularly speak on the same issues as their government counterparts, while the 17 presidential councils that aid him, involving around 700 people, are working on a broader development strategy that Nawrocki says he will unveil within months.

“I deeply believe that the presidential development strategy… will become, in the next parliamentary elections, a point of reference for all those who aspire to govern Poland,” he said.

Tusk has accused Nawrocki of trying to change Poland’s political system in practice without changing the constitution. Government spokesman Adam Szlapka described the first year of the presidency as a “bad time”, accusing Nawrocki of thinking primarily in political terms and obstructing government policy.

So far, however, the confrontation has not hurt the president much. Nawrocki remains Poland’s most trusted politician: an IBRiS poll published in late July found that 51.3 per cent of respondents trusted him.

Foreign policy has been another central part of his presidency. Nawrocki has worked hard to cultivate ties with Donald Trump and the US, while taking an increasingly confrontational line towards Ukraine over the historical legacy of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was responsible for massacres of Polish citizens during World War II.

On Thursday, he again tried to hold both positions at once. It was in Poland’s strategic interest, he said, for Ukrainian soldiers to keep Russia as far from Poland as possible. But it was also in Poland’s interest that “Banderite flags” should not fly in Warsaw, referring to the common term used for fighters of the UPA. “You can help and you can demand.”

World.title: Democracy Digest: Study Finds Slovakia Has Europe’s Weakest Spy Agency
World.content:
Police investigate Czech MP over car crash; countdown to municipal elections; Havel human rights award to be preserved

Czech police this week launched an investigation into MP and government commissioner for the Green Deal Filip Turek on suspicion of bodily harm through negligence over a car crash last month, which saw the honorary president of the Motorist Party – a ruling coalition junior partner – collide with an ambulance at a busy thoroughfare in Prague’s city centre. Caught on CCTV, the traffic accident led to the ambulance’s driver being injured and incapacitated for several days, sparking calls from opposition parties as well as President Petr Pavel for Turek to step down from both his parliamentary and government positions – although experts remain divided on who precisely was to blame for the collision. Turek has since temporarily vacated his position as the government’s plenipotentiary for climate change and the Green Deal pending the results of the investigation and vowed not to use his parliamentary immunity should the police file criminal charges against him. “I think the investigation will go well for me because I kind of know the regulations,” he told TV Nova, also suggesting the injured ambulance driver was “talked into” staying under hospital care longer than necessary for the optics.

This week was the deadline for political parties, movements and coalitions to officially register for the upcoming municipal elections, scheduled to be held across Czechia on October 9-10. Candidacies will now be reviewed by state electoral authorities by August 22. In the capital Prague, two dozen political groupings will take part in the race to win the big and hotly contested prize, a couple more than four years ago, on top of electoral fights for the city’s 57 local districts. In addition to electing their political representatives in the Czech Republic’s more than 6,000 towns, cities and municipalities, voters will also vote for a third of the Senate’s seats. About 155 candidates have registered to run for this year’s partial Senate race, less than the last ballot, mainly a result of pre-election agreements and joint candidates put forward by opposition parties.

Dagmar Havlova, the widow of the former dissident and president, along with the Vize 97 foundation confirmed this week that the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize will be preserved and continue to be awarded every year. This follows a previous announcement by the Vaclav Havel Library – which has faced an exodus of staff, sponsors and funding in recent months – that it would no longer participate in the annual award ceremony after Havlova withdrew her consent for the NGO to use the former playwright’s name. Coming with a cheque of 60,000 euros, the award was established shortly after Havel’s death in 2011 to recognise outstanding achievements in the field of human rights and has been awarded by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe since 2013 together with the Vaclav Havel Library and the Charter 77 Foundation. Past laureates include Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, Russian journalist Vladimir Kara-Murza and Belarusian activist Maria Kalesnikava.

World.title: Lands in Limbo: Danube ‘Microstates’ Dream Big Despite Lack of Recognition
World.content:
From the village of Batina in Croatia's far northeast, the only land route leads to the Free Republic of Liberland, a self-proclaimed microstate on the banks of the Danube River.

A bicycle is the only practical means of transport. The journey begins on an asphalt road before continuing onto gravel and then a dirt track, until the road disappears altogether.

The final kilometre must be covered on foot, across the dried-up bed of a Danube backwater. In summer, it feels more like walking across desert sand before reaching the dense forest that forms the "centre" of Liberland.

World.title: Letter from Brussels: Ceuta Migrant Panic Casts Shadow Over EU’s Summer
World.content:
The weeks that bridge July and August are a period when the EU buildings around Schuman here in Brussels grow quiet, and correspondents’ group chats go mute.

But this year the last week of July was far from quiet. While EU spokespersons were cycling through out-of-office messages and the unlucky ones were covering for absent colleagues, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - the largest single-day surge in irregular arrivals ever recorded on EU territory.

Dozens died. Within two days, the story had stopped being about victims. It had become a story about Europe’s political nerves.

World.title: Ice Deliveries: How Southern Croatia Coped in Summer Before Air Conditioning
World.content:
August the 7th, 2026 – Ice deliveries through the mountains was how southern Croatia coped during the intense summer heat, long before the advent and comfort of air conditioning.

Long before refrigerators and ice machines, the local people of Dubrovnik developed an incredibly organised ice-supply system. Snow was stored in special pits in winter and kept under straw and brushwood.

Imagine what summers looked like a few hundred years ago. The Dalmatian sun is strong, heating the ancient stone walls and streets; electricity doesn’t even exist, nor do refrigerators, freezers, and definitely not air-conditioners. Putni kofer/Lana Mindoljevic writes that instead of getting a full glass of ice in a few seconds, ice was an extremely precious commodity. Down in Dubrovnik, however, it existed even during the middle of summer.

Mountain snow was stored throughout the winter in special pits in the Konavle hills, kept under straw and brushwood, and in summer lowered by horses down to Cavtat and sent by boat to Dubrovnik. This precious ice was so highly valued that it was given as a gift to distinguished guests, and Dubrovnik even had an Ice Street.

Hundreds of kilograms of ice arrived in the City every summer

How was it possible that something considered a real little miracle during the hot summer days could already be found on the tables of Dubrovnik’s nobility? And not just a few accidentally preserved pieces. In the hottest part of summer, according to surviving accounts, around 260 kilograms of ice arrived in Dubrovnik every day.

Hundreds of kilograms of something that had to be produced months earlier, protected from the spring and summer sun, carried across the mountain, loaded onto horses, brought down to the sea and then transported by boat to the City. Apart from showing the fascinating organisational skill of the former Republic of Dubrovnik, this also reveals how much people already sought ways to refresh themselves in summer.

In winter they stored snow in pits and kept it until summer

Dubrovnik’s main reserve of cold lay far from the hot stone of Stradun, in the Konavle hills, in the Sniježnica area. The Museums and Galleries of Konavle write that in the time of the Republic of Dubrovnik three ice-houses (ledenice) were filled every winter – special natural or adapted pits into which snow was collected. The work was most often done in January or February. The snow was thrown in and compacted, then covered with brushwood and straw, and the ice-houses were closed and locked. The prince (knez) was responsible for their operation and maintenance, and the whole process took place under the supervision of a guard.

The ice-houses were by no means just small holes in the ground. They are located about a two-hour walk from the village of Duba and have been thoroughly explored by speleologists. The Konavle museum blog states that the Great Ice-house is 11 metres deep and 12 metres long, while the Small one is four metres deep and eight metres long.

When summer arrived, the night-time delivery operation began

Although collecting the ice was already interesting, the method of transport when summer arrived was even more fascinating. During the warmer part of the year, ice delivery from the Konavle hills to Dubrovnik was organised almost daily. Ice was taken from the ice-houses in the late afternoon, when the greatest heat had subsided, then loaded onto horses and brought down towards Cavtat.

From Cavtat, the journey continued by sea to the City of Dubrovnik. After the horse journey, the ice would set off by boat from Cavtat in the early morning hours so that it would not melt before reaching its destination.

For the year 1783, there’s concrete data: almost 16 tonnes of ice were brought to dubrovnik

How extensively the whole system was used is best shown by one surviving account. HRT’s programme Gradoplov, referring to Zdravko Šundrica’s book The Secret Box of the Dubrovnik Archive II, gives very precise figures for 1783. From 20 May to 20 August, 12,123 oka of ice arrived in Dubrovnik – that is, 15,759 kilograms. Transport required 146 horse-loads, and the whole operation cost 129 of the prince’s thalers.

in some cases, ice was brought in from herzegovina

On average, around 170 kilograms of ice arrived in the City every day during that period. In June about 110 kilograms were used, in July 170, and in August consumption rose. From 1 to 20 August Dubrovnik needed around 260 kilograms of ice daily. And every one of those kilograms first had to be produced with the help of winter alone, preserved for months and physically delivered to the city. If the winters were weak and did not produce enough snow to fill all three ice-houses, ice was obtained from the Herzegovinian mountains.

dubrovnik’s very own ice street

Over time the trade became so organised that ice had its own place in the City. HRT notes that there was an Ice Street (Ulica od leda) in Dubrovnik where ice could be bought, and interesting equipment for its use was also developed. One of the best examples was the kantiflora, a special glass bottle for cooling drinks. Ice was, of course, available only to the wealthier, so it was often given as a gift to distinguished guests. The Museums and Galleries of Konavle mention another tasty detail: ice cream was already spoken of in Dubrovnik in the 18th century.

Remains of the old ice-houses are still hidden on Sniježnica mountain today

The story does not live only in archival documents today. The Great and Small Ice-houses still exist in the Konavle hills, and in 2016 speleologists explored them and drew up their plans. The Cavtat-Konavle Tourist Board notes that the trail to the Konavle ice-houses is marked and starts in the village of Duba by the Church of St Stephen.

World.title: What Does New Pension Increase Mean for Defenders Who Worked After War?
World.content:
August the 7th, 2026 – There is set to be a new pension increase for Croatian defenders, but what will the situation be for those who did continue working after the war ended?

Index reports that the government has now presented a new model for increasing defenders’ pensions, which should apply from the 1st of January 2027 if the legislative amendments pass in Parliament. Among the beneficiaries covered by the changes are also defenders who returned to work after the war.

A defender who returned to work after the war and later retired under the old-age pension scheme basically receives a pension calculated in the same way as other workers, according to years of service and salaries. Then, as a defender, the pension is additionally increased depending on the time spent in the war, especially in the combat sector.

The position of these defenders was precisely one of the main reasons why Možemo demanded a change in the calculation method that would raise the pensions of the covered beneficiaries by up to 20 percent.

The Government today presented a different model under which the new supplement depends directly on the wartime service record. For every month spent in the combat sector the pension would be higher by three euros per month, and for a month in the non-combat sector by 50 cents.

Around 68,000 defenders are drawing pensions from the general system

In the refined proposal by Možemo, 68,561 beneficiaries are listed whose pensions are calculated primarily according to the rules of the general pension system, but with the application of defenders’ rights. On average they had around 31 years of service, and the average pension amounted to 668.37 euros.

The Ministry today presented a very similar current figure of 68,269 beneficiaries in that category.

Možemo intended its proposal primarily for defenders who returned to the labour market after the war and proposed an increase in the starting factor, which could raise their pensions by up to 20 percent. A higher factor would also apply when determining the lowest defenders’ pension.

The Government’s supplement is calculated completely differently. Its amount does not depend on the amount of the current pension, but on the number of months spent in the war and whether it was in the combat or non-combat sector.

what would an actual concrete example of that look like?

Let us take a simplified example of a defender who today receives 668.37 euros, which is the average pension of the mentioned group. If we assume that under the Možemo proposal he would achieve the full 20 percent increase, he would receive around 134 euros more per month, meaning his pension would rise to around 802 euros. Under the Croatian Government’s model, the increase would depend on the length of combat service.

In this concrete example the Government’s supplement would overtake the 20 percent increase after approximately three years and nine months spent in the combat sector.

This isn’t a universal threshold. For every defender, everything depends on their current pension and how large an increase that individual would achieve under the Možemo proposal. In this example, for simplicity, it was assumed that the person did not participate in the non-combat sector.

The length of participation in the war already today affects certain defenders’ pension rights. The Možemo proposal would not change that, but the new increase would not depend directly on whether someone spent one year or five years in the combat sector. Under the Government’s proposal that is precisely the main criterion for the new supplement. One year of combat service means 36 euros more per month, three years 108 euros, and five years 180 euros. The difference between the combat and non-combat sectors is also large. Five years in the non-combat sector would bring a monthly increase of 30 euros, while five years of combat service would bring 180 euros.

government proposals encompass a wider number of people

The Government’s increase isn’t intended only for defenders who continued working after the war. The Ministry announced today that the new supplement according to wartime service will be received by 104,560 defenders, while various proposed amendments would cover a total of 201,304 defenders and members of their families.

Defenders who continued working are thus included in the Government’s model, but they are not singled out as a special group. In other words, Možemo proposed an increase of up to 20 percent for a narrower circle of beneficiaries, while the Government proposes a supplement for a wider circle of defenders whose amount will depend directly on the number of months spent in the combat and non-combat sectors.

former pension reductions are also being scrapped

The Government also proposes the abolition of the pension reduction of 8 to 20 percent that is still applied to some retired soldiers, police officers and other authorised officials. This is a separate measure, distinct from the new supplement calculated according to the time spent in the Homeland War.

The abolition of the reduction should from 2027 cover around 34,000 beneficiaries, and the Ministry estimates that their pensions would as a result rise on average by around 70 euros per month. This measure is not limited only to defenders, but applies to all beneficiaries covered by that special pension regulation. The Government’s amendments have not yet been adopted. After public consultation they should be sent to the parliamentary procedure, and application is planned as of the 1st of January 2027.

World.title: Croatian Mountain Rescue Service Rescues Another Foreign National on Biokovo
World.content:
August the 7th, 2026 – The Croatian Mountain Rescue Service (HGSS) has had to rescue yet another foreign national stuck on Biokovo.

As Index reports, the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service (HGSS) has reported a night-time rescue of a foreign national who got lost last night in the area of Sutvid above Živogošće near Makarska, at around 1,050 metres above sea level on the southeastern part of Biokovo. HGSS received the call on Wednesday at around 18:30.

The man reported that due to high temperatures and lack of water he had become severely dehydrated, felt extreme weakness and was no longer able to safely continue moving or find the way. Four rescuers from the HGSS Makarska Station immediately set out into the field, and due to the demanding terrain they were soon joined by another four.

“After several hours of night ascent, the rescuers reached the injured person at 22:50. First aid was provided at the scene and after a rest and rehydration, accompanied by the rescuers, he began the descent towards the vehicle,” the HGSS Makarska Station announced.

The operation was successfully completed at 02:50. Photos published by HGSS show that the man had set out on the ascent in sandals. HGSS once again warns everyone not to go into the mountains without appropriate equipment and a sufficient amount of fluids.

“We’d once again like to appeal to all visitors to Biokovo to please, please carefully plan their trip before going into the mountains. During the summer months it is absolutely paramount that you bring a sufficient amount of water, avoid the hottest part of the day and use appropriate hiking footwear,” HGSS said.

World.title: This Croatian Island is Closer to Italy Than to the Mainland of its Own Country
World.content:
August the 7th, 2026 – There’s a far-flung Croatian island that is closer to neighbouring Italy than to the Croatian mainland. Only a lighthouse keeper lives there, and he’d be able to arrive on Italian shores much more quickly than he’d manage to arrive in Croatia.

Far out in the Adriatic Sea sits an isolated island from which, on a clear day, both shores of the Adriatic are clearly visible. Putni kofer writes that only a lighthouse keeper lives there, and day-trippers rarely stop by.

If you look at a map of the Adriatic and study the area from Split towards the shores of Italy, you will see the islands of Brač, then Hvar, then the more distant Vis and Korčula, followed by the open-sea island of Biševo… After that long stretch there is nothing, only deep blue emptiness, and then, almost in the middle of the open sea, another “little dot”. That’s Vela Palagruža, Croatia’s most remote island of all. It’s a narrow rocky islet barely a kilometre and a half long. From here to the Italian coast, you’ll cover just 68 kilometres, while to Split it is more than 120. In other words, this piece of Croatia is almost twice as close to foreign land as to its own.

this position made the island so important

It is precisely this position that for centuries gave Palagruža an importance out of all proportion to its size. It is the only point on the Adriatic from which, in clear weather, both the Italian and Croatian coasts can be made out, so for thousands of years the island served as a landmark and resting place on the long voyages between the Italian shore and Dalmatia.

Archaeologists have been confirming this for decades. At the Salamandrija site, on the plateau right next to the lighthouse, traces of human presence going deep into prehistory have been found, and in later periods the island became a sanctuary for seafarers. Finds of pottery inscribed with the name of Diomedes, the hero from the Iliad, confirmed that Palagruža was a place where sailors paid homage to him before setting out onto the open sea.

it remained under italian control until 1860

Until 1860, Palagruža was under Italian administration. When the Austrian authorities took it over, a lookout service was established on the island, and then in 1875 the lighthouse was built. Twenty years later a meteorological station was added. Since then Palagruža has never been without people.

The stone lighthouse stands in the middle of the island at 90 metres above sea level; with its lantern it rises to about 126 metres above the sea. A steep path about 700 metres long leads up to it – a real mountaineering stretch on which donkeys once helped the lighthouse keepers. About ten years ago they were replaced by a cable winch built specifically for this purpose.

the lighthouse keeper welcomes guests… but rarely

Today only the lighthouse keeper lives on Palagruža all year round; in the past entire lighthouse families – more than ten people – used to stay there. It is he who, during the summer, welcomes the guests who manage to reach this little piece of paradise.

And for those rare visitors that means exactly what it sounds like. There is no shop, restaurant, bar or pharmacy. There is not even the possibility of quickly buying something extra. Plovput looks after the lighthouse, and through them one can arrange summer accommodation in one of the two four-bed apartments, with a minimum stay of seven days. The building stands high on the island’s ridge, so a stay is not recommended for people in poorer health. What you get in return is hard to compare with anything else on the Adriatic: silence, the sea on all sides, and the feeling that you are on a planet of your own.

the highest number of endemic plants in all of southern dalmatia

Vela Palagruža is 1,400 metres long and only 300 metres wide, with gentler slopes on one side and vertical cliffs on the other. The climate is exceptionally mild and rainfall is scarce, so vegetation is lush in spring, autumn and winter, while in summer the coast is almost bare. Among the islands of southern Dalmatia, Palagruža has the most endemic plants. Here grow the Palagruža cabbage, Palagruža centaury, Palagruža horsetail, open-sea spurge and other species you will not find elsewhere. The archipelago around the main island also includes Mala Palagruža and a series of rocks and reefs. To the south-east lies the islet of Galijula, officially the southernmost land point of Croatia.

the former home of the richest fishing grounds in the entire adriatic

The waters around Palagruža were once one of the richest fishing grounds in the Adriatic. Today lobster and white fish are mainly caught here, and the area remains primarily a fishing zone. Visits have to be arranged with the lighthouse keepers or with one of the fishermen from Komiža; organised group excursions practically do not exist. For a place of this kind, that is probably not bad news.

World.title: Hajduk Stun Žalgiris 5-2 Away in Conference League Qualifier
World.content:
Hajduk beat Žalgiris 5-2 away from home in the first leg of the third qualifying round for the Conference League. The Split side celebrated in Vilnius thanks to goals from Michele Šego (5′, 44′), Adrion Pajaziti (56′), Dalisson (73′) and Rokas Pukštas (75′). Nikola Petković (35′) and former Hajduk man Marko Capan (86′) scored for the hosts. The return leg is in a week, on August 13, kicking off at 9 pm at Poljud.

This is Hajduk’s first away win in Europe in almost six years, since a 1-0 triumph at Renova in the second qualifying round of the Europa League. The winner of the Hajduk–Žalgiris tie will face the winner of the clash between Raków and Hammarby in the next qualifying round; their first meeting finished goalless.

Two goals from Šego put Hajduk ahead at the break

Hajduk took the lead as early as the fifth minute. Pajaziti played in Marin Šotiček, who squared the ball back from the edge of the box. Šego ran onto it, and Žalgiris captain Yuri Kendysh brought him down, conceding a penalty and picking up a yellow card in the process. Šego made no mistake from the spot, sending the keeper the wrong way to make it 1-0.

Just four minutes later, Hajduk squandered a big chance to extend their lead. Goalkeeper Vincentas Šarkauskas spilled the ball, and Pukštas crossed from the right for Šotiček, who volleyed wide from close range.

Hajduk won another penalty in the 13th minute. Šotiček again broke through on the left and entered the box, where he was brought down by Deividas Šešplaukis. Šego stepped up again, but this time Šarkauskas got down to save his effort, which was heading into the left corner.

Žalgiris pulled level in the 35th minute. Bilenkyi played in Nikola Petković, who slipped away from the attention of Hajduk’s defense unnoticed. Goalkeeper Silić misjudged the flight of the ball and pushed it into the path of the Žalgiris forward, who made it 1-1.

Hajduk still went into the break in front, however. In the 44th minute, following a foul on Pukštas, Šego produced a phenomenal strike straight from a free kick from around twenty meters to make it 2-1.

Hajduk seal the win in the second half

The second half began with a forced change for Hajduk, as center-back Alec van Hoorenbeeck was forced off through injury and replaced by Ron Raci. Hajduk continued to press forward and extended their lead in the 56th minute. After a short combination from a corner, Pajaziti got into the box and finished precisely from an angle to make it 3-1.

Hajduk then settled the tie with two quick goals. The first came in the 73rd minute, when a long ball from goalkeeper Toni Silić set up Anđelo Šutalo to assist Dalisson, who finished from the right to make it 4-1. Just two minutes later, Rokas Pukštas cut out a pass from the home side’s defense, went past his marker and scored from five meters to make it 5-1.

Žalgiris did manage to pull one back before the end. Former Hajduk player Marko Capan, who had come on in the second half, scored from a free kick from around twenty meters in the 86th minute. In stoppage time, Hajduk also had a goal disallowed, as Šotiček’s effort was ruled out for offside.

World.title: Serbian Historian: “Croatians Have Reason to Celebrate, They Got What Historically Belongs to Them”
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – Serbian historian Milan St. Protić has openly stated that Croatians have a reason to celebrate Operation Storm (Oluja), and that “they got what historically belongs to them” in a recent interview for N1 Serbia.

Index reports that the historian assessed that there’s no way out of the state the entire region has been in since the 1990s without confronting one’s own responsibility. According to him, in Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina the same rhetoric is still used, and all sides avoid responsibility while waiting for the other to first admit their own crimes. Protić notes that Operation Storm is rightly celebrated on the Croatian side and mourned on the Serbian side, and that this pattern has been repeating for decades now, and will likely continue to do so.

“Honestly, yes, the Croatians absolutely have something to celebrate. They got the result they wanted and which, historically speaking, belongs to them. Dirty things happened on both sides – that’s just what war is. There are no clean wars or ones like we watch in partisan films. Wars are horrendous, inhuman and no one can come out of them with clean hands and a totally clear conscience,” Protić said, recalling that the insane policies of Slobodan Milošević ended catastrophically for the Serbs themselves as well.

“And now the Serbs are marking the anniversary of Operation Storm, whether that be in Belgrade or in Mrkonjić Grad, it’s all being done with false pathos and crocodile tears. That emotion is, of course, fake. They don’t care about the people who suffered. If they’d cared, they would have pursued a different policy at the time or opposed it entirely. Today’s authorities in Serbia are the direct successors of those back then; they like to justify and support everything Milošević did, so it’s clear what this is really all about,” he stated.

the price of war

Protić posed the question of who “sold the Serbs in Croatia down the river” after first stirring them up, arming them and inciting them. Asked about the 200,000 people who were left with nothing and about the fact that the case still has no legal epilogue after three decades, he replied with a counter-question: which war ends in court?

“The winner has always imposed their own legal solution. War is settled on the battlefield, not in court. You lost there, and in the meantime you also sinned. The fact that others also sinned is on their conscience and their issue to deal with. The issues of the other side cannot be a justification for the things we committed,” he emphasised.

serbia’s need to finally look in the mirror

The prominent Serbian historian believes that in Serbia, people lack examination of their own actions.

“We’ve never had the courage, wisdom or will to realistically and soberly examine the responsibility, the policy and the consequences of the 1990s. We haven’t admitted to ourselves how disastrous that policy was, and we still feel its consequences of it all today,” he said, adding that this discussion must be opened if there is a desire to move forward into the future.

“If we want to step out of this swamp, then we’ll actually have to do it. We should have done it a long time ago, but we didn’t, I’d say out of weakness, despair and a sense of defeat. Of course, people will play that card. Such a wounded people as we became then is easy to manipulate,” he said. That manipulation, he added, continues. “When the Serbs beat their chests and swear that Kosovo will ‘forever’ be Serbian, deep down they know the truth. When they forge Serbian history, whether to deny Serbdom or to glorify it, they do it exclusively in their own interests,” Protić noted.

the end of yugoslavia and the birth of mature nation states

“It was clear that the Yugoslav peoples no longer wanted to live together. No one can force anyone to stay where they do not want to be. Why did our former brothers want to leave Yugoslavia? That is a question both for them and for historians. The moment someone decided to prevent that by war, the gates of hell opened,” Protić described. According to him, the solution could have been a peaceful and friendly separation. For the situation to be resolved, he believes, every nation must examine itself rather than constantly looking at what the other side did wrong.

“One must not live in the conviction that everything done in our name was ‘right’ and ‘clean’, while everything foreign was ‘dirty’ and ‘evil’. That is proof that none of these nations has matured and that they still feed on that kind of infantilism which often brings unimaginable horrors,” he said. He observed that the same rhetoric and refusal to look at the other side is used in Croatia, Bosnia and Serbia, only with different signs.

“I try my best to simply avoid talking about others; someone of their own should tell them that. That’s why I appeal that Serbs take a long, hard look in the mirror. A person, and a nation, confronts their own responsibility independently of the other. That confrontation is not mutually conditioned. Whenever it is conditioned, both on their side and on ours, it is actually just an excuse to avoid responsibility,” he said.

belgrade was the one to sell its own people down the river

Protić also stated that the expelled people from Knin served the Belgrade authorities only for political score-settling and that there was no real desire to help them. “Belgrade rejected everything that could have led to a compromise – both Rašković’s attempt with Boljkovac, and the Z4 Plan, and the opinion of the Badinter Commission. In the end they left those people high and dry, unprotected, to suffer such a miserable fate,” he said. He noted that even after 30 years there is money for EXPO, Belgrade Waterfront and various investments, but none for the refugees. He also recalled that everything possible was done to conceal their arrival in Serbia. “How can one justify that in such a large Republic of Serbian Krajina the Croatian army swept everything away in four days?” he asked.

even the “mourning” is disrespectful in serbia

Regarding the commemorations for Operation Storm in Mrkonjić Grad, Protić wondered about the appropriateness of such events.

“Is that how one mourns for any sort of victims? Heavy drinking before and after? Is that how it’s done? Or do you raise a monument to those who did unfortunately suffer, hold a memorial service and go home to grieve? What kind of paganism is this? Do Serbs do it this way?” he asked, before assessing that it is all simply abuse and that absolutely nothing of it is remotely sincere.

“They really don’t care about those who suffered. They don’t care how many young men died under their command in Republika Srpska… They don’t give a damn about those unfortunate refugees from Croatia, except for those who sided with them in order to achieve some ridiculous interests in Serbia,” he said.

World.title: Danube Recedes, Shipping Stopped: “Water Level Has Never Been This Low”
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – The Danube has receded so much that shipping has had to be stopped, with experts claiming that the river’s water level has never been this low.

An extremely low water level on the Danube has seriously hindered navigation near Vukovar in recent days. Some ships can no longer continue their journey, cargo vessels are stranded, and Croatia’s largest river port has had almost no traffic for ten days. Index reports that the water level of the Danube near Vukovar has dropped to minus 60 centimetres. In some sections of the fairway the river is only about 1.2 metres deep, forcing ships to reduce their cargo or stop sailing altogether.

The low water has exposed sandbanks, rocks and other underwater obstacles that are normally hidden at usual river levels. “We’ve now got to watch out for all the sandbanks, for the rocks – for all the underwater obstacles that until now were under water and inaccessible. Now, unfortunately, we keep having problems with them,” said Saša Piljaš, president of the Dunav Vukovar Sport Fishing Association, as reported by HRT.

two cargo vessels are stranded not far from erdut

The problems first affected smaller boats and are now making navigation difficult even for the largest vessels. “The fairway should be at least two metres deep for it to be worthwhile for shippers to transport cargo. Anything below that means sailing at reduced capacity, so profitability becomes questionable,” said Borna Čerina, head of the Navigation Safety Service at the Vukovar Port Authority. A cruise ship has been moored in Vukovar for a week, while two cargo ships are stranded near Erdut.

“In the fairway near the village of Erdut we have two cargo ships that ran aground a few days ago and are still sitting there. They will either have to lighten their load or wait for the water level to rise,” Čerina said.

no navigation at the port of vukovar for ten days

The consequences of the low water level are also being felt by the Port of Vukovar. In recent weeks shippers were still arriving with almost half the usual cargo, but even that traffic has now stopped.

“Over the last ten days we’ve had no navigability at all. All the barges are anchored either in their ports or in certain areas, waiting for a better draught,” said Marijan Kuprešak, director of the Port of Vukovar. If the water level does not rise soon, the port could lose a large part of its contracted traffic. “Partners who signed contracts with us were supposed to move around 200,000 tonnes of goods through the Port of Vukovar over the next three months – a significant tonnage for the port and significant revenue. It is now questionable whether the partners will organise some other form of transport, by cargo or by truck,” Kuprešak emphasised.

“I’ve never seen anything like this”

Retired port captain Ivan Barović, who worked on the Danube for more than 20 years, said he had never experienced a situation like this before. “There have been ice blockages around Dalj, and there have been high water levels when we had flooding at this spot. But the water level has never been this low,” Barović said.

The Danube is navigable almost all year round, and interruptions until now have mostly been caused by ice or floods. Such a prolonged suspension of navigation near Vukovar, according to Barović, has not been recorded before. “Captains have to use all their knowledge to bring ships safely into port. It’s another matter how profitable it is to load a ship to only 50 percent of its draught so it can pass certain sections,” he said. He warned that conditions like these may not remain an isolated case.

“I’m afraid we can’t be too optimistic, but we have to take certain steps. This is a situation where we have drought here and floods in some other area,” he stressed. The lowest water level ever measured on the Danube closr to Vukovar was recorded about a hundred years ago and stood at minus 110 centimetres.

World.title: Will Croatia Have Enough Electricity and Water?
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – Prolonged drought, the absence of heavier rainfall and high temperatures have seriously affected Croatian rivers, springs and pumping stations. Will Croatia actually have enough electricity and water?

As Domagoj Puljizovic reports for Poslovni, the Danube and Drava have dropped to record low levels, inflows on the coast and islands have decreased significantly, and electricity production in hydropower plants has weakened.

Despite the challenges, the director-general of Croatian Waters (Hrvatske vode), Zoran Đuroković, says that the water supply for the population is not currently under threat. The water level of the Sava has fallen to –298 cm, while historical minima have been broken on the Danube and Drava. Due to unfavourable hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava, the Krško Nuclear Power Plant (NEK) will gradually reduce reactor power to 80 percent during the night of 6 August.

This is a planned measure to ensure that the average daily temperature of the Sava does not exceed 28 °C and that the average daily temperature rise remains within three degrees. NEK has been operating continuously for 280 days since its overhaul in November 2025; if conditions worsen, power will be reduced further. The last time NEK operated at reduced power because of Sava temperature and flow was in 2003.

recovery won’t happen quickly

“There is no doubt that Croatia will have enough electricity,” Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said on Tuesday, adding that there is “no threat whatsoever” regarding NEK. Turning back to water supply:

“The situation is quite serious. This is already a prolonged low-water period,” Đuroković told HRT, warning that a rapid recovery cannot be expected. The Danube at Batina has fallen to –144 cm, surpassing the minimum recorded as far back as 1909. A historically low level has also been measured on the Drava, where the previous record of –172 cm has been exceeded with a drop to –192 cm. High water temperatures are also a problem.

The situation is even more sensitive on the coast, islands and karst areas. The long period without rain has reduced the yield of springs and pumping stations, prompting many water utilities to call on citizens and businesses to use water rationally.

“Inflows there are already greatly reduced, so capacities are being cut,” Đuroković said. In some areas pressure drops in the network are being recorded, but water supply remains stable. Conservation measures are being introduced and the use of water for irrigation, filling swimming pools and other non-essential purposes is being restricted, but the basic needs of the population are not currently threatened.

In Lika the situation is relatively stable, although the yield of some springs has decreased, particularly in the Brinje area. Đuroković warned that the disappearance of the snow cover has eliminated an important natural water-storage source for Lika watercourses.

Continental Croatia is currently in a more favourable position thanks to groundwater and large river systems. “There will be no shortages on the continent. The situation is quite good,” he said. Zagreb’s Water Supply and Sewerage company (ViO) also says there is no cause for concern, stating that water extraction in the city area is proceeding without difficulty.

“In the City of Zagreb, water extraction is taking place smoothly and there are currently no indications of possible disruptions in water supply,” ViO emphasised. The city company stresses that it continuously invests in the new network and maintenance of existing infrastructure and is implementing an action plan to reduce water losses, which last year amounted to 55 percent. They add that their water inspection service checks cases of illegal connections, and citizens can report suspicions of unauthorised water use to vodno.redarstvo@zgh.hr.

Croatian Waters has intensified monitoring and sent water-warden services into the field. Special attention is focused on smaller watercourses, which become sensitive to pollution due to low flow and high temperatures.

“Any inflow of pollution into these small rivers can cause ecological incidents,” Đuroković warned, calling on cities, municipal companies and economic entities to carefully treat wastewater. Recovery of water levels is not expected in the next five to seven days. The drought is already affecting hydropower plants, especially those on the Drava, where production has been reduced due to weaker inflows.

Croatian Waters and HEP are coordinating the use of available water so as not to endanger the biological minimum in the rivers. In Istria the key role is played by the Butoniga reservoir, which is currently sufficiently full. Larger restrictions are not expected there, but citizens are still being urged to use water rationally.

no reductions… for now, anyway

Istrian Water Supply and Sewerage Buzet has warned users in the areas of Vižinada, Kaštelir-Labinci, Višnjan, Tinjan and parts of Poreč and Kanfanar to immediately limit irrigation of green areas and washing of yards, and that if consumption is not reduced the first degree of restriction could be introduced. Vodovod Pula-Labin, which supplies the Pula and Labin areas and part of central Istria, says that water supply is regular and that reductions are not currently planned.

HEP: We’ll secure electricity from our own sources and by purchasing

In the event of a halt in production from the Krško Nuclear Power Plant (NEK), Hrvatska elektroprivreda (HEP) would secure the necessary quantities of electricity through production from its own available generation sources and by purchasing the remaining quantities on the wholesale market, HEP told Hina on Wednesday.

“In the event of a halt in production from NE Krško, HEP would secure the necessary quantities of electricity by engaging production from other available own generation sources and by purchasing the remaining quantities of electricity on the wholesale market,” HEP stated.

The Ministry of Economy, responsible for energy, says that the Croatian and Slovenian governments are taking all necessary activities to ensure that the Krško Nuclear Power Plant continues to operate stably and safely even under conditions of high Sava River temperatures.

“We are in constant communication with the Slovenian side and jointly monitoring the development of the situation, with the aim of preserving the security of electricity production and supply,” the ministry told Hina. NEK reported on Wednesday that due to the continuation of exceptional hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava, it will begin operating at 80 percent reactor power during the night of Thursday, 6 August 2026, and will announce a return to full power when conditions allow.

“Due to the continuation of exceptional hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava River, NEK will, as announced, begin a gradual reduction of reactor power during the night of Thursday, 6 August 2026. In the first step, power will be reduced to 80 percent,” NEK reported on Wednesday.

This is a planned and controlled temporary measure necessary to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Environmental Consent (OVS), according to which the daily average temperature of the Sava River at the point of complete mixing downstream of the Brežice Hydropower Plant must not exceed 28 degrees Celsius, and the average daily temperature rise must not be greater than three degrees.

World.title: Estonia earned €256.5 million from carbon quota sales last year
World.content:
Estonia's share from the 2025 auction of carbon dioxide units totaled €256.5 million, the Climate Ministry said.

Since 2013, Estonia has received more than €2.3 billion in revenue.

Since the launch of the European Union auction platform, most of Estonia's revenue has gone to transportation and mobility — €1 billion — followed by €446 million for improving building energy efficiency and €175 million for developing renewable energy and energy efficiency. Nearly €164 million has been allocated for monitoring, research and development, and €37 million for climate adaptation and nature conservation.

The ministry said last year's quota funds continued to support Rail Baltica construction, railway electrification and the purchase of six new electric trains, which are expected to arrive in Estonia by the end of 2026.

Work also continued on building shore‑power infrastructure at the Virtsu and Kuivastu ports so they can serve a new electric ferry.

To improve building energy efficiency, local government and central government buildings were renovated and nearly zero‑energy buildings were constructed.

In the renewable energy and energy efficiency sector, radars enabling wind farm development in Northeast Estonia were completed, and work continued on renewable energy solutions on Vaindloo Island.

Rail Balticu jaoks killustiku laadimine Estonia kaevanduses. Autor/allikas: Rene Kundla/ERR

Theater and performance venue lighting costs were significantly reduced. Funding also supported monitoring of Lake Võrtsjärv and the sea, compiling a climate atlas, developing geothermal pilot plants, and flood‑risk reduction projects in Paide, Sindi, Pärnu, Haapsalu, Keila, Kuressaare and Hiiumaa, as well as climate cooperation projects in Ukraine and developing countries.

Revenue from CO 2 unit sales comes from the European Union Emissions Trading System (ETS). Under the system, companies that emit greenhouse gases must pay for those emissions, encouraging investment in cleaner technologies and lower‑emission production.

A portion of the revenue from sold CO 2 units goes to Estonia, which uses it by law to fund climate and energy projects.

The system currently covers 37 major industrial and energy companies in Estonia and one aviation company. Since 2024, maritime transport has also been included, and by mid‑2026, 16 Estonian shipping companies with a total of 53 vessels will participate.

World.title: Disputes reported in Estonia detention facility as 99 migrants recently caught
World.content:
Indrek Aru, head of the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) North Prefecture border guard bureau, said that in the past two weeks police have caught 99 people who are believed to have no legal basis for staying in Estonia.

On Thursday and Friday, Estonian police did not detect any new cases involving illegal immigrants. However, Aru said the migration pressure is not expected to end in the coming days.

Police conduct daily checks on roads entering the country, as well as at Tallinn Airport and major ports. Aru said that on 4 August police caught around ten people in central Tallinn who had no grounds to be in the country. They were from Somalia.

He said that disagreements arise easily in the detention facility where the illegal immigrants are currently held. "In the past couple of weeks, there have already been quite a few conflicts," Aru added. So far, police have managed to resolve them with little difficulty.

There have been cases where police have been threatened. Generally, however, the conflicts in the detention facility are everyday disputes. "For example, people bump into each other in the food line, leading to scuffles and pushing," Aru said. There have also been misunderstandings when someone has eaten another detainee's food.

In some cases, it is possible to send a person back to the country they came from within 48 hours. In other cases, the process can take several years.

On average, police receive five to ten calls per day from citizens regarding illegal immigrants. Aru stressed that although some calls are justified, people should not assume that everyone with a different skin color is problematic. "It is better to call when a person seems lost, is in a distressed condition, or when larger groups appear to be wandering aimlessly," he added.

World.title: Adaptation of Seita Vuorela's novel 'Karikko' begins filming on Saaremaa
World.content:
The film is based on the acclaimed novel "Karikko" ("The Reef") by Finnish author Seita Vuorela, which won the Nordic Council Children and Young People's Literature Prize in 2013. The screenplay was written by Jytte-Merle Böhrnsen.

Kari is a mysterious adventure film about a sister and brother, Kathi and Mika, who travel with their mother to a former seaside camp for their summer holiday. They soon discover a wild gang of teenagers on the beach who call themselves the Wrecks, as well as a mysterious abandoned hotel. The deeper the children delve into the secrets of the place, the more the boundaries between past and present, memory and oblivion, and the worlds of the living and the dead begin to blur.

The film is directed by Australian-born director Phillip Donnellon, who gained international recognition with his short film "Bird in the Wire," which was selected for the competition program of the Cannes Film Festival in 2001. Kari is his first feature-length fiction film.

Donnellon said he was initially advised against filming on Saaremaa because it was considered too remote as a filming location.

"I come from an even more remote island in Australia myself, so I managed to convince the producers to come and take a look. When we started exploring possible filming locations, I was overjoyed – I immediately realized that Saaremaa hides real treasures. The story unfolds at a very special coastal camp that has to feel both like an adventurous nature park and a place closely connected to the sea. Mändjala Campsite, Panga Cliff and the surrounding beaches were a perfect fit for our film," Donnellon said.

German actress Nora Tschirner plays the mother of Kathi and Mika. The young lead roles are played by Leo Humphreys, Esme Hobson and Lovena Börschmann Ziegler. The Estonian young actors appearing in the film are Derek Leheste, Torm Laos, Karl Jakob Moora, Alen Aiden Mathieson, Hugo Gorski, Mia Mahala Mäe and Aimei Zuo.

Filming in Estonia will continue until September 9.

World.title: Gallery: Tartu welcomes Moby on 'Play' 25th anniversary tour
World.content:
Tartu Song Festival Grounds hosted Moby on Thursday, as the U.S. musician and producer brought his 25th anniversary "Play" tour to Estonia.

Moby's latest tour celebrates the 1999 album that marked his breakthrough, earning critical acclaim and reaching millions of listeners worldwide.

"Play" was later included on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time list.

Moby began his career in punk rock before moving into electronic dance music and rave culture.

He has since released 22 studio albums, selling more than 20 million copies worldwide, with hits including "Honey," "Porcelain," "Flower," "Natural Blues," "Bodyrock" and "Why Does My Heart Feel So Bad?"

Throughout his career, he has earned multiple Grammy, Billboard Music Awards, Brit Awards, MTV and NME nominations and wins.

His music has also appeared in films including "The Beach" with Leonardo DiCaprio, the "Bourne" series with Matt Damon and the James Bond film "Tomorrow Never Dies."

Beyond his own recordings, Moby has produced and remixed music for artists including David Bowie, Ozzy Osbourne, The Beastie Boys, Daft Punk and Public Enemy.

World.title: Paide and Flora both lose in UEFA Conference League qualifying first legs
World.content:
Estonia's representatives at the UEFA Conference League suffered defeats home and away on Thursday, as Paide Linnameeskond went down to Rapid Vienna (Austria) and Tallinna FC Flora lost 2-0 away to Inter Club d'Escaldes (Andorra).

The UEFA Conference League is the third tier of European club competition, and Thursday's games were the first leg of round three of qualifying, with a berth in the playoffs awaiting the aggregate winners.

Paide 1, Rapid Vienna 4

Paide Linnameeskond suffered a 4–1 home defeat against Rapid Vienna before 5,500 fans at the A. Le Coq Arena in Tallinn. The hosts kept the score at 1–1 before things began to unravel in the last 10 minutes.

This means they will go to Vienna for the second leg next week with a mountain to climb if they are to meet either Benfica or Hearts in the playoff round.

The 32-time Austrian champions Rapid started the match sharply and were awarded a penalty as early as the third minute, which Hungarian right-back Bendeguz Bolla duly slotted in.

The visitors kept up the pressure, keeping 75 percent of the possession in the first half, though such shots as they had were little threat to Paide's Gambian 'keeper Ebrima Jarju's goal, and some chances even began to emerge for the home side as well.

This manifested with a Paide equalizer in the 41st minute when a low corner made its way into Rapid's penalty area; a touch from striker Abdourahman Badamosi hit the crossbar before it fell to forward Daniel Luts, who fired it into the net from a few meters out.

However, Rapid got back in control of the tempo in the second half. In the 71st minute, Paide committed a poor misplaced pass near their own penalty area, though Jarju saved the resulting close-range effort. Two minutes later, it was Rapid's goalkeeper's turn to keep out a fierce shot at his near post from striker Modou Pa Sohna.

In the final 10 minutes, however, the visitors settled things once and for all with three unanswered goals. In the first of these, Jarju came off his line in time to cut out a through ball, but the ball unfortunately ricocheted to striker Moulaye Haidara, who calmly slotted it home. Just two minutes later, Bolla delivered a low cross from the right into the goalmouth, where winger Petter Dahl turned it into the net, and in the fourth minute of stoppage time, Haidara capped a fine attack to put the finishing touch on the match.

Benfica meanwhile put six past Hearts, while the latter responded with just the one goal, in their first leg of the same qualifying stage.

Tallinna FC FLora players. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Flora lose 2–0 away to Andorran champs

Meanwhile reigning Estonian champions FC Flora went down 2–0 away to Andorran league champions Inter Club d'Escaldes in the first leg of their third-round qualifier, for the same competition.

Despite being based in tiny Andorra, the hosts have picked up some notable victories in the Conference League competition in recent years. Three summers ago, they defeated Scottish Premiership club Hibernian at home in the second qualifying round of the Conference League. Then last season, they beat Romanian giants FCSB, and drew with Slovenian powerhouse Olimpija Ljubljana.

AVUI JUGA UN DELS NOSTRES!

Encamp pic.twitter.com/xapXCvX29D — Federació Andorrana de Futbol (@Fedandfut) August 6, 2026

Inter are reigning Andorran league champions, though they have only one Andorran player in their squad, who came on for the final 10 minutes on Thursday. The overwhelming majority of the squad are Spanish nationals, many of them products of the academies of major clubs. For example, Inter midfielder Juan Camara has appeared for Barcelona in a Champions League match, while Inter Club d'Escaldes 'keeper Javi Diaz has played for La Liga side Sevilla.

The first half of Thursday's match belonged entirely to the hosts: Forward Faysal Chouaib put Inter ahead as early as the fifth minute, with the Andorran champions retaining 75 percent of possession during the first half, registering 13 shots during that time to Flora's two, one of which was on target.

The visitors came out for the second half in much better shape, however, holding more possession and even creating some chances in front of the hosts' goal. One good opportunity fell to national team striker Rauno Sappinen, but he was not ready for the ball inside Inter's penalty area. However, it was Inter who doubled their lead, in the 62nd minute, thanks to a goal from winger Domi Berlanga. The hosts held on to that margin to the final whistle, taking that advantage into the second leg in Estonia next Thursday, August 13.

World.title: Estonian raspberries thrive as new methods help farms weather changes
World.content:
Estonian raspberry growers are reporting a strong season this year as farms turn to new growing methods to protect crops from increasingly unpredictable weather.

Recent years of volatile spring and summer weather have pushed growers to experiment with new ways of cultivating raspberries. This summer, those adaptations combined with favorable weather conditions have helped berry farms achieve a strong harvest.

At Tontoli Berry Farm in Põlva County, raspberries are now grown in outdoor pots instead of directly in the ground.

Owner Kardo Tamm said the plants are also set out later in spring, with early-season raspberry plants initially kept in greenhouse-like tunnels to shield them from spring frosts.

The later planting schedule has helped protect their plants from cold.

"This year's raspberry harvest has been good," Tamm said. "We haven't had heavy rains that damage the berries during harvesting, and the cold this spring didn't do too much damage."

At Joosepi Farm in Ahja, the first tunnel-grown raspberries ripened around Midsummer, while outdoor potted raspberry plants are now reaching peak production.

Owner Kaire Roositalu said their harvest is expected to continue through late August.

"We have a lot of raspberries," she said, calling this year's harvest good. She noted that the outdoor crop is only just getting started.
