“If I were on the defense, I’d call to the witness stand my private detective on retainer Persistio Bongcal, P.I. who was an office boy for Sam Spade, Philip Marlowe, and later Mike Hammer in the U.S. Definitely the expert on cloak-and-dagger confidential stuff.”

Army of secret agents

Manny buzzed Bongcal, who shuffled in with a cigarette dangling from his lips.

“Percy, tell my friend here what you dug up on VP Sara’s confidential spending.”

“Yeah? Who’s asking?” Percy shot me a dirty look that made me want to take a shower.

“Listen, buddy. Here’s the lowdown. VP Sara’s a high-class dame. She kept her inside men in nice digs, with three squares and enough drinks to sink a battleship while they sniffed out every bad egg in the schools. See?”

Apparently, VP Sara spent the confidential funds to deploy an army of secret agents — like Andy Lim and Mary Grace Piattos — to the country’s 47,831 public schools. That’s a lot of schools, and a lot of operatives.

“That’s to finger mule-headed teachers who buck DepEd Order No. 21, Series of 2023. See, they’re not supposed to put up posters that mess up the classrooms, uh-uh,” snarled Percy.

But “Mary Grace Piattos” is a dead giveaway alias–everyone would know it’s just a snack brand from a ubiquitous restaurant chain.

“Look here, pal,” Percy growled, thumping my chest. “My buddy Senator Bato de la Rosa swears there are Piattos in Davao. Said so to Karen Davila. He’s on the lam, see, and likely cooling it in their roost right now.”

Well then, I conceded, VP Sara justifiably pulled out all the stops to quash creeping insubordination among our public school teachers.

“You bet. It might be ‘Always have clean and bright teeth’ posters now but commie placards later.”

But did her confidential expenses also include payouts to sources who snitch on teachers that sell longganisa and panties to colleagues between classes?

“Unfortunately,” Manny butted in, “surveilling teachers who sell longganisa and sundry goods is neither within the purview of DepEd Order No. 21 nor are rewards for that an allowable expense under Joint Circular 2015-1 of the Commission on Audit et alia.”

“Besides,” he added, “such cases are obiter dictum—merely heard of in passing and not legally significant.”

Obiter dictum? Legally insignificant like the manifestations of Senator-judge Robin Padilla? Or when he irrationally grills a Commission on Audit witness about leftist recruitment in universities? When the DepEd is only in charge of basic-education public schools?

“Ah, well,” Attorney Manny sighed, shaking his head, “that’s because Senator Robin hears things through a different orifice. In his case it’s always obiter rectum.” – Rappler.com

Rene Ciria-Cruz is a Filipino-American journalist and writer who has worked extensively in U.S. and Filipino media. He served as US bureau chief for Inquirer.net, the official site of the Philippine Daily Inquirer, a major Philippine news outlet. During his tenure he also wrote and edited for other publications and sites including PositivelyFilipino.com and has contributed to U.S. newspapers like the San Francisco Chronicle and San Francisco Examiner as well as magazines such as California Lawyer Magazine and Filipinas Magazine.

World.title: Is Kazakhstan’s Middle Class Expanding? New Survey Reveals More Than Just Income Trends
World.content:
ASTANA — More than 93% of Kazakh citizens describe their household’s financial position as middle income or above, according to a survey by the Bureau of National Statistics (BNS) released on Aug. 5.

The survey found that 70.1% of respondents described themselves as having an average level of material well-being, while 22.9% said they were somewhat above average. A further 4.9% considered themselves relatively well-off, and 0.3% described themselves as affluent. By contrast, only 1.8% assessed their financial situation as below average or poor.

These results come at a time when expanding the middle class has become a central element of Kazakhstan’s economic agenda, moving beyond a narrow focus on household income alone. In his 2024 State of the Nation Address, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev stated that “economic growth should be accompanied by reduced social inequality and a strengthened middle class. Only in this way can we reinforce the country’s potential.”

This reflects a broader shift in economic policy thinking, where growth is increasingly assessed not only through GDP, investment, or industrial output, but also through whether it translates into higher living standards, better-quality jobs, and greater financial security for households.

Comparing 2023 and 2024: a shift in self-perception

BNS data from previous waves of the same survey suggest a modest shift in how Kazakh citizens position themselves within the income structure. In the earlier survey (2023), 74.2% of respondents identified as middle income, compared with 70.1% in the most recent 2024 results. At the same time, the share of those placing themselves above the middle has increased to nearly 23%.

Taken at face value, this could indicate a gradual rebalancing of self-perception, with fewer respondents identifying strictly as “middle” and more moving into the “above average” category. However, this should be interpreted cautiously. The change may reflect not only material improvements, but also shifts in expectations, inflation perceptions, or changing reference points for what households consider “average”. In other words, the data may suggest that Kazakh citizens are not only evaluating their income, but also redefining what “middle class” means in a changing economy.

Regional and demographic differences

The survey also highlights differences across regions and demographic groups. Among urban residents, 70.9% described their financial position as average, compared with 68.2% in rural areas. However, rural respondents were slightly more likely to identify themselves as relatively well-off (5.8%, compared with 4.6% in cities), while also being more likely to describe their situation as below average (3.2% versus 1.1%).

Men generally assessed their financial standing more positively than women. One quarter of male respondents said their income was somewhat above average, compared with 21.6% of women, while 5.7% of men and 4.5% of women considered themselves relatively well-off. This gap may reflect a mix of factors, including differences in income perception, social expectations, and variation in how respondents choose to self-report their financial status. Again, this is an interpretive observation rather than a statistical conclusion.

Beyond income perception, the survey indicates broadly positive attitudes toward household finances. 38.2% of respondents said they were satisfied with their financial situation, while 59.6% reported being partially satisfied. Only 0.5% said they were dissatisfied. Similar results were recorded for assessments of overall household economic conditions, with 39.6% fully satisfied and 57.9% partially satisfied.

Perception vs. objective indicators

The distinction between perceived and actual economic status is important because perceptions of prosperity do not always align with traditional macroeconomic indicators. A range of international research in behavioral economics and sociology, including work by the OECD, the World Bank, and studies published in journals such as the Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, has shown that households often assess their financial well-being relative to expectations and to the living standards of those around them, rather than by income alone.

As living standards rise, expectations tend to rise as well, which can reshape how people define what it means to be “middle class.” This means that a stable or even improving economy can still produce shifts in self-assessment that do not directly mirror income growth statistics.

What the trend may suggest

Taken together, the comparison between 2023 and 2024 suggests a gradual shift in how Kazakh citizens locate themselves within the income distribution, with fewer identifying as strictly middle income and more placing themselves above that threshold.

Whether this reflects real income growth, inflation-adjusted improvements, or changing social benchmarks remains open to interpretation. However, the direction of self-perception combined with consistently high levels of reported financial satisfaction may indicate that Kazakh citizens are, at minimum, not experiencing a deterioration in perceived living standards, and may be gradually adjusting upward in how they define their economic position.

As policymakers continue to emphasize inclusive growth alongside headline economic performance, these perceptions may become an increasingly important lens through which they can understand how economic change is experienced on the ground.

World.title: EAEU Trade Nears $100 Billion as Bloc Shifts Focus to Digital Integration
World.content:
ASTANA — Trade among Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states is on track to surpass $100 billion for the first time in 2026, as the five-country bloc shifts its focus from traditional market integration toward digital trade, artificial intelligence and the removal of non-tariff barriers. Speaking at the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council meeting in Cholpon-Ata on Aug. 7, Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said mutual trade within the EAEU reached $95 billion in 2025 and is expected to grow by 7.3% to $102 billion this year.

The milestone also reflects the bloc’s continued importance for Kazakhstan’s external trade. As previously reported by The Astana Times, trade with fellow EAEU member states reached $9.87 billion in the first four months of 2026, up 13.3% year-on-year. Russia remained Kazakhstan’s largest trading partner within the union, accounting for 87.6% of Kazakhstan’s trade with EAEU members, followed by the Kyrgyz Republic, Belarus and Armenia.

The discussions reflected what officials increasingly describe as the next stage of EAEU integration. While the bloc was initially built around the free movement of goods, services, capital and labor, policymakers are now focusing on digital integration, harmonized regulations and more efficient cross-border trade.

At the meeting, the prime ministers discussed measures to further develop the EAEU’s internal market, deepen sectoral cooperation and strengthen financial and economic coordination. The agenda also included the digitalization of freight rail transport and international transport corridors, e-commerce, climate cooperation and the integration of artificial intelligence into the union’s information systems.

The meeting concluded with the signing of six documents, including an Agreement on Electronic Commerce, aimed at creating a more unified regulatory framework for online trade, expanding opportunities for businesses and improving market access across member states. Participants also approved an agreement on the mutual recognition of academic titles and adopted several decisions aimed at advancing regional cooperation.

Rather than focusing primarily on tariff liberalization, the EAEU is increasingly prioritizing the removal of non-tariff barriers, digital customs and logistics, and common digital rules designed to make businesses more competitive across the union. For Kazakhstan, that next phase of integration also means addressing long-standing barriers affecting exporters.

Bektenov said Kazakhstan’s exports of animal and plant products, as well as processed food, reached nearly $7 billion in 2025 and totaled $3.6 billion in the first five months of this year. At the same time, he pointed to concerns raised by businesses over restrictions affecting poultry and dairy exports to EAEU markets.

Kazakhstan called for systematic monitoring of market access conditions for food products to ensure member states comply with their obligations under EAEU rules, arguing that a more consistent approach to resolving trade barriers would provide a significant boost to intra-union commerce. The proposal reflects a broader effort to address non-tariff restrictions, which have increasingly replaced customs duties as one of the main obstacles to deeper economic integration within the bloc.

Digital transformation emerged as another central theme of the meeting. The discussions build on commitments made at the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council summit in Astana in May, where member states adopted a Joint Statement on the Responsible Development of Artificial Intelligence. Speaking at that summit, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for integrating national digital systems to accelerate customs procedures, identify bottlenecks and forecast cargo flows in real time.

“New technologies should not become the cause or source of digital gaps. They are designed to become an instrument of economic interconnectedness and powerful synergy of cooperation between our countries,” Tokayev said.

In Cholpon-Ata, Bektenov also highlighted Kazakhstan’s own digital ambitions, noting that 2026 has been declared the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence. Among the country’s flagship projects is the planned Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz, where the first 125 megawatts of computing capacity is scheduled to come online in June next year.

“The project will create digital infrastructure of international standards and strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as one of Eurasia’s digital hubs,” Bektenov said, inviting businesses and technology companies across the EAEU to participate in the initiative.

The meeting also reflected Kazakhstan’s close economic ties with fellow member Kyrgyzstan. During a collective meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Bektenov conveyed greetings from President Tokayev and noted that bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan has doubled over the past five years to $2.2 billion, with both governments continuing efforts to expand commercial ties.

The next meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council is scheduled for Oct. 1-2 in Minsk, Belarus, where member states are expected to continue advancing the bloc’s digital integration agenda.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Services Exports Near $13 Billion as Digital Sector Gains Momentum
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s services exports approached $13 billion in 2025, with transport remaining the backbone of the sector. But while logistics continues to generate nearly half of the country’s services export revenue, the fastest growth is increasingly coming from digital industries, pointing to a gradual shift toward higher-value exports.

According to Energyprom.kz, Kazakhstan exported $12.8 billion worth of services in 2025. Transport services remained the country’s largest export category, generating $5.7 billion, or 44.8% of total services exports, up 5.2% from a year earlier. Freight transportation accounted for $4.5 billion of that total.

Travel-related services ranked second, increasing 12.4% to $2.9 billion, driven largely by spending by foreign visitors traveling to Kazakhstan for tourism, education, medical treatment and personal visits.

Sustaining that growth, however, will also require continued investment in logistics infrastructure. In a report, the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) identified modern warehousing as one of Central Asia’s biggest untapped opportunities, estimating demand for nearly 2 million square meters of new warehouse space and investment needs of up to $1.5 billion.

EDB Chief Economist Evgeny Vinokurov said in an interview with The Astana Times that Kazakhstan is particularly well positioned to capitalize on the trend due to its location at the intersection of major Eurasian trade routes.

“Kazakhstan is particularly well-positioned. Where North-South and East-West routes intersect, synergies emerge. We see at least three major logistics nodes: Almaty, Astana and Shymkent with strong potential for warehouse development,” he said.

But transport is no longer the whole story

Among the major service categories, telecommunications, computer and information services recorded the fastest growth, rising 35.6% to $1.4 billion. Together with transport and travel, the three categories generated nearly 78% of Kazakhstan’s total services export revenue.

The biggest breakthrough came from computer services. Their exports climbed 36% to $1.1 billion, surpassing the $1 billion mark for the first time. Even excluding digital asset mining, which accounted for $367.6 million, computer services exports reached $775.1 million, reflecting continued expansion of Kazakhstan’s technology sector.

The milestone also fulfills a strategic objective set several years ago. In his 2023 State of the Nation Address, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for Kazakhstan’s IT services exports to reach $1 billion by 2026, identifying digital industries as one of the country’s future growth engines. The latest figures indicate that the target has effectively been achieved ahead of schedule.

Much of that growth has been supported by Astana Hub, whose resident companies exported IT services worth $681 million in 2025 to 111 countries, underscoring the expanding global footprint of Kazakhstan’s technology sector. According to previously reported data, the innovation hub is now home to more than 1,700 companies and continues to serve as the country’s primary platform for technology exports. Maintaining that momentum, however, may prove more important than reaching the milestone itself.

Computer services exports also remain highly concentrated geographically. Astana accounted for more than 90% of the country’s total, exporting around $1 billion worth of computer services in 2025. The concentration reflects the capital’s growing technology ecosystem, centered around Astana Hub and the newly launched International AI Center Alem.ai. Together, Astana and Almaty generated more than 96% of Kazakhstan’s computer services exports.

The figures suggest Kazakhstan is gradually broadening its export base. While transport continues to capitalize on the country’s strategic location at the crossroads of Eurasian trade routes, digital services increasingly demonstrate its ability to compete through innovation, technology and human capital.

The shift also reflects broader changes in the global economy. According to the OECD, services generate more than two-thirds of global GDP and attract more than three-quarters of foreign direct investment in advanced economies. Increasingly, countries compete not only by exporting physical goods, but also by selling knowledge, software, financial services and other high-value expertise.

For Kazakhstan, that transformation carries significance beyond the technology sector. Expanding services exports is increasingly viewed as a key pillar of economic diversification, reducing dependence on commodities while creating higher-value jobs, boosting productivity and strengthening the country’s long-term competitiveness.

The momentum continued into 2026. During the first quarter, Kazakhstan’s services exports increased 14.1% year-on-year to $3.1 billion, while imports rose 8.8% to $3.3 billion. As export growth outpaced imports, the country’s services trade deficit narrowed by 34.5% to $219.1 million. Transport remained the largest contributor, with exports rising 20.7% to $1.6 billion, while travel-related services increased 10% to $559.5 million.

Services are central to economic transformation

While transport remains Kazakhstan’s largest services export today, the country’s fastest long-term growth is increasingly coming from digitally delivered services. That shift mirrors broader changes in the global economy. WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has described services as “the fastest growing component of world trade over the last two decades,” adding that the digital revolution has “super-charged this trend.”

“Services are now central to economic transformation in developing countries. That is why mainstreaming services into national development strategies is no longer optional. Services are a necessity for diversification, productivity and resilience,” she said.

According to the WTO’s latest forecasts, digitally delivered services are expected to grow by 5.6% in 2026, significantly outpacing transport services, whose growth is projected to slow to 1.8%.

For Kazakhstan, the trend signals that the country’s next stage of export growth may increasingly depend not only on moving goods across borders, but on exporting technology, innovation and specialized expertise. If transport reflects Kazakhstan’s geographic advantages, the rise of digital services points to something equally important: the country’s growing ability to export knowledge and compete in the global economy through human capital rather than natural resources alone.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Copper Output Places It Among World’s Top 10 Producers
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan ranked among the world’s 10 largest copper producers in 2025 after mining 710,000 tons of the metal, reinforcing its position in a market where demand is expected to accelerate as countries expand clean energy and digital infrastructure.

According to data from the Energy Institute (EI) and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Kazakhstan shared ninth place with Indonesia, with both countries producing 710,000 tons of copper last year.

Chile remained the world’s largest producer with 5.3 million tons, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo with 3.2 million tons and Peru with 2.7 million tons. China ranked fourth with 1.8 million tons, while Russia produced 1.3 million tons. The United States (US), Zambia and Australia also ranked ahead of Kazakhstan.

Together, the world’s 10 largest producers mined 18.39 million tons of copper in 2025, accounting for the bulk of global output, which reached 23 million tons, according to the Energy Institute.

Kazakhstan’s ranking comes as demand for copper continues to rise. According to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), global demand for the metal is projected to increase by more than 40% by 2040, driven by the expansion of renewable energy, electricity grids, electric vehicles and digital infrastructure. Meeting that demand could require around 80 new copper mines worldwide, underscoring growing concerns over future supply.

Copper is widely used in power transmission networks, electric motors, batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and other technologies underpinning the global energy transition. As a result, it has become one of the minerals increasingly classified as critical for economic security and industrial development.

The latest ranking also aligns with Kazakhstan’s broader strategy of positioning itself as a reliable supplier of critical minerals. As previously reported by The Astana Times, the country has expanded partnerships with the European Union, the United Kingdom, the US and other international partners to attract investment, boost geological exploration and strengthen critical mineral supply chains.

With global competition for critical minerals intensifying, Kazakhstan’s place among the world’s top copper producers reinforces the country’s growing role in supplying one of the key resources needed for the energy transition and advanced manufacturing.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan Join Forces to Pursue New Export Markets in Syria and Iraq
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are expanding their economic partnership beyond bilateral trade by jointly targeting new export markets in Syria and Iraq, reflecting a broader strategy to position Central Asia as a supplier to rapidly growing reconstruction and import-dependent economies. Business delegations from the two countries are expected to travel to Aleppo in late September and Erbil, the capital of Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, in early October following agreements reached during the Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan Business Forum in Tashkent on Aug. 5, Uzdaily reported.

The initiative signals a shift in regional trade strategy. Rather than competing for overseas markets, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are increasingly seeking to combine their industrial strengths to reach destinations where demand is being driven by reconstruction and infrastructure development.

Chairman of Uzbekistan’s Chamber of Commerce and Industry Davron Vakhabov proposed assembling a delegation of 20 to 30 companies for Aleppo, where a trilateral business forum involving Uzbek, Kazakh and Syrian businesses is planned. The visit will coincide with the official opening of Uzbekistan’s trade house, which began operating in March.

Syria’s reconstruction creates demand

According to representatives of Uzbekistan’s trade house in Syria, the country is experiencing growing demand for food products and construction materials as reconstruction accelerates following years of conflict. Officials estimate that around six million housing units are planned, creating sustained demand for building supplies.

Among the products in demand are construction materials, sunflower oil and meat products. Kazakh manufacturers could also benefit from exports of galvanized steel and other metal products, which are not produced in Uzbekistan. One example of the emerging cooperation is sunflower oil manufactured in Uzbekistan using raw materials supplied from Kazakhstan.

Kanat Sharlapayev, chairman of the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, said Syria deserves separate attention as a destination for Kazakh businesses, noting that Atameken already has contacts with a Qatari holding company involved in reconstruction projects there.

“This is an extremely important direction for both Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan,” he said.

Iraq as a regional gateway

The second joint business mission will focus on Erbil, a major commercial hub in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region. According to forum participants, around 180 entrepreneurs from the region visited Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan roughly three weeks ago to explore business opportunities. Sharlapayev noted that much of the imported goods entering Iraq’s Kurdistan Region are subsequently distributed across Iraq or re-exported to neighboring Türkiye and Iran, making the region an attractive entry point into a broader market.

Forum participants estimated Iraq’s annual imports at around $95 billion, while nearly all of its $109 billion in exports come from crude oil, underscoring the country’s dependence on imported manufactured goods. Iraqi partners have already expressed interest in importing seven to eight truckloads of Uzbek confectionery products every month, along with porcelain tiles produced in Uzbekistan’s Fergana Region. Business representatives also highlighted opportunities to export semi-finished products, such as unpackaged household chemicals and polyethylene granules, allowing final processing and packaging to take place locally while reducing production costs.

Looking beyond traditional markets

Vakhabov also contrasted the challenges of entering mature European markets with the opportunities emerging in countries undergoing reconstruction.

“No one is waiting for your products in Germany because the standards are extremely strict. But in countries where domestic production was disrupted for many years, such as Syria and Iraq, the situation is stabilizing, creating significant opportunities,” he said, pointing to Kazakhstan’s rapidly growing exports to Afghanistan as an example of how businesses from Central Asia are finding new demand in neighboring emerging markets.

The trend is reflected in recent trade figures. Bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and Afghanistan reached $342.4 million in the first four months of 2026, up 2.3 times compared to the same period a year earlier. Kazakh exports accounted for $338.5 million, driven primarily by shipments of wheat, wheat-rye flour, sunflower oil and other agricultural products. Kazakhstan has also set a long-term goal of increasing exports to Afghanistan to $3 billion, while discussions are underway to expand banking cooperation to facilitate trade and settlements between the two countries.

Logistics as a competitive advantage

According to Vakhabov, approximately 350,000 Turkish trucks transit Uzbekistan every year and often return empty. Because Turkish drivers do not require visas to cross Turkmenistan, these vehicles could be used to transport Central Asian exports to Syria and Iraq. According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Uzbekistan, shipments along this route cost between $2,900 and $3,500 and take eight to ten days, compared with $6,000-$8,000 for conventional transport routes.

The planned business missions come as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan continue to deepen their strategic economic partnership. The two countries have set a target of increasing bilateral trade to $10 billion. Trade turnover exceeded $4.1 billion last year, supported by new commercial agreements worth more than 80 billion tenge (US$146 million) signed in July, as well as ongoing work on cross-border industrial cooperation centers, trade hubs and transport corridors.

Rather than focusing solely on expanding trade between themselves, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are increasingly positioning their partnership as a platform for jointly entering third-country markets. The upcoming business missions to Syria and Iraq represent one of the clearest examples yet of that strategy in practice.

World.title: Kazakhstan Takes First Step Toward Air Taxi Era With Passenger eVTOL Flight
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has taken its first practical step toward urban air mobility after a passenger completed the country’s first flight aboard an autonomous electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, signaling that the country’s air taxi ambitions are beginning to move beyond government plans into real-world testing.

According to the Committee of Civil Aviation (CCA), the EH216-S, a two-seat autonomous aircraft developed by Chinese manufacturer EHang for short-distance passenger transport, carried a passenger during a demonstration flight over a specially designated area in Astana as part of the Games of the Future 2026 on Aug. 6, marking Kazakhstan’s first-ever passenger eVTOL flight.

The electric aircraft can travel up to 35 kilometers at speeds of up to 130 kilometers per hour and is designed to operate without a pilot onboard.

The demonstration follows a series of policy announcements made earlier this year. In May, the government outlined plans to develop an urban air mobility ecosystem, including regulations for eVTOL aircraft, vertiports and unmanned air traffic management, while targeting the launch of pilot air taxi routes between Alatau, Almaty and Konayev as early as 2027.

The CCA said the first phase could include demonstration and sightseeing routes lasting between five and 30 minutes over Kazakhstan’s natural, cultural and historical landmarks. In the longer term, authorities see autonomous aircraft supporting emergency medical response, medicine deliveries, firefighting and logistics—applications where speed and rapid deployment are critical—alongside passenger transportation.

Beyond operations, Kazakhstan also plans to localize production of passenger eVTOL aircraft through an international partnership. If implemented, the initiative could position the country not only as an early adopter of advanced air mobility technologies but also as a regional manufacturing hub for an industry that

remains in its early stages globally.

The Ministry of Transport, with other government agencies, is developing the legal and infrastructure framework needed to introduce urban air mobility. Legislative amendments have already been adopted to regulate the operation of eVTOL aircraft, vertiports and unmanned air traffic management systems, laying the groundwork for the safe integration of these technologies into Kazakhstan’s transport network.

Unlike helicopters, eVTOL aircraft rely on electric propulsion, making them quieter and potentially less expensive to operate over short distances. Industry experts view the technology as part of a broader shift toward Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) — a new transportation system intended to complement rather than replace conventional road and air transport.

Several countries, including the United Arab Emirates, China and the United States, are already conducting pilot programs or preparing for commercial eVTOL services, although widespread deployment remains several years away. Initial applications worldwide are expected to focus on airport transfers, tourism, emergency medical services and connecting remote communities before broader urban deployment.

While commercial passenger services remain several years away and will require further testing and regulatory development, the demonstration marks Kazakhstan’s transition from planning to practical experimentation with technologies that could eventually reshape short-distance transportation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Sustainable Aviation Fuel Industry With Alatau Pilot Project
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan took a step toward entering the emerging market for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) after signing a memorandum with Hong Kong-based Full Vision Capital to explore building an integrated production ecosystem in Alatau, a project that could position the country within the global aviation industry’s decarbonization efforts.

The memorandum, signed on Aug.4 following a meeting between Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Full Vision Capital founder Dr. Peter Lee, outlines plans to study the creation of a complete SAF value chain from cultivating agricultural feedstock to processing and producing aviation fuel. The partners will also assess opportunities to deploy smart energy technologies and nickel-hydrogen energy storage systems to support renewable energy integration.

The agreement brings together the Alatau City Authority, Kazakhstan’s Ministries of Energy, Agriculture and Transport, and Full Vision Capital under the Green Kazakhstan initiative.

Speaking during the meeting, Bektenov said Alatau’s special legal regime creates favorable conditions for international investors.

“The Constitutional Law on the Special Legal Regime of Alatau City provides legal certainty, stable tax conditions and a one-stop-shop mechanism for investors. Alatau can become a pilot platform for localizing technologies and your development expertise,” he said.

Lee described the initiative as the beginning of a long-term partnership focused on sustainable urban development.

“We hope to introduce innovative technologies that will help Alatau and Kazakhstan more broadly establish a new international benchmark for sustainable urban development,” he said.

Why sustainable aviation fuel matters

The project reflects a broader global shift as aviation seeks to reduce carbon emissions. Unlike electric aircraft, which remain impractical for most commercial flights, sustainable aviation fuel is widely viewed as one of the few near-term solutions capable of significantly lowering emissions from existing aircraft without requiring major changes to airport infrastructure or airline fleets.

International airlines are also facing growing regulatory pressure to increase SAF use, particularly in Europe, where blending mandates are gradually taking effect. Those requirements are expected to drive long-term demand for new fuel suppliers outside traditional markets.

For Kazakhstan, which possesses extensive agricultural resources and is seeking to diversify its economy beyond conventional energy exports, SAF represents an opportunity to move further up the value chain by producing higher-value, low-carbon fuels rather than exporting raw materials alone.

Alatau as a testbed for green technologies

The project also reinforces Alatau’s role as Kazakhstan’s flagship innovation city. Established under a special legal framework offering tax incentives and simplified administrative procedures, Alatau has been positioned as a testing ground for advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and clean energy solutions.

Rather than focusing solely on fuel production, the memorandum envisions a broader ecosystem combining renewable energy, energy storage and industrial processing, suggesting Kazakhstan aims to integrate green manufacturing with wider urban development.

The memorandum does not commit the parties to immediate construction, but it signals Kazakhstan’s intention to explore participation in a sector expected to expand rapidly over the coming decades. It also reflects a broader shift in the country’s investment strategy from attracting capital for traditional energy projects toward developing industries linked to the global energy transition.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Launches New World Tour
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen has announced a new world tour titled DiMENSIONS, presenting the project as his most personal stage production to date and the latest step in an international career that has steadily expanded beyond music.

According to the artist’s official website, the new program is designed not as a journey through time and space, but as an exploration of the person behind the performer, revealing the different dimensions of Qudaibergen as a singer, composer, producer and individual.

“The world has long known him for his unique voice. This concert is intended to reveal the person behind that voice, presenting a deeper and more complete portrait of the artist,” reads the statement.

Organizers describe the production as a narrative built around emotions, memories and defining moments in Qudaibergen’s life. Rather than presenting isolated episodes, the performance seeks to unite them into a single story shaped by his connection to Kazakhstan, personal values, artistic ambitions and ongoing search for self-understanding.

The announcement comes as Qudaibergen continues to expand his international presence through performances and cultural initiatives. Last October, he performed to a sold-out audience of 15,000 at Mexico City’s Palacio de los Deportes following his first solo concert at the Auditorio Nacional, further strengthening his popularity across Latin America.

His international recognition has also extended beyond the stage. In December, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) appointed Qudaibergen as a Global Goodwill Ambassador in recognition of his humanitarian engagement. Earlier this year, he received the Ambassador of Turkic World Culture order, TURKSOY’s highest distinction, honoring his contribution to promoting Turkic cultural heritage. He was also named Cultural Figure of the Year at Kazakhstan’s People’s Favorite awards.

The announcement also reflects Qudaibergen’s evolving position in Kazakhstan’s cultural diplomacy. While his vocal performances first brought him international recognition, recent years have seen his role expand through humanitarian initiatives, international cultural awards and appearances across new markets. As his audience continues to grow across Asia, Europe and Latin America, Qudaibergen has become one of Kazakhstan’s most visible cultural representatives abroad.

World.title: Azerbaijan FM visits Ukraine amid thaw in Russia ties
World.content:
Azerbaijani FM visits Ukraine

Azerbaijan‘s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov paid an official visit to Ukraine on 6 August. It was the first visit by an Azerbaijani foreign minister to Kyiv since the start of Russia‘s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Bayramov began his visit with a trip to Irpin, where he viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones and laid a wreath at a memorial to fallen defenders at Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. He also held meetings with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, President Volodymyr Zelensky, Head of the Presidential Office Andriy Yermak, Defence Intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov and National Security and Defence Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

One of the most notable announcements was Azerbaijan’s stated willingness to supply Ukraine with natural gas if needed. The two sides also discussed the possible use of Ukraine’s underground gas storage facilities to strengthen regional energy security.

These developments are significant both regionally and internationally, particularly in the context of Azerbaijan’s relations with Russia. In mid-July, Bayramov met Sergei Lavrov in Moscow and said the “difficult period” in bilateral relations was over and that ties had been fully normalised. A few weeks later, in Kyiv, he reaffirmed Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, while also signalling Baku’s interest in expanding energy cooperation.

The visit illustrates Baku’s multi-vector foreign policy. While maintaining dialogue with Russia, Azerbaijan has continued to provide humanitarian assistance to Ukraine and has expressed its readiness to support the country in the energy sector if required.

Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan🇦🇿 @Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @IhorKlymenkoUA, Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The importance of maintaining peace, stability and sustainable… pic.twitter.com/k59QcGZuU1 — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

Symbolic and practical significance of the Irpin visit

Irpin was one of the towns where the Russian advance on Kyiv was halted in 2022. Hundreds of civilians were killed during the fighting, and more than 70% of the town’s housing stock was destroyed.

Azerbaijan has contributed to Irpin’s reconstruction.

The minister laid flowers at the bust of academician Zarifa Aliyeva in the park named after her, and visited the Zarifa Aliyeva Linguistic Lyceum and Irpin Central City Polyclinic, both rebuilt with Azerbaijan’s support. He was also briefed on future reconstruction projects, including plans to restore the town’s House of Culture.

In his statement, Zelensky said Bayramov had visited a school, a hospital and a rehabilitation centre supported by Azerbaijan. The visit to Irpin was seen as a demonstration of humanitarian solidarity with Ukraine, as well as Azerbaijan’s willingness to share its experience in rebuilding territories recovered from occupation.

I received Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, @Bayramov_Jeyhun. This is the Minister’s first visit to Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. He began his visit in Irpin, where he visited a school, a hospital, and a rehabilitation center supported by… pic.twitter.com/7HTLIaz3EF — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) August 6, 2026

The visit to a town devastated by Russian forces, together with Bayramov’s review of reconstruction efforts and Azerbaijan’s continued support, was seen as underscoring Baku’s intention to reaffirm its longstanding position despite the “normalisation” of relations with Moscow, particularly its commitment to the principle of territorial integrity.

Following the official welcoming ceremony at the Foreign Ministry, Bayramov and Sybiha viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones. They then laid a wreath at the Memorial to the Fallen Defenders of Ukraine and observed a moment of silence in their honour.

Meetings and gas supply pledge

During expanded talks with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, the two sides discussed their strategic partnership, trade, energy, transport, humanitarian cooperation and regional security. Bayramov reiterated the need for an early end to the fighting and a diplomatic settlement based on international law, while reaffirming Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

He said Azerbaijan’s total humanitarian assistance to Ukraine had exceeded 50 million US dollars. Bayramov also highlighted reconstruction projects in Irpin and rehabilitation programmes for children.

During his meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the discussions focused on Russian attacks, the situation in the Black Sea, the disruption of grain export routes, defence cooperation, and cooperation in the energy, oil and gas, and agricultural sectors.

Zelensky thanked Azerbaijan for its energy and humanitarian assistance, as well as for maintaining constructive dialogue. Bayramov, in turn, spoke about the post-conflict situation in the South Caucasus and reconstruction efforts in the territories regained by Azerbaijan.

As part of his official visit to Ukraine 🇺🇦, FM of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 @Bayramov_Jeyhun visited the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Kyiv.



The Minister met with the Embassy staff and received a comprehensive briefing on the Mission’s activities. pic.twitter.com/UPqN5Hn9rx — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

At a joint press conference, particular attention was drawn to Bayramov’s remarks on possible gas supplies: “If the need arises, we will be ready to supply gas to our friendly Ukraine.”

He highlighted SOCAR’s long-standing presence on the Ukrainian market, as well as the importance of Ukraine’s underground gas storage system – the largest in Europe – for regional energy security.

The statement can be seen as signalling Azerbaijan’s willingness to contribute to the diversification of Ukraine’s energy supplies, while also supporting alternative routes for Caspian gas exports to Europe. Against the backdrop of Russia’s strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Ukraine, Baku’s offer also underscores the importance of competition and diversification in the energy sector.

During meetings with Kyrylo Budanov and Ihor Klymenko, the sides also discussed regional and international security, as well as prospects for energy cooperation. They reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of state sovereignty, territorial integrity and the inviolability of internationally recognised borders.

Expert: “Azerbaijan will continue to provide Ukraine with political, economic and humanitarian support”

lkhan Shahinoglu, head of the Atlas Research Centre and a political commentator considered close to the Azerbaijani authorities, wrote that the visit is being closely watched by Russia:

The Kremlin will closely monitor Jeyhun Bayramov’s meetings in Kyiv. Azerbaijan’s partnership with any country is an exclusive sovereign right, and no other state has the right to interfere in that process.

At the same time, Russia, which is waging a war of conquest against Ukraine, closely watches those who cooperate with Kyiv. President Ilham Aliyev‘s response to the same question from Ukrainian journalist Gordon, asked at the Shusha Global Media Forum two years in a row – that ‘Ukraine should not reconcile itself to occupation’ – angered chauvinistic circles in Russia. They believe Azerbaijan should accept the annexation of Crimea and the occupation of Ukrainian territories.

Just as Jeyhun Bayramov visited Moscow some time ago, he has now travelled to Kyiv. Ukraine is Azerbaijan’s partner, and Baku will continue to provide it with political, economic and humanitarian support.”

World.title: Giga Avaliani case: Two more arrested 10 months after Georgian teacher’s murder
World.content:
Two more arrested in Giga Avaliani murder case

Two more suspects have been identified in the high-profile murder case of a 28-year-old teacher in Georgia. On 5 August 2026, two teenage girls – Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili – were arrested.

Giga Avaliani, a mathematics teacher, was killed in October 2025. Five people have already been convicted over his murder, while the trial of a sixth defendant is still under way. With the arrest of the two girls, the total number of suspects in the case has risen to eight – all of them minors.

The arrests of Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili, after several convictions had already been secured, mark an unexpected and significant development in the Giga Avaliani case.

Nia Imnadze was one of Giga Avaliani’s former students and the girlfriend of the principal defendant, Aleksandre Gabashvili. Prosecutors accuse her of incitement to commit the crime.

According to local media, Anastasia Beruashvili is a friend of both Nia Imnadze and another convicted defendant, Giorgi Rikadze. She has been charged with failing to report the crime.

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics tutor, was returning home late on 1 October 2025 when he was attacked outside his apartment building. He fell into a coma following the assault and died on 24 October without regaining consciousness. Investigators say the attack was motivated by jealousy and what they describe as “unwanted communication with a girl”. The defendants have given a similar account. According to their version of events, Avaliani sent sexually explicit messages to his student Nia Imnadze, who told her boyfriend, prompting him to confront the teacher. Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, rejects that account. She says Nia had been skipping lessons and that Avaliani informed the girl’s mother, angering the student. According to Kupatadze, the attack was planned afterwards.

The Giga Avaliani case has become one of Georgia’s most high-profile criminal cases in recent years. Much of the public attention surrounding it has been driven by Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, who campaigned for what she said should be a thorough and impartial investigation. Her efforts also helped generate significant public pressure over the handling of the case.

From the outset, Kupatadze maintained that Nia Imnadze bore primary responsibility for what had happened and repeatedly called for her arrest. The recent detention of the two girls has therefore raised new questions.

But the key question remains: if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, why were the two girls not arrested earlier? Was their detention the result of new evidence, or did it come only after sustained public pressure and Eka Kupatadze’s campaign?

Detention of two girls

Both girls were arrested late on the night of 5 August, in what appeared to be coordinated operations. News of the arrests first emerged through a video of Nia Imnadze’s detention, which was released by her lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili.

The footage is deeply distressing. It shows a large number of police officers arriving at Nia’s home. Her mother, visibly distressed, pounds on the front door, shouting: “Come in, all of you!”, “Maniacs!”, “Murderers!”, “Do you know that Niako is innocent?!”

The girl’s father, meanwhile, tells the police: “You are going to make me do something the whole of Georgia will be talking about. If you treat my child so unjustly, I will do it.”

Police officers try to calm the distraught parents.

“Why are you taking my child? On what grounds? What does the court order say?!” the mother asks.

“The lawyer has reviewed the court order,” one of the officers replies.

“Giorgi, on what grounds are they arresting her?” the mother asks the lawyer.

“On the basis of a court order containing only formal wording, nothing specific,” the lawyer replies.

Nia sits in the hallway on a sofa, curled up with her face buried in her hands. The video is being filmed by her lawyer, who occasionally strokes her hair.

Shortly after the video was released, reports began circulating on social media that the second girl, Anastasia Beruashvili, had also been detained. No footage of her arrest was made public, but the Ministry of Internal Affairs later confirmed that she had been taken into custody.

During her arrest, Nia Imnadze became unwell and was taken to hospital, where she spent the night. On 6 August, she was transferred to a pre-trial detention centre. Anastasia Beruashvili was also taken there.

Minors charged in Giga Avaliani's murder case in Georgia – read more Five people have already been convicted in connection with Giga Avaliani’s murder: Aleksandre Gabashvili – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. He was the principal defendant in the case and was found guilty of organising a group assault and intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm as part of a group, resulting in the victim’s death. Giorgi Rikadze – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. A friend of Aleksandre Gabashvili, he was convicted on the same charges. Demetere Chikovani – sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was convicted of attempted intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm in the Avaliani case, as well as organising group violence in connection with the case and four other incidents. Ani Naskidashvili – sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. She was found guilty of failing to report a particularly serious crime. Another minor – sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He was convicted of giving false testimony. The nature of the false statements has not been disclosed. His case was heard behind closed doors, lawyers involved in the proceedings are bound by a non-disclosure order, and the teenager’s parents have declined to speak to the media. According to TV Pirveli, the boy is named Luka Klatkin. Giorgi Malania – arrested in July 2026 and charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. Malania is the son of a former senior Interior Ministry official, who served as deputy interior minister between 2016 and 2019. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered.

Eka Kupatadze’s reaction

“Georgia has won another battle against the killers of a healthy, innocent and talented young man – Giga Avaliani!” Eka Kupatadze said in response to the girls’ arrests.

Giga Avaliani’s family has always maintained that those who carried out the attack were not the only people involved. They have consistently called on investigators to identify and prosecute all those who may have played a role in the crime.

The family has paid particular attention to the alleged role of the two girls. Eka Kupatadze has repeatedly said that they knew the attack was being planned.

Until recently, however, prosecutors had taken no apparent action against additional suspects, prompting repeated criticism of the investigation from Avaliani’s family.

Kupatadze even appealed for help to Ekaterine Khvedelidze, the wife of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling party and widely regarded as Georgia’s “informal ruler”. Khvedelidze replied to her letter, expressing sympathy and support for the mother who had lost her son.

“As far as I am aware, the investigation has not yet been completed. I am confident that the relevant state authorities will see it through to the end and that all the circumstances will be thoroughly examined, so that no question surrounding the terrible tragedy that has befallen you remains unanswered,” Ekaterine Khvedelidze wrote in her reply.

Formal charges

On the evening of 6 August, both girls were formally charged.

Nia Imnadze at the time of her arrest

Nia Imnadze has been charged with incitement to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm committed by a group. The offence carries a maximum sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment.

Anastasia Beruashvili has been charged with failing to report a particularly serious crime, an offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

Under Georgian law, sentences imposed on minors are reduced by one quarter.

“The investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs under the supervision of the Prosecutor’s Office established that, in September 2025, Nia Imnadze began taking mathematics lessons with Giga Avaliani. The accused, Nia Imnadze, told her friends Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Malania that her teacher, Giga Avaliani, had allegedly shown her excessive attention. By doing so, the accused incited Aleksandre Gabashvili to attack Giga Avaliani together with his accomplices,” the Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

According to the statement, Aleksandre Gabashvili, together with Giorgi Rikadze, Giorgi Malania and Demetere Chikovani, “decided to act on that incitement.”

What defence says

The defence has denied all the charges.

According to Nia Imnadze’s lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili, there is no evidence in the case to support the allegation that she incited the attack.

The lawyer also rejected reports that prosecutors had obtained data and messages from Meta, and that the arrests followed an examination of those materials.

“Criminal proceedings cannot be based on suspicion. They must be based on lawfully obtained evidence, and no other standard can override that principle,” Lekishvili told reporters.

Ketevan Vardanashvili, the lawyer representing Anastasia Beruashvili, made similar arguments. She said Anastasia had not witnessed any crime and that she and Nia Imnadze had seen each other only once, for a few minutes.

“They had no friendship and no contact,” the lawyer said.

As for Anastasia’s relationship with the convicted defendant Giorgi Rikadze, Vardanashvili said that “even if she was his girlfriend, that does not mean she had any knowledge of the crime.”

Complaint or incitement?

The arrests of the two girls have sparked intense debate on social media. Many commentators agree that everyone responsible for Giga Avaliani’s death should be held accountable and that justice should be served. Many have also expressed sympathy for Eka Kupatadze.

At the same time, some have questioned the actions of the law enforcement authorities. They have asked whether prosecutors have sufficiently strong evidence against the two girls, particularly Nia Imnadze, who faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.

The Prosecutor’s Office statement says only that Nia Imnadze told her friends that Giga Avaliani had allegedly shown her excessive attention. It does not explain whether she knew an attack was being planned or whether she urged her boyfriend to take any specific action.

“Does complaining to friends amount to incitement?” some social media users have asked.

Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Odesa in summer 2026: Life between sea and war. VIDEO
World.content:
Beaches, bomb-damaged homes and explosions in broad daylight. In the summer of 2026, Odesa is caught between its traditional seaside resort atmosphere and the constant threat of Russian attacks. While some people relax by the sea and stroll through the city centre, others sift through the rubble left by the latest strike.

JAMnews visited Odesa to show what life in the city looks like today.

Odesa and the surrounding region remain frequent targets of Russian strikes. Residential neighbourhoods, critical infrastructure and port facilities have all come under attack.

Russia has carried out combined attacks using drones and missiles, seeking to overwhelm Ukraine‘s air defence systems.

The impact of these attacks is visible across the city. Residential buildings have been damaged, windows blown out and flats destroyed. Strikes have also hit Odesa’s historic centre, including heritage buildings and universities.

Ports in Odesa Region, along with the logistics hubs and warehouses that support them, are also regularly targeted. Attacks on port infrastructure have disrupted Ukraine’s transport network and Black Sea export routes.

The strikes often occur in broad daylight, when the streets are busy, cafés and shops are open, and beaches are filled with residents and visitors. At any moment, the familiar sounds of the city can be interrupted by explosions, air defence fire or the buzz of attack drones.

On several occasions, missiles have been intercepted directly over the coastline while beaches were crowded with people.

Today, it is possible to spend the day at the beach and the night in a bomb shelter.

World.title: Armenia’s growing number of large families: Statistics, one couple’s story and expert insights
World.content:
Surge in large families in Armenia

In recent years, more young families in Armenia have chosen to have a third or even fourth child. According to the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, around 8,300 third and subsequent children were born in 2018. By 2023, that figure had risen to more than 12,400, before easing slightly to around 12,000 in 2024. Overall, the number of third and subsequent births increased by about 45% between 2018 and 2024. Full-year data for 2025 are not yet available, although figures up to September show that 8,070 third and subsequent children had been born.

Experts cite a range of reasons why families choose to have larger families. Conversations with parents of three or more children suggest there is no single explanation, but the most common responses include: “Two children didn’t feel enough“, “We wanted a child of the opposite sex“, and “We were thinking about the country’s future.”

“We planned to have a large family, regardless of state support”

Vanuհi and Tigran married in 2013. For seven years, they were unable to have children. Eventually, they turned to in vitro fertilisation (IVF). In 2021, they became parents to triplets – a girl and two boys.

“We were asked how many children we wanted. We could have chosen one or two. But we decided to take the risk and become parents of triplets, even though we knew the risks were higher,” Vanuhi says.

Parents celebrate their triplets’ birthday.

According to Vanuhi, both she and her husband grew up in large families. From the outset, they wanted a big family of their own – at least three children and, ideally, as many as six.

“I received so much love and care from my brothers and sisters that I found it hard to imagine a family with just one or two children. My parents are no longer alive, but I feel stronger and more complete because I have my brothers and sisters,” says Tigran Hovakimyan.

The couple raised the triplets on their own, without relying on grandparents or other relatives. When the children turned three, they started nursery. Then came another surprise: Vanuhi became pregnant with their fourth child.

Vanuhi says they were astonished, as doctors had told them they had virtually no chance of conceiving naturally.

“We now have four young children. We both work and can provide them with good food, clothes and opportunities for leisure. We also receive state benefits. Because we had triplets, the government counts each of them as a third child and pays 50,000 drams (about $137) per child each month. We now receive an additional 50,000 drams for our fourth child, as well as 30,000 drams (about $82) because my wife is temporarily unable to work while on maternity leave,” Tigran explains.

He says that part of the money is deposited into savings accounts opened in the children’s names, while the rest is spent on their activities and recreation. The family has bought a large inflatable swimming pool for the garden of their home, as well as bicycles, and the children also attend paid extracurricular classes and sports clubs.

Family vacation.

The couple are also setting aside modest savings to help ensure all four children can receive a good education.

“You know, many families have children because of state benefits or other government support. We don’t judge them, but our story is different. We always planned to have three or more children without relying on state assistance. It wasn’t something that influenced our decision. In the early years of our marriage, both my wife and I worked several jobs at the same time so that we could afford to buy a large house, hoping one day we’d have a big family,” Tigran says.

“If we were still paying off a mortgage, we would probably depend on the child benefits that families receive until their children turn six,” Vanuhi adds.

How state encourages higher birth rates

In 2022, Armenia introduced a state support programme under which families receive a monthly payment of 50,000 drams ($137) for a third and each subsequent child until the child reaches the age of six.

By 2025, more than 45,000 children were covered by the scheme.

Under a separate programme, the state repays part of a family’s mortgage principal following the birth of a child. The subsidy amounts to:

up to 500,000 drams ($1,377) for a second child,

for a second child, up to 1 million drams ($2,754) for a third child,

for a third child, up to 1.5 million drams ($4,132) for a fourth child.

The scheme applies to mortgages that meet certain social eligibility criteria and is regarded as one of the government’s key measures to encourage higher birth rates.

In addition, amendments to Armenia’s Labour Code that came into force in 2026 introduced new benefits for working parents. In particular, parents with children under the age of 12 are now entitled to a “parental hour” – a shorter working day without any reduction in pay:

parents with one or two children can finish work 30 minutes earlier;parents with three or more children are entitled to a one-hour reduction in their working day.

The benefit can be used by either the mother or the father.

Families also receive a one-off payment of 500,000 drams ($1,377) for every child, including their first.

More recently, the government approved a new housing programme for families raising six or more children under the age of 18, an initiative proposed by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs.

“Under this programme, large families will be able to purchase property or build a detached house in any regional community in Armenia with 100% state funding,” ministry spokesperson Gayane Karagezyan said.

The programme does not cover property purchases in Yerevan, however, reflecting the government’s policy of promoting balanced regional development.

“More targeted measures are needed”

Demographer Rubina Grigoryan says the government’s efforts to encourage larger families have produced some results. While the increase in births is evident, she believes it is still not enough.

“New, more targeted programmes are needed. They should be tailored separately for Yerevan and the regions. They should also go beyond financial assistance. The recently introduced ‘parental hour’ is one example of an effective incentive. I believe more should be done to expand access to nurseries and kindergartens. Just look at how many private childcare centres cater for children under the age of two. If the state increased the number of places in public childcare facilities, more women would consider having additional children.”

Grigoryan says attitudes towards large families have also become more positive in recent years. They are not only receiving greater state support but are also more valued by society.

“However, many of these families may face difficulties once their children grow older, particularly with the costs of education and other financial pressures. State support is available only until children reach the age of six. After that, families seem to be left without much assistance. This is something policymakers should also address. As for the recent rise in birth rates, I see one particularly significant factor. The increase in births between 2021 and 2023 was largely influenced by the aftermath of the Karabakh war. Many families decided to have children after the war, each for their own reasons – from a sense of responsibility towards those who died to a desire to help build a stronger country for the future,” Grigoryan says.

World.title: First digital bridge beneath Caspian Sea: How Sumqayit-Aktau cable reshapes Eurasia’s geostrategic landscape
World.content:
Sumqayit-Aktau cable reshapes Eurasia

Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan have completed a key milestone in the implementation of a Caspian Sea project, with the subsea section of the Sumqayit-Aktau Trans-Caspian fibre-optic cable now in place.

The roughly 380-km line is the first fibre-optic infrastructure to be laid on the bed of the Caspian Sea. With a capacity of more than 400 Tbps, the system is being developed by AzerTelecom International and Kazakhtelecom through their joint venture, CaspiLink B.V. The project is being financed entirely by the operators, without any state budget funding.

Offshore works began in July and were completed in early August. The connection of the onshore infrastructure and system testing are scheduled for the autumn, while commercial operations are expected to begin by the end of 2026. The project is more than a technical achievement. As one of the flagship components of Azerbaijan’s Digital Silk Way initiative, it strengthens the digital dimension of the Middle Corridor and has the potential to reshape regional data flows.

Technical and organisational aspects

The capacity of the fibre-optic cable significantly exceeds that of the existing terrestrial routes in the region. This provides the foundation for transmitting large volumes of data and supporting the development of cloud services and future artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The project is being implemented by AzerTelecom International, part of NEQSOL Holding, and Kazakhtelecom through an equal partnership under their joint venture, CaspiLink B.V. Registered in the Netherlands, the company is responsible for both the construction and future operation of the cable. The project is financed entirely with private funds, reducing its exposure to the political and bureaucratic risks associated with state funding. At the same time, its long-term success will depend on the commercial viability of the operators and the stability of the regional political environment.

Laying the cable along the Caspian seabed presented significant technical challenges, as no such operation had previously been carried out there. The route was designed to avoid anchorage areas and military exercise zones. Engineering surveys and environmental approvals were completed in 2025.

The cable was manufactured and tested in China before being shipped to Baku via Kazakhstan’s Kuryk port. Installation was carried out around the clock using a specialised vessel with a displacement of more than 20,000 tonnes. Around 70 specialists took part in the operation. The next phase will involve integrating the onshore landing stations and conducting system tests.

Although commercial operations are scheduled to begin by the end of 2026, the cable’s actual utilisation rates and transit volumes are unlikely to become clear before 2027.

Can Caspian cable provide alternative to Russia and Red Sea routes?

The answer is: to some extent, yes, but not entirely. At present, internet traffic from Central Asia and the South Caucasus largely relies on two main routes: via Russian networks to the north and via the subsea cable systems in the Red Sea and the Mediterranean to the south. In recent years, both have faced geopolitical and infrastructure-related risks, including sanctions, cable damage and network congestion. The Trans-Caspian cable helps reduce this dependence by creating an alternative route that bypasses Russia and Iran, connecting Europe via Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey, or linking eastwards through Kazakhstan to China.

Its impact, however, is unlikely to be immediate or comprehensive. The cable covers only the Aktau-Sumqayit section of the route. A fully functioning digital corridor will also require sufficient terrestrial network capacity in Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan, a well-developed network of data centres, and commercial agreements between telecom operators.

From a latency perspective, the Caspian route appears competitive. According to available data, round-trip signal latency between the two shores is around 3.7 milliseconds. However, the extent to which it strengthens digital sovereignty will depend on whether substantial volumes of traffic are rerouted through the new link and whether regional operators gain greater control over traffic routing.

For Central Asian states, the project offers an opportunity to reduce, at least partially, their dependence on Russian transit infrastructure. For the South Caucasus, it strengthens the region’s position as an emerging digital hub. Full digital independence, however, remains a distant prospect, as a significant share of traffic handled by major providers, as well as data flows between China and Europe, will continue to rely on established routes.

Synergy between Middle Corridor and Digital Silk Way

Combining freight transport and digital infrastructure within a single geographic corridor offers practical advantages. The Middle Corridor, or Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, has seen container traffic grow in recent years but continues to face constraints in competing with routes through Russia and other alternative corridors.

Adding a digital dimension makes the corridor more technologically advanced by enabling real-time transmission of logistics data, digitalising customs and border procedures, and accelerating insurance and financial transactions. Azerbaijan’s ambition to become a regional digital hub is closely linked to this synergy. Complementing existing energy pipelines, railways and seaports, the fibre-optic cable enhances the country’s appeal as a transit hub for data flows.

A realistic assessment, however, is warranted. Although Azerbaijan’s geographical location is advantageous, becoming a fully fledged digital hub will require large-scale data centres, affordable electricity, a highly skilled workforce and the presence of international cloud service providers. At present, these conditions have only been partially met. Strengthening terrestrial links with Georgia and Turkey, together with laying additional subsea cables across the Black Sea, would help unlock the full potential of the Digital Silk Way.

For Kazakhstan, further development of Aktau port and the modernisation of the country’s east-west digital infrastructure will be equally important. Ultimately, the benefits of this synergy will depend on both countries developing their respective infrastructure at a comparable pace.

Private funding model and risks

The advantages of delivering the project without state funding are clear. It reduces the risk of delays linked to political decision-making, places commercial incentives at the forefront and makes the project more transparent to international investors. CaspiLink B.V.’s registration in the Netherlands also provides greater legal certainty and a well-established framework for dispute resolution. The main vulnerabilities of the model stem from the financial position of the operators themselves and their political connections.

AzerTelecom is part of NEQSOL Holding, a privately owned business group with significant regional influence. Kazakhtelecom, by contrast, is a telecommunications operator with close ties to the Kazakh state.
