World.title: Teen gunman watched violent videos before killing seven in shooting rampage
World.content:
Graphic content WorldAsiaMass shooting Teen gunman watched violent videos before killing seven in shooting rampage Zach Hope Updated August 8, 2026 — 3:35am ,first published 3:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content. Bangkok: The Thai teenager who shot his grandparents dead at home and then killed at least five people at his high school had been watching online videos about mass shootings in the days leading up to his rampage, police say. Royal Thai Police spokesperson Trairong Piwpan said police were also examining the 14-year-old’s apparent taste for violent video games, while Prime Minister Anunit Charnvirakul, who visited the scene on Friday, said the boy had previously shown off the 9mm handgun that he used in the killings on Instagram. A man carries two girls outside the school. AP Photo/Wason Wanichakorn Piwpan said that after the boy killed his grandparents early on Friday morning, he went as usual to Debsirin Nonthaburi School, on the north-west outskirts of Bangkok, and sat in class until about 10am before pulling the concealed gun from his bag and opening fire.



He then went beyond the classroom and began firing in other areas of the school grounds, discharging more than 20 rounds. “He eventually reached the last building, where police officers had already begun securing and cordoning off the area,” Piwpan said. “At that point, the suspect took his own life.” Five teachers and administrators were left dead or dying and about 30 people, including students, were wounded by gunfire or while trying to escape, as many as 10 of them critically. Anutin said the gun was legally registered to the boy’s grandfather.



A schoolgirl is comforted outside the school. AP Photo/Sakchai Lalit “I understand that his grandfather and grandmother – his grandmother is a teacher – wanted him to do well in his studies, so they were quite strict and rigorous,” the prime minister said when asked by reporters about a possible motive. “We learned from the police interrogation ... of his close friend that he was experiencing stress in this area and complaining about it.” Piwpan said the shooter had also been complaining to friends about assignments and homework. People gather the Debsirin Nonthaburi School. AP Photo/Sakchai Lalit



Videos and photos shared on social media on Friday showed students running from classrooms, sheltering beneath desks and climbing through windows to stand on ledges. In one photo, a person can be seen lying on a stretcher outside an ambulance, while another is attended by a medic. An 18-year-old student at the school said he initially thought the sound of gunfire was firecrackers or someone banging an object. “I didn’t think it was a gun at first,” he said. “There were many shots: bang, bang, bang! Then it went quiet. Then it started again.” Loading



The Bangkok Post reported family members saying that he usually kept to himself and spent most of his free time playing video games. “We also found evidence that he had searched for and researched several past shooting incidents, and some of those searches appear to be connected to this case,” Piwpan said. Emergency worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, 47, said he arrived at the scene during the shooting and his team treated students with injuries to the back, chest and arms. They found a male teacher lying dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds in her chest and arm.



Police patrol outside the school. AP Photo/Wason Wanichakorn Police stand guard after the shooting. AP Photo/Sakchai Lalit He said he was called to treat the teenage shooter after hearing a final shot. “We rushed up and found that the perpetrator had shot himself in the right side of the head and collapsed. When we got up there, we checked his pulse, he still had one, so we started CPR,” he said. The suspect was then taken to the hospital, he said, where he later died.



Police search the suspect’s home. AP Photo/Sakchai Lalit The school has about 3100 students and 147 teachers, according to district authorities. The prime minister said he would discuss gun control with the country’s police chief. “This is terrible for something like this to happen,” Anutin told reporters. “I’m sad for those who died and sad for something like this to happen in our country.” Gun ownership is common in Thailand, but school mass killings are not.



The tragedy on Friday has triggered memories of the 2022 massacre at a daycare facility in north-east Thailand in which a former police officer killed 36 people, including 24 children. In 2020, a soldier stole weapons from a base and went on an hours-long rampage at a military camp and shopping mall in central Thailand, leaving almost 30 people dead. In February, a teacher died and a student was injured in southern Thailand’s Hat Yai district after a gunman opened fire at a school. Crisis support is available from Lifeline on 13 11 14. World.title: Four years overdue: The $4m social housing project left half-built
World.content:
NationalWAPublic housing Four years overdue: The $4m social housing project left half-built Indigo Lemay-Conway August 8, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Social housing in one of Perth’s southern suburbs has been left standing with no completion date in sight, even though it was due to be finished four years ago. The Hilton housing revitalisation project should have delivered 14 architecturally designed timber-frame social housing homes across the suburb by 2022. WA Greens leader Brad Pettitt at one of the half finished social homes in Hilton. Indigo Lemay-Conway But as of this month, construction has only begun – and stalled – on six of the Bernard Seeber Architects homes, with the remaining eight given a standard home-build design instead. WA Greens leader Brad Pettitt said the years of delays and multiple builders entering into liquidation resulted in half-finished homes that could have been used during the current housing crisis.



“There should be two families living in here now, but despite repeatedly pushing the state government on this, they’re failing to finish these properties,” Pettitt said. “Most depressingly, this is not an isolated incident. These are scattered all over this suburb, unfinished houses in the middle of a housing crisis. “The government needs to get on and actually finish this housing. It’s a really good design by a really great local architect, and it’s outrageous that it’s not completed.” Pettitt was the mayor of Fremantle when Bernard Seeber Architects won the design competition in 2017 for the social housing project. The 14 houses were to be built on seven different sites in Hilton and were anticipated to cost $200,000 per house at the time of the design.



But Pettitt says more than $4 million has been spent on the project to date. One of the half finished social homes designed by Bernard Seeber Architects in Hilton. Indigo Lemay-Conway “If they had delivered it on time, at the time, these would have been both inhabited and delivered much more cheaply than they have now. But instead, we’re going to spend way more than needed to be spent, whilst failing to even deliver these houses,” he said. “And you can see the amount of money that’s been wasted here on toilets and security, and all those things, rather than getting in and finishing houses.” Pettitt said the original builder assigned to the project went broke, as well as the builder who was hired after.



Small builder Jaguar Constructions currently holds the contract for the homes and told 9 News Perth it took over the project in 2024, but hasn’t worked on site since December. The company says it’s ready to finish the homes on a slim profit margin, but is waiting on the state government before construction can resume. Meanwhile, it’s covering the cost of maintaining the site. Hilton residents said it was frustrating to see homes sitting idle while so many people are searching for somewhere to live. “This has been going on for a number of years, and our poor neighbours on the street have been living right in front of a building site all this time with a young family, so that’s really unfortunate,” Louise Goodes said. “A lot of people are looking for somewhere to live now, and these houses could have been that answer.”



Rocky Terry said it was “totally ridiculous” the homes were still empty. “I’m a resident here, and Hilton’s a wonderful place to live, and these social houses here at the back have been going on for years,” Terry said. Hilton resident Louise Goodes. Indigo Lemay-Conway “It’s just totally ridiculous with the housing crisis that we haven’t got people in them. Now a lot of people say, ‘It’s good you haven’t got any neighbours’. No, I’d like to have neighbours, because that’s what we’re trying to do for people. And it’s got to happen. “They’re so close to finishing it now. I mean it’s past lockup, and they should be in there. They should have been in there a couple of years ago. It’s just not on. It’s just incompetence by someone.”



Bernard Seeber Architects director Georgina Willis said the idea behind the design for the homes was to create new infill density for rear strata lots at an affordable price. “The City of Fremantle granted special dispensation that allowed for two individual dwellings, so we set out to create inclusive, diverse, site-responsive architecture that is also humble and recognises the history and the culture of Hilton,” Willis said. She said the dwellings were meant to be built within a year of construction commencing. But despite the time it’s taken to get the buildings complete, the team would still like to see them come to fruition. “Ultimately, we’d like to see the completion of this project and whether that be this project or another new project with these sort of dwelling typologies, and that would be great if it’s in conjunction with the Department of Communities or Housing and Works,” she said.



An artist impression of what Bernard Seeber Architects social homes would have looked like. Bernard Seeber Architects “Because ultimately, it’s the community that benefits. The intention is to provide quality living for people who are vulnerable in communities and so Fremantle can benefit as well as the broader community.” Housing and Works Minister John Carey said the state government has delivered more than 4300 social and affordable homes to date. “In the vast majority of cases, projects are delivered without issue; however, we are not immune from the challenges in the construction market,” Carey said. He confirmed the original builders for the project went into administration and therefore had their build contracts terminated.



“Eight of the 14 Hilton homes were delivered under a new builder and tenanted after shifting to a design and construct model,” he said. “The Department of Housing and Works is also working with a new builder to complete the remaining six Hilton homes.” WA Premier Roger Cook said he didn’t know the details of the specific homes in Hilton, but there could be a range of reasons why a property might be vacant. “Firstly, it might be part of a broader development in the area. There may be other issues associated with the infrastructure for the area. So we’ll always make sure that we can get our social housing stock back into the market, so we can get roofs over the heads of people as soon as possible,” he said.

World.title: A hotel fit for a king, a tsar and Princess Di doesn’t disappoint
World.content:
★★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews A hotel fit for a king, a tsar and Princess Di doesn’t disappoint Michael Gebicki August 8, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel Mandarin Oriental Old Cataract, Aswan, Egypt Checking in The hotel is perched on granite cliffs overlooking islands in the River Nile. I like a hotel that takes things in its stride without batting an eyelid, and I arrive at this venerable hotel in possibly the most beat-up Peugeot station wagon on the planet. Sitting beside the driver is a villainous looking teenager in a white gallabiyah with a red keffiyeh, with his sidekick – a mischievous but persuasive youth of about 10 – who have together procured this inelegant conveyance for me. The driver realises there is no possibility of being allowed inside the cool, manicured domain I am about to enter, and so I am dumped unceremoniously outside the gate, but the fez-topped staff are an unflappable breed and praise be, my name is on the guest list.



The look 



My garden suite, a step-down from the river-facing suites, has brown curtains and a separate sitting area with a brown couch and a brown desk. The dimensions are palatial, the bathroom is huge but the furnishings and fabrics might have come from the parlour of a dowager aunt whose taste atrophied in the 1950s. There are two separate buildings with very different rooms. The Palace Wing is the original while the Nile Wing was built in 1961 to house Russian engineers working on the Aswan High Dam. These are functional rooms, and while they share the Palace Wing rooms’ riverside location, they lack their grandeur and opulence. In May, management of the hotel was transferred from the Accor group to Mandarin Oriental. The hotel is currently undergoing a renovation expected to last until July 2027, and some rooms and suites will be unavailable in the meantime. Expect lighter, prettier colours, panache and a style uplift from the Mandarin Oriental makeover. Food + drink When the current makeover is complete the hotel will have six dining venues. Al Saraya serves an Ottolenghi-does-Egyptian dishes, handmade pasta, fish from the Nile and the yummy treats of the Levantine kitchen. A sundowner on the Terrace, perched high above the river, almost justifies the room rate. The bar is terrific. You can imagine Winston Churchill here with brandy and a cigar, or Orson Welles with Rita Hayworth, but the barman isn’t telling any tales. Some of the former restaurants are closed for renovation. When the current makeover is complete the hotel will have six dining venues. Out + about



A felucca ride is the proper thing to do in the late afternoon. You’re probably only staying two nights, with an early morning visit to Abu Simbel taking up most of one day. There’s not too much to tempt you into Aswan, the souk is nothing special and the merchants are merciless hagglers. The unfinished obelisk and the Nubian Museum are within walking distance of the hotel. Just to the south, the Temple of Isis at the Philae temple complex was the last major temple built in the classical Pharaonic Egyptian style. A felucca ride around Elephantine Island is the proper thing to do in late afternoon. The hotel will arrange it, with a bar on board. You’ll be besieged by small children on surfboards who will anchor themselves limpet-like to your vessel singing “Frere Jacques” in expectation of a reward. The song hasn’t changed in 20 years. The verdict There’s not too much in Aswan to tempt you away from the hotel. The location is sublime, the suites in the Palace Wing are palatial, the pedigree is uplifting, but it feels frozen in a time warp. It needs to shake off the stodge, and the Mandarin Oriental group has what it takes.





Highlight Sunset cocktails on the Terrace overlooking the swan-like feluccas on the Nile. Lowlight Service was glacial in the breakfast room when I stayed under Accor management, but hopefully the Mandarin Oriental will inspire waitstaff to lift their game. The writer stayed at his own expense.

“This was a punishing victory... one that’s re-awakened the spirit within the whole group. “If they get into the top four with a double chance, look out. “They [Brisbane] took on a team that many had thought might be ready to challenge, and they showed them in no uncertain terms that they have a long way to go.” Work to do: Jack Gunston and Sam Mitchell’s Hawks. That was perhaps exactly the motivation the Lions needed to rebound from their 76-point capitulation against the Blues last week, after they were heavily criticised for their lack of pressure at the end of what had been a seven-game winning streak, and their premiership credentials called into question as a result.



Aside from that opening Gunston goal, the Lions never trailed, and a second quarter surge – kicking 6.5 to Hawthorn’s 3.1 – proved the momentum swing needed to put the foot down on their fellow top four threats. The hosts went on to kick five goals to two in the third quarter – beginning with Sam Draper’s snap at close range and ending with top-10 draftee Daniel Annable’s first AFL goal in his comeback from shoulder surgery – and consolidated in the final term, as 250-game milestone man Ryan Lester fittingly helped himself to a goal and Cam Rayner joined him on the scoreboard. “We love Ryan Lester, what he’s been able to do in his career is one of the great stories ... he’s just a tale of absolute persistence, and he’s playing his best footy in his 30s,” Fagan said of the man better known as “Froggy”, who has been dropped more than a dozen times throughout his career. If Morris, Lohmann, Hipwood and Cameron hitting their straps wasn’t good news enough for the Lions faithful, the sight of marquee recruit Oscar Allen back in the AFL – having returned from a three-month foot injury lay-off through the VFL in the past fortnight – only adds a new layer to the two-time reigning premiers’ forward line heading towards September.



“Oscar didn’t have a lot of the ball, but that’s often what happens when you have three of them [tall forwards] there, but between them, they caused a bit of chaos,” Fagan said. “I thought Kai Lohmann’s performance tonight was one of the most special performances I’ve seen from a small forward player. He got a lot of the ball, his tackle pressure was sensational, and he kicked five goals, so it’s a pretty good night by him too. “He’s just got his pressure right, he doesn’t have to worry about those freakish things – they just happen. When he focuses entirely on putting pressure on, his game seems to come together.” Every time Hawthorn struck throughout the contest and threatened to get back in the fight – Massimo D’Ambrosio, Jarman Impey and Connor Macdonald all scoring at key stages – the Lions were quick to respond and ensure they maintained a commanding lead. Despite the Hawks leading the inside-50 count at the major break (31 to 29), Lions co-captain Harris Andrews and his backline contingent were near impenetrable.



Even as the Lions’ superstar midfield was contained in the opening quarter, they eventually exploded to keep Hawthorn scrambling – Will Ashcroft leading the charge with 39 touches and seven clearances, with Lachie Neale (35 disposals, six clearances, three goal assists) hot on his tail. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Prove it’: Sam Mitchell urges outclassed Hawks to bounce back after Lions lesson
World.content:
Geelong great Tom Hawkins has called out the Cats hierarchy for not speaking to the public on Thursday and explaining their actions regarding the secret concussion waiver with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

“It’s hard to formulate an opinion when there has been so little information given,” Hawkins said on Kayo Sports on Friday night.

Geelong’s games record holder Tom Hawkins and 355-gamer Joel Selwood with their former teammate Mark Blicavs ahead of his 300th game. AFL Photos

“As a football spectator now, I was frustrated with the process, that it has taken so long to hear from the Geelong Football Club. We heard from Steve Hocking. It was a misstep.

“I don’t know – I think there is still more to be played out. I just find it staggering that yesterday [Thursday], they [Geelong] didn’t front the media and talk us through the process of what has actually happened.”

World.title: Two charged, stolen car recovered after Heidelberg West alleged hit-run
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

A woman accused of running over a man while stealing his car will face court on Saturday, after a dramatic arrest where police officers were allegedly forced to jump out of the way of a moving car while conducting a search warrant.

The 51-year-old woman was one of three arrested at Narvick Crescent, Heidelberg West on Friday, almost a week after an incident in nearby Blackwood Parade that left a 68-year-old man fighting for life.

Earlier this week, police urged a woman to hand herself in after she allegedly ran over a man who was trying to stop her from stealing his car in Heidelberg West. Victoria Police

In Friday’s incident, officers were conducting a search warrant at Narvick Crescent, when a vehicle parked in the driveway allegedly drove at them, forcing them to jump out of its path.

“The vehicle lost control, crashing into a wall before allegedly ramming an unmarked police vehicle,” police said in a statement on Friday night.

World.title: Roosters pip Bulldogs to draw level with league leaders
World.content:
Sydney Roosters have edged past Canterbury in a 20-18 win that has blown the race for the NRL’s minor premiership wide open.

On a pivotal night in the make-up of the top four, the Roosters moved up to second with a late win at Allianz Stadium that puts Trent Robinson’s men level on 36 points with ladder-leading Penrith.

Loading

The Panthers, who sit first as a result of their superior for and against, host the Roosters next Thursday and look set to be without captain Isaah Yeo.

Even without facing Yeo, the Roosters will have to turn things up a notch against the Panthers as the race for the minor premiership looks set to go to the wire.

Robinson’s side led 8-2 at half-time on Friday but were stunned when a try from Lachlan Galvin and a Jacob Kiraz double in a 12-minute second-half spell catapulted the Bulldogs into an unlikely lead.

But a miscommunication at the back by Bulldogs fullback Connor Tracey allowed Salesi Foketi to dive on a loose kick and claim the match-winning try in the 69th minute.

Loading

The victory gave the Roosters a seventh-straight win but also puts a major dent in Canterbury’s top-eight aspirations after they threatened to upset the home side.

Stephen Crichton kicked a penalty to get the Bulldogs on the board after sixth minutes before Sam Walker and Hugo Savala combined down the left to send Billy Smith in at the corner.

Then after Matt Burton failed to gather a Daly Cherry-Evans bomb, Siua Wong touched down for the Roosters who led 8-2 at half-time after Walker failed to convert both kicks.

The Bulldogs had struggled for spark in the first half but they came back after half-time with a bang as hooker Bailey Hayward burst up the middle of the field and found a supporting Kiraz.

The Canterbury winger scored under the posts as Crichton converted to tie the game up.

Galvin then put the Bulldogs ahead for the first time when the five-eighth drifted across field and darted through a Reece Robson tackle to score.

Galvin set up Kiraz for his side’s third but Canterbury were unable to find a knockout blow and the Roosters clawed their way back into the game.

Smith added a second with 15 minutes left before Foketi was in the right place at the right time, touching down a Walker bomb that Tracey failed to take to score the decisive try.

AAP

World.title: Timor-Leste: The new tourism frontier
World.content:
For the adventurous traveller, finding somewhere genuinely undiscovered has become almost impossible. Modern travel, globalisation and social media have left few blank spaces on the map. One country, however, has so far escaped mass tourism: Timor-Leste, a peaceful nation with a complicated history, a distinctive culture and a special bond with New Zealand. Anna Thomas reports.

Timor-Leste, or East Timor, is a name most New Zealanders would recognise but few could probably locate on a map. The most direct route is by flying to Bali, then taking a two-hour flight to the capital of Dili. But while Bali attracts 16 million visitors a year, Timor-Leste receives just 26,000, even then, most of those are ex-pats or business travellers.

Change, though, is arriving quickly. Since joining ASEAN in October 2025, development in this small South East Asian nation has accelerated. New hotels and restaurants are opening, roads are being sealed, and the international airport is undergoing a US$240 million upgrade.

With Timor-Leste due to chair ASEAN in 2029, a large convention centre is under construction on Dili's waterfront and thousands of political leaders, media and visitors are expected.

Supplied/Anna Thomas

Roughly the size of Hawke's Bay, the country has a population of 1.4 million. It has a rich and complex history marked by colonisation, conflict and occupation but as 'independent' Timor-Leste, its history is still being written.

It remains the poorest country in South East Asia, with almost half its people living below the poverty line. Ironically though it is also one of the most expensive countries with the majority of its goods imported. While oil and gas reserves remain the country's main revenue earner, tourism is increasingly seen as a potential golden goose.

A Kiwi connection

Diane Clayton has been living in Timor-Leste for a year. After 10 years with Tourism New Zealand, she and husband Tristam decided they needed an adventure. She signed up with Volunteer Service Abroad with the plan to help Timor-Leste develop eco-tourism. While the well-travelled couple were given a lengthy brief before arriving, she says nothing can quite prepare you.

"It's really quite a crazy place", she laughs "especially the lack of infrastructure, the heat, and the pollution. But very quickly we were made to feel at ease because the Timorese are so friendly."

VSA worker Diane Clayton with Timor-Leste Forestry Rangers. Supplied/Diane Clayton

Clayton has been working alongside tourism operators sharing her knowledge on everything from marketing to basic customer service. She explains that very few of the locals have experienced being a tourist themselves sowhen you're advising on hospitality you're starting from scratch.

And while health and safety wasn't part of her job description, Clayton discovered first hand, it needed to become a priority.

"On day two of my job I was asked if I'd like to join a group of Australian tour operators heading to Atauro Island."

The island is roughly 36km from Dili, about 1.5 hours by a small boat, and it has one of the world's most biodiverse coral reefs. The waters around Timor-Leste also have at least 24 species of whales and dolphins living or travelling through them. Clayton says the weather wasn't ideal and from the beginning she had a bad feeling.

"Because of the wind and swells the trip was on-again off-again but the call was made to proceed. There were 14 of us in a 10 person boat with no lifejackets.

The trip over was OK but when we arrived visibility wasn't good enough for snorkelling. So we had lunch and decided to return to Dili. However, halfway across the channel, the boat just stopped. We had run out of gas."

Diane and Tristram Clayton on Atauro Island. Supplied/Diane Clayton

The crew couldn't speak English and refused to use the boat radio but luckily there was some phone coverage. "Calls were being made but because of the deteriorating weather no one wanted to bring out extra fuel. As the hours ticked by, and the seas got rougher passengers were scared and a few of them were throwing up.

Finally, after waiting four hours, help arrived." Clayton told me it was the first time she had ever feared for her life.

As a result of that incident, Clayton has been working on health a safety protocols. But like most things in the country, developing industry standards is a work in progress.

One of the many picturesque rivers around Timor-Leste. Supplied/Anna Thomas

VSA volunteers like Clayton have been making a small but important contribution in the tourism sector. Clayton's predecessor, Jonty Crane, spent a year producing tourism videos and articles that remain the country's most visible promotional material online.

Australian expat Barry Hinton, who owns 'Barry's Place' one of Atauro Island's original eco-resorts credits Crane with doing more for Timorese tourism than anyone else. Hinton arrived in 2001 to teach English, later settling on Atauro and marrying locally.

Up to 85 percent of guests at 'Barry's Place' are Australians who are drawn to the island's marine environment.

Barry Hinton is an ex-pat Australian who owns the ecolodge Barry's Place on Atauro Island. Supplied/Anna Thomas

Hinton employs 30 local staff, doesn't advertise and books entirely through WhatsApp. His main frustration is bureaucracy. "The laws are changed all the time," he says.

"They (government) want investment, they want tourism, but they don't get how difficult they've made it." Still, he stays for the lifestyle. "It's just the rawness and the beauty of a very simple life and meeting guests who want an ethical holiday."

The next generation

'Friendly' and 'resilient' are the two words most commonly used to describe Timorese. Despite the poverty, the people of Timor-Leste are always smiling.

Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida is a 24-year-old tour guide from Dili. He is sharp, enthusiastic and hungry to learn. He started work in a car rental firm and when customers kept asking for recommendations of what to do and where to go, he saw an opportunity.

He's been running his business MaunTimor Guide for three years.

Varela Belo de Almeida says because Timor-Leste is an expensive country, it's not really suited to backpackers. Most of his clients are Australians and some New Zealanders, who want to learn more about the country where many of their soldiers served first in WWII and then again from 1999 as part of a multinational force restoring peace to the newly independent country.

Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida, 24, has been guiding tourists around Timor-Leste for three years. Supplied/Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida

Varela Belo de Almeida says an ideal itinerary is about six days; a couple of days in Dili, visiting Christo Rei (a smaller version of Rio's Christ the Redeemer), Santa Cruz cemetery, markets and museums, then Baucau to see Portuguese architecture, and then up to the remote and pristine Jaco Island.

Supplied/Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida

He says getting around the island can be challenging. "The roads can be dangerous at times and you could travel for hours only to discover the guest house you booked has increased the price, given away your room or has run out of food."

A typical washed out road in Timor-Leste. Supplied/Anna Thomas

While guiding can't support him full time yet, he says the knowledge and expertise he's received through Clayton has been invaluable. "I have learnt so much in her workshops on story-telling, hospitality and customer service, and especially marketing. I'm hoping as a result business will grow."

As Clayton's one year posting comes to an end she says volunteering gives you a rare insight and access to this young nation.

She is looking forward to returning in a few years to see how the country has developed. And for those considering visiting Timor-Leste, Clayton has some advice. "Come with your eyes wide open. Have low expectations and you'll be delighted."

World.title: Transport Agency refuses to release documents about tolling roads
World.content:
The Transport Agency is refusing to release briefings and records about tolling roads.

The government has moved to have tolls considered on all big projects and to change the rules so the revenue raised could be spent more widely.

RNZ asked Waka Kotahi for copies of any ministerial briefings on tolling this year and of any board minutes where tolling came up this year.

It identified two briefings and two lots of minutes from April and May.

But it has withheld all four on various grounds.

The first briefing, related to tolling consultation of the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass project, where decisions had not been made, was withheld on constitutional conventions for the time being which protect the confidentiality of advice.

The second briefing and boths sets of minutes contained commercially sensitive information so were withheld, NZTA said.

World.title: In China-US rivalry, NZ remains isolated but not insulated
World.content:
With China and the US vying for status as the major world superpower, New Zealand is caught walking a careful line.

In China-US rivalry, NZ remains isolated but not insulated The Detail Download MP3 22m

China sees an opportunity - created by US President Donald Trump and the global chaos he is creating - to influence New Zealand's actions in the world, according to an expert on the Chinese Communist Party.

"If you're a propagandist sitting in Beijing, Trump is the gift you never thought you'd get," says Sam Chetwin George, a senior fellow at the Asia Society's Centre on US-China Relations in New York.

China has been issuing more critical statements about New Zealand in the past year or so, coinciding with a realignment in New Zealand's foreign policy towards a traditional, US-led security framework.

But with Trump's disregard for international rules, New Zealand could be feeling more exposed, says George.

George is a Kiwi: he was a New Zealand Prime Minister's Scholar, learning Mandarin in Taiwan, and he also studied at Oxford and Stanford. He recently published a piece in Foreign Affairs magazine about how Beijing is making the most of this "age of anarchy".

"The New Zealand economy is in difficulty," George says. "We're facing an energy crisis. Our manufacturing base is at risk. The global economy is not looking great, and so it might just be that [China thinks] there's strategically an opening to apply pressure in a way that might be more effective now."

Earlier this year, China sharply criticised New Zealand's participation in a United Nations sanctions-monitoring mission focused on North Korea, and put a travel ban on four New Zealand MPs who visited Taiwan, a self-governing island that Beijing considers part of its territory.

It has also been encroaching further into the Pacific diplomatically, economically, and militarily. Last year, a Chinese naval task force group conducted live fire exercises in the Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand. Last month, Beijing launched a nuclear-capable missile into the nuclear-free South Pacific.

Still, Chinese leader Xi Jinping is casting himself as the stable alternative to the unpredictable Trump.

The Chinese Communist Party has long portrayed the US as bullying, hegemonic, greedy and expansionist - and Trump is proving some of those stereotypes, George says.

Beijing is now benefiting from the geopolitical rivalry between the world's two superpowers that's playing out in public.

"Countries like New Zealand are in the unenviable position of having to navigate that."

A recent survey from the Asia NZ Foundation found that, for the first time in a decade, Kiwis are more likely to see China as a friend than the United States. Similar trends were reported in a Pew Research survey of 36 countries, which found views of China have improved while opinions of the US have worsened, to the point where China is now seen more positively than the US.

So is China the guardian of stability in the world?

"Of course they're not," George says. "They're like any big power: they are focused on their own interests and they're focused on their own objectives."

But they're just being smarter about it. For example, the way Beijing is funding and supporting Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.

"America is so overt in its military adventurism, and China has just very carefully and very cleverly, I think, kept its support at a level that's plausibly deniable," he says.

Xi is "obsessed with strength" and returning China to what he sees as its rightful position in the world as a great civilisation and a great country, George says. That means cementing the absolute leadership of the Chinese Communist Party but also challenging the leadership of the US, its principal adversary in the world.

World.title: Way forward on merger unclear for Wellington councils
World.content:
The way forward for Wellington councils remains unclear, despite agreeing to submit amalgamation proposals to ministers this weekend.

Despite hours of productive discussions on Friday, a consensus across all parties could not be reached.

One proposal called for a region-wide merger; the other for a Wairarapa-only authority.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little said it was too early to know what changes would look like but he expressed optimism.

"I'm confident with the discussion that we've had today there is a lot of goodwill between the councils in the Wellington and Wairarapa region, and depending on what the government decides, regardless of whether it's one or two proposals they agree to, we've got a good chance of putting something good together for the region," he said.

He said there would be a number of benefits to amalgamation in the long run - inlcuding a stronger voice for the region, standardised processes and more cohesive economic and social strategies.

He said past amalgamation had not caused places to lose their distinctive characteristics.

"People's connection to their place, people's connection to land isn't dependent on who's administering their rights and who's issuing their dog licence and those sorts of things.

"It's about what happens in those areas, and that comes from communities."

But he said it might take time for benefits to become evident, "but it shouldn't stop us trying".

The Wellington region. Screenshot / Google Maps

He said balanced economic management was already happening through the Greater Wellington Regional Council, to everyone's benefit.

But the details around amalgamation had not been laid out: the next step is ministers deciding which proposals to take forward.

"Obviously, if we do get approval from ministers to proceed with whatever change happens, then council is going to have to communicate well and effectively to their communities. But in practice, nothing changes before 2028.

"Until the detailed work is done and again until ministers approve the detailed work, which will be the next phase, we won't know what things look like."

And the fight is not over for Kāpiti Coast District Council, whose proposal to become a singular authority was shot down by the other councils on Friday.

Mayor Janet Holborow said Kāpiti is looking to form a unitary authority under current legislation as the Head Start programme for reforming local governments had not been passed into law yet.

"We'll be talking to our local MP, to ministers, to MPs from the opposition, just to make our position very clear because we've done the analysis and we've done the work and we know that Kāpiti is in a strong position to form a unitary authority."

Kāpiti Coast Mayor Janet Holborow. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

She said as a unitary authority, Kāpiti could run its own services and set its own rates, "so that we're not subsumed into the problems of Wellington or any other council".

She told RNZ the council was also exploring possible mergers with Horowhenua and Palmerston North.

"We simply haven't had time to do that in this rushed process."

Holborow said if a structure were imposed on the council, "then we'll always just be putting our best foot forward on behalf of our community".

She said only 18 percent of residents in Kapiti were in favour of merging with the rest of Wellington.

Upper Hutt City Council also opposed amalgamation, it did not sign any Head Start proposal.

But its views were acknowledged in the proposals put forward.

Upper Hutt Mayor Peri Zee. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"It's obviously tough to include everyone's different views, but we've done the best we can collectively to make sure that everyone's views are incorporated, including ours, which was not to support the proposal," said Mayor Peri Zee.

She said she hoped the inclusion of Upper Hutt's opposition would let the council have an out from mergers later as discussions progressed.

"For Upper Hutt, the costs and benefits are quite different than other places: we have low rates already, quite an efficient council, and we wanted to protect our local democracy.

"So we heard that loud and clear that those were the key concerns for our community, and this proposal doesn't meet those concerns largely."

She said the council would fight a merger one step at a time as there was still much uncertainty over the reforms.

"I think there's certainly concerns with local government and even widely acknowledged concerns with local government, particularly around funding and financing. I don't know that this solves that problem."

Wellington City Councillor Diane Calvert. RNZ / Dom Thomas

Wellington City Councillor Diane Calvert said she was surprised to see the council endorse a region-wide propposal.

"On Thursday, Wellington City Council voted that our preference was that there should be two unitary authorities within the Wellington region, one for the Wairarapa and one for the metropolitan area, whoever was in that area, but primarily Wellington City, Porirua, Lower Hutt and Upper Hutt."

She said Wairarapa and the metropolitan Wellington area had different needs and ressources.

"And we're quite different. We're totally different catchment areas. We are divided by, geographic divide - not just a line on the map from one street to the next. So, there is quite a distinct difference," she said.

World.title: Hutt Hospital neonatal upgrades underway, long-promised maternity ward delayed
World.content:
A new maternity ward at Hutt Hospital promised for years has been put in the back seat in the lead-up to building work to add neonatal cots swinging into action.

Instead of getting upgrades of both the ward and neonatal unit, the downsized project only includes the latter.

Yet it is costing is about a million dollars more than the original, bigger multi-part project agreed by the previous government in 2020.

Health Minister Simeon Brown is putting the blame there.

"They never did the work to make sure all of it could actually be delivered," he told RNZ this week.

Some work in stage one and two was done but then paused in 2022 over seismic worries with the main hospital block. By the time it was recosted it was three times more or $31 million.

Health Minister Simeon Brown. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

'Off track'

"Off track," was how a Treasury report put it last year.

"Faced with that blowout, Health New Zealand recommended proceeding with stage 4, the neonatal unit, within the remaining funding," Brown's office said

"It required only an additional $950,000 to complete."

This meant dropping the maternity ward work, a rescope that Brown approved in January, another Treasury report showed.

The neonatal budget is $6.9m, part of what was a $9.5m - now $10.5m - women's health service redevelopment programme at Hutt Hospital. It relocated the community midwives and involved an upgrade to a unit that does assessments.

A tender was then put out only for neonatal, with an aim to start work in April, expanding it from 12 to 14 cots. Lack of cots has meant some premature babies having to transfer to Wellington Hospital.

The start was delayed and the $950,000 completion work began last week, when Brown visited.

'Insufficient planning'

Hutt South MP and Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop heralded the start online though a Facebook post of his did not mention maternity was not part of it.

Hutt South MP and Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop (L) and Health Minister Simeon Brown (R) visit the construction site. Supplied / Chris Bishop via Facebook

Clinical leaders supported prioritising neonates, said Brown's office, adding staff were told in March that maternity was progessing separately.

Health NZ said it communicated the revised scope directly with staff and key stakeholders, including community midwives.

"Labour was quick to announce this project back in 2020, but like many of the projects this Government inherited, they never did the work to make sure all of it could actually be delivered," Brown said in a statement.

"Even the Ministry of Health has noted it 'illustrates the risks of insufficient planning at the time of approval.'"

Brown went to the hospital last week to view the construction underway, speak with staff, and, "importantly, seek assurances about the current maternity ward and discuss the next steps for its upgrade", his office told RNZ.

Health NZ was doing minor refurbishment work in the ward meantime.

"The maternity ward upgrade remains a priority," said Brown's office.

"The community can be assured they will continue to receive quality maternity care at Hutt Hospital."

Labour's health spokesperson Dr Ayesha Verrall. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Labour's health spokesperson Dr Ayesha Verrall said the government could not keep blaming the opposition for "its own failures and broken promises".

"This is another example of the Government's stop-start approach to hospital infrastructure - as we've seen in Dunedin and Nelson where plans for hospital upgrades and rebuilds have been made but the National Government has scaled them back, reduced services, and delayed projects by years," she said.

World.title: Pacific Islands Forum fails to reach consensus on anti-missile statement against China
World.content:
Disagreement from some China-aligned Pacific Islands countries has prevented regional countries within the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) issuing a joint statement against missile testing in the Pacific.

At their meeting in Suva on Friday, PIF foreign ministers failed to agree on a unified statement against China after it fired a nuclear-capable missile into Pacific waters last month, despite deep concern among most countries about Beijing's actions.

It is understood there was a majority of countries represented at the meeting who wanted a clear joint regional statement condemning such missile testing in the nuclear-free Pacific.

However, the Forum's usual Pacific decision-making by consensus could not be met because Kiribati and Nauru were opposed to a strong statement condemning the testing.

New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters told media some Pacific nations were using the consensus system because they were more concerned with external partners' wishes than those that belong to the Pacific Islands Forum, something he described as an "unusual view".

"They didn't actually lay out any reasons, apart from their disagreement, and not wishing for us to make the clear statement such as 'we are opposed to missiles being fired into the Pacific'.

"That's what the statement should have said, and we're still waiting for that to get laid out."

Foreign Minister Winston Peters speaking to reporters in Fiji ahead of the Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Ministers' meeting on Friday. Supplied / screenshot

Some governments have pointed out that China is not the only country testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific. The US regularly conducts tests into the Marshall Islands.

Peters said that testing in the Marshall Islands was done with the country's consent.

Security agenda

The PIF Foreign Ministers Meeting was held to set the agenda for the annual Leaders' Meeting in Palau later this month.

A Solomon Islands proposal for a regional security treaty was one of the discussion points, although it's clear more consultation is required on the matter.

The Solomon Islands' Foreign Affairs and External Trade permanent secretary George Hoa'au told RNZ Pacific that there was already a range of regional security mechanisms in the Forum fale.

"The missing part is to have a common thatched roof over them," he said.

"The proposal for this single security treaty by Solomons is to provide an umbrella on top of what is already regional MOUs which are non-binding."

World.title: Warriors shock NRL table-topping Panthers in Metcalf comeback
World.content:
Halfback Luke Metcalf made a triumphant return to the NZ Warriors, leading his current team to a stunning 28-12 victory the NRL table-topping Penrith Panthers at Auckland's Go Media Stadium.

Metcalf was summoned into the Warriors line-up, after Te Maire Martin pulled out with a hamstring injury, and celebrated his comeback with two tries and 16 points, as the home side never really let their rivals into the game.

They pounced early with a try to lock Erin Clark, before Metcalf grabbed his first, looming in support of break by second-rower Kurt Capewell.

Five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita added another try before halftime, as the Warriors took an 18-0 lead into the sheds.

They had not lost a game that they led at the break this season and they took another step towards victory, when fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad - another forced to wait his turn this season - was first to score after the restart.

Penrith threatened to spoil the party, when they scored back-to-back tries to halfback Nathan Cleary and fullback Jaxen Edgar, both masterminded by Cleary.

They crossed for a third to wing Paul Alamoti, but it was overruled for offside in a kick chase.

Moments later, Metcalf sealed the win with his second try.

The result consolidates the Warriors' position in the top three - it puts them second on points difference, with Sydney Roosters yet to play this weekend - now two points behind Penrith.

World.title: Dargaville man faces multiple firearms charges after shooting into a garage
World.content:
A Dargaville man faces multiple firearms charges after firing a shot into a garage and sparking a major police operation on Thursday night.

The 37-year-old appeared in the Whangārei District Court on Friday charged with discharging a firearm in a house, discharging a firearm to intimidate, presenting a firearm at a person, unlawful possession of a firearm, and unlawful possession of ammunition.

The drama began on Ranfurly Street in Dargaville, close to Selwyn Park Primary School, just after 6.30pm.

Local residents reported seeing the police Eagle helicopter circling over the town, as many as 10 police cars, and spikes being laid to stop any fleeing vehicle.

Other residents attending a public meeting in town were told not to leave the building.

Inspector Maria Nordstrom, Whangārei-Kaipara Area Commander, said police responded to reports of a man pointing a firearm at a person during a family harm incident.

He then allegedly fired a shot into an unoccupied garage on the property.

"Our staff responded into the area, and took this man into custody," she said.

"Police would like to reassure the community that this was an isolated incident, involving parties known to each other."

Police enquiries were continuing.

World.title: New jumper revealed as NRL grants Perth Bears salary concessions
World.content:
The NRL's newest side, the Perth Bears, have unveiled their inaugural playing jersey on the same day they were granted salary cap concessions ahead of their entry to the competition in 2027.

In an event coordinated between Perth and North Sydney, where the unveiling was live-streamed, the Bears revealed the jersey by dropping the design from the famous WACA Ground light towers.

The design, which features red hoops on a black background, pays homage the North Sydney Bears, which left the NRL at the end of the 1999 season and currently play in the NSW Cup competition.

Peter V'landys (second from left) announced the concessions alongside WA Premier Roger Cook (speaking), Bears CEO Anthony De Ceglie, and Perth coach Mal Meninga (left). (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

The unveiling of the jersey marks a major step towards the Bears' entry into the NRL, which club chief executive Anthony De Ceglie said was on track to have 35,000 members by the beginning of the 2027 season.

Salary boost

In a big boost to the club, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys announced the Bears would be granted a concession for signing a marquee player.

"They will be given a 20 per cent dispensation for any player above a million dollars [salary]," V'landys said.

"If the player is worth $1.5 million, they can pay another 20 per cent from a sponsor and that won't be counted in the salary cap.

" So that gives them the opportunity to get somebody because they've got a 20 per cent bonus for that player from the sponsor. "

The Perth Bears will play in the 2027 NRL season. (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

Additionally, the Bears will have first rights to any player who wants to leave their club but is under contract for 2027.

"You may have a marquee player that's not happy in a particular club and the club and the player want to separate. That player can only go to Perth in the first instance," V'landys said.

"There will be some good players that will come up and be given the opportunity to play in Perth."

The concessions will help the Bears land a high-profile player, which has so far being lacking in their signings.

Meninga happy with progress

Bears inaugural coach Mal Meninga says he is "really happy" with the club's progress to date and talked down the need for a marquee player.

"We've worked within the conditions of obviously our entry into the NRL and you know … let me be frank with this … I'm really excited about the roster we've built," he said.

"You look through the team, we've got some high-profile players already.

"We've certainly got players of the future, there's no doubt.

"I really appreciate Peter and the club's great concessions, but I'm really happy with where we are at the moment."

Bellamy excited

Veteran Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy said the arrival of the Bears was exciting for the league.

And he said the club was in good hands with coach Mal Meninga steering the ship.

"I worked with Mal, I played with Mal and I know the amount of work that he puts in and the amount of work he will put into the coaching," he said.

"I'm sure it will be a very successful venture."

The Storm has already seen two of their players, Nick Meaney and Tyran Wishart, sign on with the Bears, but the coach was magnanimous about their departure.

Tyran Wishart of the Storm will line up for the Bears next season. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

"They're very excited to be coming over here," he said.

"They're obviously doing what they think's best for them and best for their families.

"They're still doing a great job for us.

"That's just the way the game is."

World.title: 'Doesn't look great': Fears Penrith captain could miss rest of NRL season
World.content:
Penrith captain Isaah Yeo may miss the rest of the NRL season after injuring his pectoral muscle, while the Sydney Roosters joined the Panthers on top of the table after defeating the Canterbury Bulldogs.

Yeo came off in the first half of Penrith's 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors in Auckland on Friday night, with the Auckland-based side solidifying their status as a genuine premiership threat in 2026.

Yeo was clutching his pectoral muscle after reeling out of a tackle, with scans needed to confirm if he has sustained a tear.

Should scans confirm a pectoral tear, he could be out for the rest of the season.

"It doesn't look great," Panthers coach Ivan Cleary said during his press conference.

"Obviously Yeoy's a big loss and hard to replace, but that's how it goes.

"If that's the case, we'll have to (replace him)."

The Roosters have joined the Panthers on 36 points at the top of the NRL ladder, surviving a scare to pip the Bulldogs 20-18.

The Roosters held an 8-2 lead at half-time, but the Bulldogs scored three tries in 11 minutes to take an 18-8 lead with 25 minutes to play.

But two quick tries in the final 15 minutes for the Roosters earned them a hard-fought win.

Meanwhile, Craig Bellamy says he will be coach of the Melbourne Storm in 2027, despite recent health issues.

World.title: De Minaur haunted by Montreal Masters double-fault drama
World.content:
A double fault has proved costly for Alex de Minaur with the Australian star blowing a match point before falling to Briton Cameron Norrie at the Montreal Masters.

Third-seeded De Minaur was up 5-2 and 40-30 in the second set, but stumbled to allow Norrie back into their third-round match.

He had another chance when serving for the match at 5-4, but again double-faulted to surrender the game on Norrie's fourth break point.

World number 37 Norrie then dug deep to record a 5-7, 7-6 (5), 6-1 victory after two hours and 52 minutes in difficult, humid conditions.

Norrie said he had to weather de Minaur's early onslaught with the newly married Aussie starting with a bang.

"From the beginning, Alex came out firing and I was like, 'Woah, this is a crazy level', and I had to match it," Norrie said in his on-court interview.

"I managed to go up a break [in the first set], but he stayed really tough and I know he's so tough as a competitor and stole that first set.

"He was looking good in the second set, and I think he took the foot off the gas very slightly and I managed to free up, steal the tie-break and then it was just a battle.

"It was a great match to win, and to test my level and I can take so much confidence from this one."

Australians through in Montreal Alex de Minaur and fellow Australians Alexei Popyrin and Tahlia Gibson all record encouraging wins three weeks out from the US Open in New York.

Entering Thursday's (Friday AEST) match, de Minaur was the highest seed remaining at the hard court tournament, also known as the Canadian Open, with defending champion and fifth seed Ben Shelton taking over that title.

In some good news for de Minaur, because American Taylor Fritz and Italian Flavio Cobolli have also exited the event early, he can only possibly drop from seven to eight in the rankings, and that's only if Shelton wins the title.

That means the Australian, who broke through for a career-high number five ranking in July, will keep his top-eight US Open seeding intact for now.

De Minaur is looking to improve on quarter-final finishes at Flushing Meadows in the past two years.

Norrie will next take on 18th seed Arthur Fils, who earlier cruised past Mariano Navone 6-3, 6-2 to maintain his impressive record at Masters 1000 events this year.

AAP

World.title: Ex-AFLPA boss calls for independent tribunal over Cats concussion waiver
World.content:
Former Richmond player and AFL Players Association (AFLPA) chief Joel Bowden has criticised the AFL, Geelong and the AFLPA for their handling of the secret concussion waiver signed by an unknown Cats player, calling for a Senate committee hearing to investigate.

The Cats have avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Speaking to ABC Radio Melbourne on Friday, Bowden said he found it "absolutely outrageous that a young person's been taken advantage of", calling it "gambling with a young [player's] health and safety".

Dogs coach on concussion controversy Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge gives his view on concussion in the AFL following revelations of Geelong putting a waiver into a player's contract.

Bowden — who is also a former trade unionist and member of the Northern Territory parliament — pointed to the close ties between the club and the AFL, with former Geelong president Craig Drummond the chairman of the AFL Commission and Geelong chief executive Steven Hocking being the former general manager of football at the AFL.

"How this has got through, how people have thought that this is possibly OK is now ever more outrageous with the facts that have been put on the table," Bowden said.

Loading...

"It's conduct unbecoming. The AFL will fine players, they will fine people who are involved in the community sport — if you breach the code of conduct anywhere in the AFL at a game of community football you can be brought in front of a tribunal.

"And this AFL club, Geelong, have gone and signed a contract outside the standard playing contract and I would say outside of WorkSafe Victoria's legislative framework to provide a duty of care and a safe workplace.

"And now they're going to say: 'Nothing to see here, let's move on and watch the footy.'"

Bowden took aim at his former organisation the AFLPA for putting out a joint statement with the AFL over the issue and saying that the association had to "act more like a union, the union they are."

"They [the AFLPA] are too close [to the AFL] and this example says to me that the industry has got control of the Players Association," Bowden said, citing the AFL's funding of the AFLPA "to the tune of millions of dollars per year".

He called for Geelong to be brought in front of an independent tribunal to get to the bottom of the issue.

"I don't think there's been a press conference where anyone from the AFL or Geelong has stood there and taken questions," he said.

"Concussion is the nmber one issue in the AFL at this point of time. It's going to be huge in years to come, the CTE research and understanding now, the history that we know.

"They're all too close and the industry is too close at times so maybe it needs to go to a Senate estimates committee hearing or something and get David Pocock to ask some questions and get independent senators and Sarah Hanson-Young to level these to the AFL.

"A young man has been put at risk and been asked to sign a secret waiver that says he'll exonerate the club from any future issues with his health. That needs to be investigated and that's not OK."

Asked if he thought Geelong would end up being sanctioned over the waiver, he replied:

"Yes I do. I think the court of public opinion will demand that they be sanctioned because this type of behaviour in modern AFL but also in workplace safety laws is not acceptable. Independent separate contracts are unacceptable."

A Victorian government spokesperson responded on Friday.

"Players safety must never be compromised," the spokesperson said.

"The AFL must have evidence-based policies and procedures in place to protect their players.

"The AFL, as the governing body for Australian rules football, has responsibility for managing concussion within the code."

World.title: Athletes go missing after Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

'No idea what type of asylum'

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Former Iranian footballers granted citizenship Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Dogs coach says he would have signed concussion waiver to keep playing
World.content:
As the AFL and Geelong continue to face questions about their handling of a concussion issue, Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge believes players are looked after better than ever.

The Cats avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

The Cats also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

Geelong avoided punishment and said it would remove the waiver in the unnamed player's contract. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

When asked about the bombshell revelation out of Geelong, Beveridge spoke generally about concussion rather than commenting directly on the Cats' case.

"I think every player wants to keep playing until your boots fall off," Beveridge said after the Bulldogs' shock loss to North Melbourne.

"All I know that when I was playing, we all had concussions, and if I had to sign a waiver to keep playing, I would have.

"We're so careful with our players now.

"The way we train, as far as the duty of care goes, we really look after them."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kangaroos coach Alastair Clarkson, who earlier this year sprayed insurance company Zurich for rejecting concussion insurance claims, insisted he knew nothing about Geelong's case.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the statement from the AFL.

Deciding not to front the media to explain the situation, Drummond issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy and former number one pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham "Polly" Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.
