World.title: Some of rugby league's truest believers await the NRL in Perth
World.content:
Most of the time when we talk about an expansion team it's all about firsts.

It starts with the first signing, then it's the first look at the jersey, then on to the first match, first win and first loss as they settle into their new place in an older world.

The Perth Bears are midway through that process right now. With 27 players on their books, their roster has well and truly come together and on Friday afternoon they'll reveal their playing strip to the world ahead of their NRL debut next year.

But amid all the firsts there will also be a last. The jersey unveiling will be held in conjunction with Melbourne's game against Manly this weekend, which is the final NRL game that will be played in Perth before the city has a team of its own.

The next NRL game Perth Oval hosts will be the local side's home debut. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

As the old world dies, plenty expect the new one to struggle in birth.

Much has been written and said about the new franchise's lack of star power and whether they can be competitive as they fight against the tyranny of distance and the money monster of their fellow expansion team in Papua New Guinea.

But their entry goes both ways as the beginning looms. It's not just about what awaits Perth in the NRL, but what awaits the NRL in Perth.

With the elite level of the sport about to finally put real roots down, how fertile is the soil? The spark of the game has been flickering for decades, but can it catch fire? Ahead of the last game before the start of forever for the Bears, what is rugby league in Perth really like?

A player's life at the outpost

Samisoni Langi is used to life on rugby league's frontiers. It's where he spent his finest playing days and where he helped make history.

The 33-year old got his start with the Sydney Roosters back in 2013, playing a handful of NRL matches before a long career in Europe, highlighted by five years with Catalans Dragons in France.

Langi played five-eighth for the Super League club when they won the Challenge Cup in 2018 to become the only non-English side in the competition's 125-year history to win the trophy.

He also represented Tonga while he was in the NRL and played for France at the last World Cup after qualifying through residency.

After finishing at the top level at the end of the 2023 season, Langi resettled in Perth to be closer to his wife's family and before long rugby league came calling.

Langi spent five years playing with Catalans Dragons in France. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton )

"It wasn't anything to do with footy, just for family. But a few clubs reached out when they found out I was here," Langi says.

"The players and the clubs here, they live and breathe rugby league. The people in the background are so passionate, they love their club and they love the sport.

"When I first came over there was only five teams in the first grade competition, that's up to nine now. It's a tough competition with lots of pride that's growing each year.

"There's so many volunteers who are at the fields setting up from 6am on Saturday for seniors and they all back up for the juniors on Sunday.

"They love it so much, and they're looking forward so much to the Bears."

Langi linked up with South Perth Lions, a local powerhouse with 20 premierships to their name since their formation in 1948, and got into the world of West Australian rugby league.

Langi played the 2025 season with South Perth Lions and was named the competition's player of the year. (NRLWA)

As Langi got about in that first season, which ended with him being named the competition's player of the year and the Lions making the grand final, the Bears slowly came to life.

In the 18 months since, they've put together their roster and now their first pre-season is well and truly on the horizon.

The discerning football fan might notice a lack of big names, but according to Langi that won't matter to most in Perth.

Australian Rules remains the biggest game in town by an indomitably huge margin and rugby union is firmly in second with the Western Force celebrating its 21st season this year.

For league to carve out a niche the key isn't in brand name players, as much as they'd help the on-field prospects, but in the name of the team itself.

There's a core of league fans that can provide a base for the club — crowds for NRL matches in the west have held steadily over 30,000 for the double headers at Perth Stadium and over 10,000 for one-off matches at the Bears' future home, Perth Oval.

Attendances and interest at NRL matches in Perth have held steady. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But for the Bears to become part of the fabric of the city they need to tap into the general sports population and the way to do that is strengthen the links to the community as much as possible.

In terms of sustainability, local pride beats imported star power every time and parochialism is a way of life in rugby league which should serve the city well, given Perth fans would show up to a letter-opening, so long as it's a letter about Perth.

"Everyone's excited to have a team of their own. A lot of footy people still have their teams from back east, the Roosters have come over and the Sharks and Raiders were here a few months ago, but having the Perth Bears will be different," Langi says.

"Nobody's too fussed about the players, they're just excited a team will be here.

"The biggest thing is being visible and accessible. Spend time in schools, visit junior clubs, support local competitions, build genuine relationships in the communities across Perth. Young players need to see the club as something they can be a part of.

"Whenever there's an NRL game coming here it's always big. The entire comp either has the week off or we push our game to Friday night or Sunday afternoon so everyone can get along to the NRL.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"You can feel the buzz around the city. It also inspires young players and they can see what's possible and dream to be out there playing professionally. Even the captain's run is big — I teach at a high school and nobody comes the day before the game, all the kids go to the open training session."

Langi doesn't just teach at Baldivis College to the city's south, he also runs the school's girls rugby league program, the first of its kind anywhere in Western Australia.

Finding a game for his charges isn't always easy but their enthusiasm is inspiring to Langi and while it could take the better part of a generation for work like his to bear fruit, the fact that the Bears are coming into a world where that work is already being done bodes well for their future.

"At the start I didn't know what I was getting myself into — the first thing they want to do every session is tackle, they're always asking when we're going to start tackling and I have to say 'we have to go through technique first, we have to catch and pass' and all these other things. But they love it," Langi says.

"The girls so look forward to games and sometimes they get cancelled and that can be disheartening.

"But we're trying to grow the game and with the Bears coming it should get a really good push, I'm looking forward to that."

Langi will be on the frontlines to see it as well. This year he transferred from the Lions to the newly promoted Kalamanda Bulldogs and he is keen to run around again in 2027.

"I'm just trying to help some of the young guys find their way. The club has come into first grade from reserve grade this year, so it's been a big step up," Langi says.

"We're pushing for the finals right now but next year and past that they'll be able to give it a real crack.

"I'll play for another year or two, then it'll be into coaching. I don't think I'll ever give up footy."

The age of the Bear begins

Perth's rugby league future might be more upscale than its past but it'll be nowhere near as colourful.

South Perth Lions, Langi's old club, have enough yarns alone to fill many a front bar session.

There was the time in the 1950s when a local dairy owner auctioned off one of his milk cart horses to raise money for the club but neglected to mention the horse in question had passed on after being hit by a car the day before.

This was around the same time the Lions home ground was next door to Perth Zoo and due to a lack of facilities players would wash in the zoo's artesian hot pools after matches.

A few decades later the team had managed to build its own clubhouse but were having trouble getting a liquor license because it required permission from the nearest publican.

After much resistance from the proprietor of said boozer, two enterprising club officials managed to win him over by approaching him on a Sunday morning in a moment of weakness as he battled a hangover that could kill a brown dog and a nasty bout of gout.

Perth hasn't had a team in the NRL since the Western Reds folded at the end of 1997. (Getty Images)

The club's end of season parties were always a highlight, particularly the year when, in an effort to keep the players out of the local watering hole, each pub donated an 18-gallon keg. It took them four days to get through all 15 of them.

Then there was the time the club had a partnership with a local company to unload produce trucks, which was put in jeopardy when the players unloaded watermelons by forming a makeshift backline and spiral passing them along.

Or the day a plane crashed on Como Reserve during an off-season game of cricket and the boys sprang into action to save the passengers, who fortunately survived the crash, with one man freeing them while still wearing his wicket-keeping gloves.

Some of these stories might be truer than others, but what's certainly true is they're all stories.

What's more iron-clad is South Perth's brilliant record on the field. Amid producing NRL talent like former Newcastle forward Cory Paterson, brothers Bronx and Bryson Goodwin and former Manly prop Kurt de Luis, they have 20 premierships to their name since 1948, the most of any team in the competition.

Other sides, like Joondalup Giants, Fremantle Roosters and North Beach Sea Eagles, had their glory days over the years but those same days never seemed to come around for the Willagee Bears, competition stalwarts since 1966.

When current coach Nelson Davis, who has lived in Perth for more than two decades, first took more than ten years ago the club had played for half a century without ever winning a first grade premiership.

Davis has lived in Perth for over 20 years and been involved with Willagee Bears for a decade. (NRLWA)

Davis, who had been coaching since he was 16 back home in Auckland, was initially daunted when his best mate and current assistant coach, Conrad Ramea, asked him to lend a hand.

"I said 'I'm only a juniors coach, I wouldn't know what to do with seniors.' But I've been at the Bears ever since," Davis says.

"We started from rock bottom. We had a really good base of players and at the time we were one of the strongest junior clubs, we had nearly one team in every grade.

"A lot of our players would come through the 16s and 17s but going to other clubs because we didn't have a first grade team.

"We did go up for two years in 2018 and 2019 and we lost every game. We learnt a lesson then."

After a few years away from the sidelines as the club's coaching co-ordinater, Davis took the reigns of the first grade side again in 2023 and was determined to learn from the pain of the past.

Willagee's trip to the grand final last year was years in the making. (NRLWA)

"I was ambitious. I gave the club a list of things we'd need to go up to first grade because I knew we had to learn those hard times," Davis says.

"I talked about paying players, upskilling staff, getting more support in terms of strength and conditioning and assistant coaches and my president, the man he was, came back to me a few months later and made it happen."

The Bears got to work, signing enough players to give their kids a team they could aspire to and setting new standards.

The results were remarkable. Just a few years after they could barely win a game, Willagee won the club's inaugural first grade premiership by downing Langi's Lions in the 2025 grand final.

It was a triumph of vision, development and self-belief, amid a transformation that would have made any club proud.

Nine of the players in the grand final side had played in the club's reserve grade team the year before and the club's entire spine and front row were local boys.

Willagee scored their breakthrough premiership in 2025 after a lifetime of waiting. (NRLWA)

"Just talking about it now makes me a bit teary. It was one of the greatest days and nights of our lives, to do it with my family and my best mate, it's what rugby league is about — those memories, the people, the bonds and the friendships you make," Davis says.

"That's what matters more than anything, more than any trophy.

"I look back at us getting belted 80-0 five or six years earlier and I never thought I'd be there for a Willagee first grade premiership.

"I thought I might have an influence on it if it happened a long way in the future but for it to happen so quickly was surreal.

"There were so many people who put in so much hard to work to get us there."

When Davis said it was a win for the many he's not kidding — Willagee has 411 people registered at the club and nearly a quarter are volunteers.

Loading Instagram content

Davis doesn't take a salary and several of his players now say they'll play for the club for free.

"That's the passion the guys have for the club and that's what drives a lot of clubs over here — the passion, the loyalty, the community feel and the family environment," Davis says.

"We aren't the biggest club, but we pack a punch and we have high aspirations for where we want to be."

Said aspirations are quickly being realised. Willagee have backed up their breakthrough premiership with a season for the ages and are undefeated at the time of writing just a few weeks out from the finals.

Their reserve grade side is set for the minor premiership as well and a clean sweep could be in the offing given their under-17s team is top of the table.

The family feel is already coming through with their links to their NRL big brother. Davis pinpoints Kaino Gudgeon, man of the match in last year's grand final win, as the club's key signing for their turnaround and his brother Ammaron, a local product, will take up a train and trial deal with Perth over the summer after a standout season with North Sydney in NSW Cup.

Plus none other than Mal Meninga himself, living Immortal and the NRL's sides foundation coach has been along to several Willagee matches and for Davis, those efforts to forge a link with the local league scene will be crucial.

Meninga's role in strengthening the Bears ties with the community will be vital. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

"Mal's been to a few of our games already and that means a lot to the players and the coaches," Davis says.

"There's a lot of kids I coach who have dreams to play in the NRL and you have to be straight up with them about how hard it is and what the pathways are like — I just hope the Perth Bears can create that for them.

"I do believe there's some real talent here and some kids who could be knocking on the door.

"I know the Bears have big plans with the Tracks Academy and there's some very, very good 16 and 17-year olds, even in our club.

"I've got one player and I'd have had him in first grade the day he turned 17 but his mum won't let him."

Few would dispute that Perth Bears have a huge task ahead of them, but Willagee Bears are proof of what's possible.

People like Davis and the army of volunteers across the clubs that have kept the flame of rugby league alive so far from the game's strongholds have not just given the NRL side an example to aspire to, they've given them a community to serve, a rock on which the elite level of the game can build its church.

For decades, love of the sport was all that kept the lights on and now those lights are about to be so bright as to be dazzling.

Their game has come to them at last and it is a reward they never expected for a passion that never waned.

"People walk around with the Bears shirts on around the streets. When I'm wearing Willagee Bears gear everyone thinks it's for Perth," Davis says.

"There's a strong core community here, it's not the biggest, but it'll only grow with them coming. Even if we have teams already - I'm still a Warrior because I have been since day dot - we're all foundation members, I can guarantee you that.

"I just hope they can be semi-competitive those first few years and give the locals something to turn up for.

"It's been a positive impact already and we're so excited. Every club has seen an increase in numbers already. The banners are up, the billboards are up. I can't wait."

World.title: Le Court wins Tour de France Femmes stage as Reusser keeps overall lead
World.content:
Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius overcame earlier difficulties to emerge victorious in a reduced sprint and win stage six of the Tour de France Femmes, as Swiss rider Marlen Reusser held on to the overall lead with three stages remaining.

Le Court joined a small breakaway group 10 kilometres from the finish, launched her sprint with 300 metres to go and held off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands coming in third.

The 30-year-old Le Court suffered a mechanical before the final climb and had to change bikes, but, thanks to her teammates, made it back in time to launch her telling move.

"They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the last climb, which was a really big effort," Le Court said.

"Then I just tried to stay patient, try to recover from this big effort. Riejanne Markus and I bridged to the breakaway, and we got to the front."

There was no change at the top of the standings after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, with Reusser holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering. Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney is third, 1:17 off the leader.

A group of three riders built an early lead of over two minutes but were brought back with 54km remaining.

World champion Magdeleine Vallieres set a blistering pace at the front on the penultimate climb of Col de Lalouvesc, which split the peloton, leaving a reduced bunch of about 30 riders to go for the stage win.

A group of six then got away, before they were joined by Le Court and Markus. The breakaway managed to hold off the chasing pack, and Markus made a move with one kilometre left.

The Dutch rider was unable to make her attack count, and it was left to Le Court to claim an almost carbon copy victory of her stage win last year when she outfought Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney in a seven-rider sprint to the line.

Tech.title: Sony could release a cheaper version of its WH-1000XM4 headphones, according to leaks
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Following the release of its premium and very expensive $650 The Collexion headphones in May, Sony could be taking its 1000X line of wireless noise-canceling headphones in a cheaper direction next month. The company is reportedly planning a refreshed and more affordable version of its six-year-old WH-1000XM4 headphones that will feature similar performance and specs as the original but at a lower price point, according to reliable leaker billbil-kun.

The WH-1000XM4C are expected to launch in early September 2026 in black, silver, and lavender color options for €249.99 or £219.99, which is around $289 to $297 after currency conversion.

The original WH-1000XM4 launched in 2020 for $349.99, while the WH-1000XM6 debuted at a much steeper $449 last year. The new 1000XM4C’s features will include ANC powered by Sony’s QN1 chip (the 1000XM6 use its newer QN3 chip), spatial audio, support for hi-res audio, and earcup touch controls. The only compromise, according to the leaks, is slightly reduced battery life on the new version. The original 1000XM4 maxed out at up to 38 hours with ANC off, or up to 30 hours with noise-canceling on. The 1000XM4C will only offer up to 34 hours of playback, or up to 27 with ANC.

Although there have been two major updates to Sony’s 1000X headphone line since the 1000XM4 first launched, there are still devoted fans of the older model’s design. Sony introduced a major redesign of the line with 2022’s 1000XM5 that eliminated the folding earcups necessitating a much larger carrying case. The company reintroduced the folding mechanism with last year’s 1000XM6 that also added a wider and more comfortable headband, but some (myself included) still prefer the 1000XM4’s design. For those of us with the aging older models suffering from reduced battery life, the 1000XM4C could be a solid replacement.

Tech.title: Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra is more of the same, but better than ever
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

What makes the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra so Ultra? Samsung’s first foldable with the Ultra name isn’t a souped-up version of the regular Fold 8, as you might expect. Where the Z Fold 8 is squat and wide, the Fold 8 Ultra retains the thin outer screen and square inner panel of the previous Folds. It does have a substantially better triple rear camera system and a slightly larger battery. But with no support for the S Pen stylus and no Privacy Display, it’s not Ultra in the same way as the Galaxy S26 Ultra.

But compare it to last year’s Z Fold 7 and the upgrades look more substantial. Samsung has improved the displays, battery, charging, cameras, chipset, and crease. Most of these are only iterative, but taken together the package is impressive.

Does that make it Ultra? I don’t know, and it doesn’t really matter. This is a meaningfully more capable phone than last year’s, albeit for $100 more, and it offers something different than its wider new sibling. Samsung will have to hope that’s enough to hold up against whatever Apple has coming with its expected foldable iPhone next month.

Closed, the Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 6.5-inch cover screen that’s taller than most phones but skinnier too; open, there’s an 8-inch flexible display that’s almost square in its aspect ratio.

At a glance, you’d struggle to tell it apart from last year’s Z Fold 7. It’s the same size, shape, and weight, apart from being fractionally thinner at 4.1mm thick when open. The cameras are in the same spot and look just about identical. In fact, the new set of colors — dark grey, cream, purple, and green — is really the only way to differentiate the two generations by sight.

Closed, it feels unusually thin and tall. Open, it’s good for split-screen work but less well-suited to video.

Samsung argues that while the new Z Fold 8 is designed for content consumption, the taller Ultra is more useful for productivity. The extra vertical space helps if you’re trying to cross-reference documents or navigate multiple inboxes. Personally, I’m more likely to use the larger inner screen for watching video, so I would take the Z Fold 8 over this, but I do see the benefits of the larger space. I wrote two whole articles for my food newsletter across a couple of flights using the Z Fold 8 Ultra’s on-screen keyboard, something I would never consider with a regular phone or even the smaller Z Fold 8.

Both displays are brighter than before, now with a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, making them easier to use outside. The inner screen benefits further from a new anti-reflective coating and a small resolution bump to 2256 x 2504.

Just as importantly, Samsung has reworked the main screen’s innards, incorporating a new titanium alloy film and a flexible titanium plate. These make the foldable screen thinner and more durable — and combined with the anti-reflective coating, they also make the crease harder to see and feel. Head-on, it’s now almost invisible, though still relatively clear when the light catches it at an off angle. Oppo’s solution in the Find N6, which involves using 3D printing to fill surface-level gaps in the hinge, seems more effective at eliminating the crease, but it’s hard to imagine anyone finding this version especially bothersome.

As ever, Samsung offers seven years of software support with its flagship foldable. AI features including Now Brief return, though new additions are limited.

The biggest year-over-year upgrade is the battery. For the first time, Samsung has adopted silicon-carbon battery chemistry, which makes it possible to fit higher-capacity batteries into the same-size space. As a result, the Z Fold 8 Ultra has jumped from a 4,400mAh battery last year to 5,000mAh, despite being fractionally thinner. The phone easily lasts a day, even with a few hours of inner screen use, and I usually have 30 to 40 percent left when I head to bed.

The bigger battery has been bolstered by faster charging — 45W wired and 20W wireless — though the phone is still only Qi2 Ready, meaning there are no charging magnets inside, and it requires a Qi2 case to hit top wireless charging speeds. That helps keep it thin, in fairness, so may be a worthy tradeoff.

An IP68 rating is another major omission; the IP48 rating here means good water protection but limited guarantees against dust and sand. Samsung removed S Pen support in last year’s Z Fold 7, and it’s still missing here. There’s also no sign of the impressive Privacy Display technology introduced in this year’s S26 Ultra.

Unlike the regular Z Fold 8, you get three rear cameras on this phone.

Then there are the cameras. If you’re picking between the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra, then form factor aside, this is the only difference that matters. The Ultra gets the same 50-megapixel, f/1.9 ultrawide as the Fold 8, but its 200-megapixel main camera is substantially superior in both detail and light capture. And the presence of a 10-megapixel, 3x telephoto adds a welcome versatility that the regular Fold 8 lacks. It’s far from the best telephoto in any phone — it’s an area where manufacturers like Vivo and Xiaomi have devoted considerable resources, including larger sensors and superior stabilization — but just having the option makes this a more flexible camera. I wouldn’t push the zoom much beyond its 3x optical range though, with significant noise creeping in above 6x or so.

There’s an impressive level of consistency between the three lenses in most conditions, though just occasionally the ultrawide comes out a little differently. It’s usually more muted, though at least once, it took the most vivid shot. Low-light performance across all three lenses is good, though they’re all guilty of over-lightening the nighttime sky and creating flare around brighter lights.

Previous Next















































1 / 25 The Z Fold 8 Ultra’s main camera is the same as the Z Fold 7’s, and just as capable.

Samsung’s software updates this year are relatively slight. There’s My FanCam, a video editing feature that uses AI to crop videos in on a specific person. Google’s Gemini Intelligence task automation is supported, but so far isn’t available in the UK, meaning I haven’t tested it. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel Magic Cue, has apparently been updated to suggest helpful contextual actions (like adding an event to your calendar) to carry out in split-screen. In a week of using the phone, I haven’t seen it pop up once, even after subjecting myself to Samsung Keyboard the whole time because some reports suggest that’s a requirement.

Samsung’s stark and simple design language is still among the best out there.

I’ve been more impressed than I expected by the Z Fold 8 Ultra. I thought it would struggle to compete with recent excellent foldables from Oppo and Honor, but in reality, it’s a fairly close contest — and unlike those phones, it’s actually on sale in the US.

Its cameras still aren’t at the level of Oppo and Honor’s, and without an S Pen or a Privacy Display, I’d quibble over how Ultra it all really is. But for those who prefer the tall, square foldable form factor, this is a worthy follow-up to the Z Fold 7. The substantially larger battery alone justifies the $100 price hike.

I don’t know which of Samsung’s two Z Fold 8 phones I’d buy this year — really, I want the Z Fold 8’s form factor with the Ultra’s cameras squeezed in — but that indecision is testament to the fact that you can’t go too far wrong with either.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, you must agree to: Google Terms of Service

Google Play Terms of Service

Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS

Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.”

Samsung End User Licence Agreement

Samsung Privacy Notice

Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services

“Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”

Send usage and diagnostic data to Google

Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant

Turn on Samsung offline finding

Samsung news and special offers

Samsung personalized advertising

Bixby personal data intelligence

Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements.

Tech.title: Werewolf transformed my old gadgets into USB-C powered ones
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When I haul my 27-inch desktop monitor into the garage to film fun gadget videos… or want to play Japanese SNES games with friends… or lose the AC adapter for my old external hard disk… I can now power them with a USB battery instead.

None of them came with USB-C ports; the entire USB protocol was barely a twinkle in its creator’s eye when Nintendo shipped the Super Famicom in 1990! But a tiny programmable dongle, from a company called Werewolf, can transform old power ports to accept USB-C electricity. I’m so impressed, I just bought a second kit for a friend’s birthday.

With these dongles, there’s no surgery required to add USB-C. You plug the $8 Werewolf VFLEX dongle into your phone to program it, plug it into your USB charger or battery, then attach a $4 barrel jack tip.

It’s like having a universal A/C adapter, one you don’t even need to plug into the wall, because modern USB-C batteries offer far more power than yesteryear’s gadgets did.

Here’s my Asus monitor, my Super Famicom, and a cheap RCA-to-HDMI adapter all powered by a single Shargeek 300 portable battery and two VFLEX adapters:

Yes, Mega Man X would look better on my CRT, but it doesn’t have a barrel jack. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

At its current rate of drain (2W for the game, 24W for the monitor, and less than 1W for HDMI), that big battery will last hours this way. With my wife’s original 1989 Game Boy, which I measured draining just 0.33 watts playing Tetris, even my pocket battery could theoretically power it for over 90 hours straight.

I have non-theoretical examples, too: When I held a classic gaming party on the Fourth of July, I genuinely powered this Super Famicom with a VFLEX for some five-player Bomberman.

When I recorded my Steam Machine video, I used an old Atomos recording device whose aging batteries died too fast — so I used a VFLEX to plug it in.

And when I shot my Sharge Disk Pro 2 video just the other day, I didn’t want to rip my monitor’s carefully cable-managed power supply out of my desk just to film in my garage for a day. I turned it into a portable monitor by plugging in a VFLEX and a USB-C battery.

This Litepanels Croma takes six AAs, but it also has a barrel jack… Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

It’s practical, and it doesn’t require surgery, but the VFLEX does take some forethought. Before you plug it into a gadget, you should always plug the USB-C end into your phone to set the right voltage. It does store settings in non-volatile memory, but I hate to think what might happen to my vintage Game Boy if I accidently shoved my monitor’s 19 volts into it.

The genius of Werewolf’s system is that it doesn’t need to convert voltage — it asks for the power you want. It uses the same protocols that other USB-C gadgets do to negotiate power, only here you get to specify how much.

But you can’t just buy a VFLEX and expect your existing chargers to do everything else. For example, my Apple 140W USB-C power adapter, the most powerful the company makes, can’t deliver the 19 volts my desktop monitor wants. Like every 100W USB-C PD charger, it’s comfortable delivering 5V, 9V, 15V, or 20V, and because it’s a 140W Extended Power Range (EPR) charger, it can do 28V as well.

You can add your own devices for easy selection. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Those voltages might be fine for many of your gadgets, and Werewolf claims the VFLEX can even go up to 48V if you’ve got a 240W USB-C power adapter to feed it. But if you need USB-C voltage below or between the standard 5, 9, 15, 20, 28, 36, or 48, you need what’s called a programmable power supply (PPS), and Apple’s charger isn’t that.

Thankfully, you don’t need to think about most of this. You can save profiles for each gadget and charger to the Werewolf app — and use the VFLEX dongle itself to test your power sources. Press the scan button, plug the dongle into your charger, plug it back into your phone, and the app will store your charger’s capabilities.

Not every power supply is equal. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

When it’s time to plug in my 19-volt monitor, I don’t need to pick “19 volts” or remember which of my chargers can deliver — I just tap the picture of my monitor, and the app tells me which of my saved chargers are compatible. Tap that charger, hit “Update” to program the dongle, then plug everything in correctly.

How did I know my monitor needed 19 volts to begin with? The VFLEX can’t test a dumb barrel jack, unfortunately. I had to look up that spec on the monitor itself, or the old power brick. Usually, you’ll find the device’s input voltage or the charger’s output voltage, though you can also look them up online.

The VFLEX is modular; you can swap out different barrel jack tips by yanking them out. They only fit one way. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

But there is one additional wrinkle: Some devices, including guitar pedals and my Nintendo Game Boy and Super Famicom, have a negative center pin instead of a positive one, so you have to use a reverse-polarity connector to avoid feeding them backward. The Werewolf app doesn’t let you program this (even though there’s a non-working toggle there) and you can’t just flip the connector upside down.

If you see the center negative symbol on your gadget, you need to use an orange-tipped plug:

These are both the same size barrel jack, but the orange one is wired center-negative. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Werewolf’s Kevin Spangler (who has since left the company) said the team knows VFLEX “may not resonate with the average consumer” because of these wrinkles; it’s working on specific adapter cables for retro gaming consoles, CPAP machines, and M12 connectors for industrial environments too. And founder Luke Beno says he’s planning to slowly phase out the orange connectors in favor of a reverse-polarity version of the VFLEX itself.

“The main reason why is that it can convert any adapter size to reverse-polarity, so we do not need to build two variants of each connector,” he says. Once that happens, the Werewolf app will also be able to warn you if you’ve got the wrong type of VFLEX connected.

I’m selfishly loving my modular USB-C power trip, and I want my Werewolf to be even more powerful and flexible than it is already. The dongles are already firmware updatable, there’s a public API and a web app, and Spangler said the company might even build its own power supplies to unlock more voltages in the future.

Tech.title: The best classic slasher movie you’ll never watch
Tech.content:
Starting with the original in Camp Miasma in 1980, the horror franchise went on to have a long life. There were multiple sequels, spinoffs in the form of arcade cabinets and board games, and just about every kind of merchandise you can think of, from alarm clocks and lunch boxes to Halloween costumes and action figures. It got so popular there were even knockoff costumes at party stores. For several decades the franchise exerted a powerful, albeit dwindling, impact on the world of horror. But if you haven’t heard of Camp Miasma, that’s okay, because it doesn’t really exist. It’s a fictional franchise at the heart of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, the latest film from I Saw the TV Glow director Jane Schoenbrun.

In order to convince audiences that Camp Miasma — an ongoing saga about a character called Little Death who terrorizes a summer camp — could be real, the production designers had to create a whole lot of objects that detailed the movie franchise’s fake history. “We probably could’ve spent three years only making stuff for Camp Miasma if those were the marching orders,” says production designer Matt Hyland.

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma tells the story of a budding director named Kris (Hannah Einbinder) who has been given the green light to reboot the long-dormant Camp Miasma franchise. Before doing so, she decides to meet up with Billy (Gillian Anderson), the final girl from the first film in the series, who has spent decades isolated in the woods. Kris tries to convince Billy to join the project, and from there the two go on an intimate journey, where they connect over sex, slasher movies, and KFC.

Image: Mubi

But before that, there’s Camp Miasma. The film — the real one — wastes no time in quickly telling the history of the franchise during the title sequence. Through old movie posters, VHS tapes, toys, photographs, and even film reviews and news articles, you learn how the series started off strong before steadily dwindling, going from box office success to direct-to-video dreck over the span of around 30 years. Those objects become a powerful and efficient tool — though the process of creating them wasn’t quite so quick and efficient.

First, the designers spent a long time doing research, looking at existing slasher series like Friday the 13th, Sleepaway Camp, A Nightmare on Elm Street, and Halloween in order to get a sense of how those films looked and how they permeated culture at large. From there, they made a kind of historical document, informed by Schoenbrun’s script, which outlined the entire existence of Camp Miasma: when each movie came out, who directed it, how it was received, and what kind of merchandise was released. Then they sat down with the director in order to figure out what items they actually needed to tell this story. “We locked ourselves in a room with Jane and the cinematographer and mapped out the sequence beat by beat, and every beat was an object we needed to fabricate,” explains Brandon Tonner-Connolly, the film’s other production designer.

Image: Mubi

Most of the items only appear on screen for a brief moment, but the work that went into them was extensive regardless. The Camp Miasma board game, for instance, is fully playable, with a complete set of instructions. Even something seemingly simple, like VHS boxes or movie posters, took a lot of effort: The team had to not only determine how they should look, but also make sure to include information like the production and distribution companies and the film’s tagline. That work was necessary to create a level of believability, even if the object in question only had a fleeting moment on camera.

“You can’t make decisions based on screentime,” says Hyland. “If it’s a board game, we’re making a board game, even if it’s on camera for half a second. That’s a resource challenge. It’s part of our process to assign priorities to things. But the truth is that Jane is so full of ideas and very excited, and gets us very excited, so that unlike other movies, this felt like a pencils-down moment. We just wanted to keep making stuff and coming up with ideas, and we only stopped because the camera was ready and we simply ran out of time.”

Image: Mubi

The attention to detail was also in part a nod to fans. “Jane has such an incredible following that you know that people will pause the movie and read the review, or read the instructions for the board game,” adds Tonner-Connolly. That meant ensuring everything was consistent; the team made multiple tie-in lunch boxes, for instance, and made sure the designs were different to reflect if they would’ve been released in 1983 versus 1997.

Nailing the details was important, but the duo also say that their goal wasn’t to 100 percent re-create existing designs and slap the Camp Miasma name on them. Instead, the objects “needed to look and feel like the memory of watching” those movies. According to Tonner-Connolly, it’s the same approach that was used on I Saw the TV Glow, which similarly had a story revolving around a Buffy the Vampire Slayer-style ’90s drama. “We know that we’re technically proficient enough to exactly replicate these [classic slasher movies], but what we’re actually interested in is relying on these fragmented memories of childhood, and how things are remembered and misremembered,” he explains. “We wanted to play with those emotions and create this new thing.”

It’s that combination of detail and emotional resonance that allows the film to tell Camp Miasma’s multi-decade history with just a handful of snapshots. And that helps make everything in the rest of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma — which includes a long sequence pulled straight out of the film that started it all — feel grounded in something that seems real before taking more fantastical turns. “It’s hard to convince an audience that for the last 30 years this thing has been in the cultural conversation,” says Hyland. “People can smell a phony pretty quickly.”

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is in theaters on August 7th.

Tech.title: Why does Apple keep banning Telegram, but never X?
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For roughly an hour this week, Telegram vanished from Apple’s App Store. Even during that blip, it was a stunning absence for such a major app: an avenue of communication for more than 1 billion users around the world, used widely as a secure platform for people who live in countries under censorship. Apple later revealed that it had removed the app due to the presence of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and restored it once that content was removed.

But the decision once again stirred up questions and confusion about Apple’s moderation policies and how it treats different companies. And one company in particular sprang to many people’s minds: X, the Elon Musk-owned platform that stayed on the App Store even as sexualized Grok-generated images of children flooded the platform. What led to Telegram’s removal but X’s ability to stay online?

The answer may be more political than technical. “When you are enforcing your content moderation policy against an entire platform, you are subjecting yourself to the blowback that will happen,” Anupam Chander, a professor of law and technology at Georgetown and affiliate of Harvard’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, tells The Verge.

Both Telegram and X have had their fair share of controversies. Telegram, which is headquartered in Dubai, garnered a reputation for having a laid-back approach to content moderation.

“Removing X would have likely caused a firestorm of political response against Apple.”

That’s all to say that, while large and important, Telegram is also seen as a nuisance politically and a problematic platform in its own right. “X has a far stronger base of political support in the United States than Telegram does,” Chander said. That means “removing X would have likely caused a firestorm of political response against Apple” to a degree it wouldn’t receive for taking down Telegram. It was not a first for Apple, either; the company previously removed Telegram due to a CSAM violation in 2018, for a similarly brief period of time.

One instance of illegal content can be enough to get an app removed from app stores, but Apple appears to have taken a very different approach when it came to X’s latest controversy. Late last year, X rolled out an update giving users the ability to edit images on the platform using X’s Grok AI chatbot. Soon after, AI-generated deepfakes that undressed adults and children began spreading across the platform.

Despite all of the pressure on Apple, the company kept X in its store. Instead, it began communicating with X behind the scenes to request changes.

Apple reached out to the teams behind the X and Grok apps “after it received complaints and saw news coverage of the scandal,” according to a letter Apple wrote to US senators seen by NBC News. Apple asked the developers to “create a plan to improve content moderation,” NBC News reports. While Apple later found that X “substantially resolved its violations,” Apple reportedly told Grok’s team that they needed to make additional changes “or the app could be removed from the App Store.”

Musk issued a statement in January, saying: “Anyone using Grok to make illegal content will suffer the same consequences as if they upload illegal content.” xAI later sued a man for allegedly using Grok to generate and distribute CSAM. During this period, Apple removed neither X nor Grok and never has, even though the AI chatbot within both apps generated undressed images of minors.

”Removing X would have had to be a decision made at the very top, a decision that you’re willing to suffer the political consequences, including a very irate Elon Musk,” Chander said. Apple is certainly aware of what can happen. In 2022, shortly after he bought Twitter, Musk began publicly complaining that Apple was trying to restrict the app; the dispute ended with Tim Cook giving Musk a tour of Apple’s campus and resolving the apparent “misunderstanding.”

Meanwhile, Durov claims that Apple removed Telegram before ever contacting the company. Apple declined to comment on the moderation differences between the two apps.

Apple closely guards the process behind its moderation decisions, so it’s hard to tell exactly how the company works with developers behind closed doors. But Apple’s recent actions suggest the rules have some flexibility — at least when the world’s first trillionaire is involved.

Tech.title: Cloudflare launches Kitesurf, a browser built for AI agents
Tech.content:
Cloudflare is the latest company to join the race to build a new web browser. But instead of pitching a Chrome alternative to consumers, the internet infrastructure provider launched Kitesurf, a cloud-hosted browser designed specifically for AI agents.

AI software is evolving from chatbots that answer questions to agents that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. Browsers are a critical part of this transition, as they’ll need to navigate the web and use websites, as humans do.

Unlike traditional web browsers built for humans, a browser built for AI agents doesn’t care about visual elements, like themes, tabs, or browser extensions, Cloudflare explained in its announcement. A browser designed for AI agents needs to manage context windows, performance, token costs, and scalability. It also faces a different threat model because an AI browser could be subject to vulnerabilities like prompt injection attacks and more, the company noted.

With Kitesurf, AI developers will be able to build software that can navigate websites, fill out forms, and complete other browser-based tasks, without having to build their own browser software.

Cloudflare says it decided to build Kitesurf just 12 weeks ago, and it runs entirely on top of the company’s serverless platform, called Workers. Kitesurf is available for free while in beta in Browser Run, which lets developers programmatically control and interact with headless browser instances on Cloudflare’s network.

For developers, Cloudflare’s pitch is that this enables AI agents to use the web more efficiently while using less computing power than Chromium, which keeps costs down.

“Kitesurf is significantly more efficient in CPU and memory consumption than Chromium for common agentic tasks like screenshots and HTML extraction,” according to the company.

Image Credits:Cloudflare

The browser itself was built from other technologies, including a modular rendering engine from Blitz; Firefox’s CSS parser, Stylo; and Boa JS, a Rust ECMAScript engine. Everything else runs inside Cloudflare Workers. Although still new, Cloudflare says Kitesurf already passes around 215,000+ web platform tests, and it’s adding hundreds more, passing tests every week.

Cloudflare also credited the open source Rust headless engine, Obscura, for inspiring it to develop Kitesurf, noting that the first proof of concept was a port of Obscura to Workers.

The company said the browser correctly renders pages like TodoMVC, a popular benchmark application for comparing JavaScript frameworks, along with Wikipedia, Hacker News, the Cloudflare Blog, and much of the Cloudflare dashboard.

Tech.title: Computer maker Framework notifies ‘all customers’ of a data breach
Tech.content:
In Brief

Framework, a company that makes modular repairable computers, said it has notified all of its customers that hackers stole their names, email addresses, phone numbers, and physical addresses, due to an incident at a company that provides business intelligence.

On Thursday, several Framework customers said on social media that they had received an email from the company notifying them of the data breach.

Framework’s spokesperson Eric Schumacher told TechCrunch that the breach affected “all customers,” but declined to specify a specific number. Framework computers are relatively niche products, but some estimates say the company sold hundreds of thousands of devices.

According to the notification seen by TechCrunch, the company blamed the data breach on an upstream cyberattack at Metabase.

Metabase disclosed its own breach in a blog post on its official website, where it said that it was hacked by someone using an unknown security flaw, a so-called zero-day. The company said the hackers exploited the bug to give them the ability to access customers’ databases stored on Metabase’s cloud servers.

In its email to customers, Framework also included the email Metabase sent to the company, which says hackers accessed Framework’s cloud instance. The computer maker said it investigated the incident and found that hackers had stolen its customers’ personal data, but did not include their payment information.

Metabase did not respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Trump administration has spent nearly $4B to cancel offshore wind farms
Tech.content:
In Brief

The Trump administration is paying another $1.2 billion to cancel an offshore wind lease, this time to German utility RWE.

The energy company said in an announcement that the wind farms would have been built off the coasts of California, Louisiana, and New York. Instead, RWE will spend $900 million to buy a small stake in a Louisiana liquid natural gas export terminal.

The New York wind farm would have generated more than 3 gigawatts, according to Heatmap News.

The remaining $300 million will go toward buying natural gas turbines to power 15 peaking power plants around the country. Peaking power plants are among the most expensive and most polluting natural gas power plants to operate. It’s unclear when those will be completed — there’s currently a backlog for new turbines stretching into the early 2030s.

RWE isn’t backing off its offshore wind investments elsewhere, though. The company said it bought 6.9 gigawatts of capacity in the U.K.’s recent auction.

The Trump administration has paid $3.93 billion for the 12 leases it has coaxed developers into abandoning.

Tech.title: Chinese AI model Kimi escaped its cybersecurity testing environment, researchers say
Tech.content:
In Brief

Kimi K3, the latest AI model made by Chinese company Moonshot, escaped an environment set up to test its cyber capabilities, researchers said in a blog post published on Friday.

The news shows once again that companies and independent organizations are struggling to contain their AI models designed for hacking.

In recent weeks, frontier LLMs at U.S. artificial intelligence labs at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, as well as the U.K.’s AI Security Institute, all escaped testing environments in different ways and ended up hacking real targets that were not part of the experiment. This is starting to happen so often there’s now a website tracking all these incidents called Felony Bench, a nod to the fact that these LLMs may be committing crimes — at least theoretically speaking.

In the case of this Kimi test, the sandbox designed to contain the experiment was not properly configured. While the sandbox disallowed the AI model from accessing certain web traffic, the model instead bypassed the sandbox by relying on command line tools, according to the researchers at AI-focused cybersecurity firm Frontier Security.

“This suggests that some of the evaluations on cybersecurity the community uses are susceptible to security vulnerabilities and allow models to cheat, and that there are models that intentionally seek loopholes and vulnerabilities which allows them to cheat on evaluations,” the researchers wrote.

If you are keeping score at home, according to Felony Bench’s tally, Moonshot now joins OpenAI and Anthropic, which have seven recorded incidents each, and Meta, which has one.

Tech.title: Airbnb says AI is helping it ship features faster as it tests a new search function
Tech.content:
Airbnb might be taking slow steps to roll out AI features to its consumer-facing interface, but the company is rapidly adopting the tech to build product. Earlier this year, the company said AI is writing 60% of its code. In its latest earnings call, co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky said AI is helping Airbnb create features a at rapid rate.

Chesky said that because of AI, the company has reduced time from conceptualization to finally shopping features by 60%.

“Today, we’re building, testing, and iterating faster than we could just a year ago. Across some of our key initiatives, we’ve reduced the time from concept to launch by as much as 60%. And compared to the same six months last year, we’ve increased the number of features and improvements we shipped this year by nearly 80%,” he said during the company’s second-quarter earnings call.

He pointed out that AI has helped the company in areas like search, sign-up, checkout, and payments. Airbnb has also released features designed to help hosts with things like quicker onboarding flow.

Airbnb’s adoption of consumer-facing AI features has been slower, and mostly isolated to features like review summaries and listing highlights.

Until now, Chesky has maintained that just adopting a chatbot-like interface won’t work for travel use cases. Instead, the company has focused on developing an AI for search, discovery, and support.

Chesky said during the earnings call that the company will finally start testing AI search. Even with the new test, Airbnb doesn’t want to impose AI search on customers who are used to the current search and filter feature on the app. To accommodate that, Airbnb is adding a toggle that lets users switch to AI search, where they can type in natural language to get results, which would be in a visual format.

“The titles [in the answer] could actually be AI-generated and they can be conversational as if you’re reading a chatbot, but more visual. Then you get to the product description page and the highlights are AI generated in real-time and personalized to you,” Chesky said.

On the back end, customer support is one area where Airbnb has heavily deployed AI. The company launched its AI-powered bot in North America in 2025, and this year, it has expanded it to more than 50 languages with plans to make it available for voice calls later this year.

The company said that nearly 45% of the customer issues that start with its AI agent are completed without any human intervention. Because of this, the company’s support cost per booking is down 16% year-over-year.

Airbnb posted positive results for the quarter ended in June with revenue up 17% year-over-year to $3.6 billion and adjusted EBITDA jumping 21% to $1.3 billion.

Tech.title: SpaceX’s Terafab will rely on natural gas power plants, not Tesla solar panels
Tech.content:
SpaceX said this week that it will build natural gas power plants to supply electricity to the Terafab semiconductor factory it plans to build in Texas, according to a report from Bloomberg.

Riley Trettel, who leads energy and data center development for SpaceX, said in a public meeting on Wednesday that his company will be “bringing our own power” for the project, which will also include “very large battery arrays.”

Notably absent from the Bloomberg report — and other SpaceX announcements related to Terafab — is any mention of terrestrial solar power for the facility. Tesla, which is also a solar developer, is a partner in the project.

Despite his investments in solar power, SpaceX and Tesla’s CEO Elon Musk has bet heavily on natural gas lately. The xAI data centers in Memphis run almost exclusively on the fossil fuel. Musk also recently bought a company that specializes in natural gas power plants, and SpaceX has said it plans to buy $2.8 billion worth of gas turbines over the next three years.

Terafab will be built in Grimes County, which is about 45 miles northwest of downtown Houston. SpaceX, which recently went public in an IPO that raised $87.5 billion, received a 100% tax abatement from the county in exchange for spending at least $5 billion by 2030 and creating at least 1,800 full-time jobs by 2035. Texas is also providing $30 million in incentives.

The initial phase of the fab unit is expected to cost $16.8 billion, though SpaceX had previously estimated it would cost $55 billion. The fab is intended to build chips for data centers that will be run by SpaceX and its xAI subsidiary.

The AI data center boom has driven a surge in proposals for new natural gas power plants across the industry, which has in turn driven up costs for natural gas power plants by 66%. Google, Meta and Microsoft have all announced massive projects in recent months.

Texas has been ground zero for these so-called “bring your own power” data centers, and more than 70 gigawatts of capacity has been charted out.

Such schemes are intended to speed up project development while addressing concerns about rising electricity prices for consumers, but natural gas turbines can release significant amounts of pollution. SpaceX subsidiary xAI has been sued over its use of unpermitted natural gas turbines in one of the most polluted parts of the country.

Tech.title: The 7 Best TV Shows to Stream This Month
Tech.content:
The big screen is having a moment. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is breaking box office records, while Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey has people dusting off Homer for the first time since high school. But television is keeping pace with a slate of can’t-miss new releases and beloved old favorites that are worth revisiting.

While plenty of outlets will tell you what everyone is watching (see: Ted Lasso), that’s not our goal. As always, the TV shows we’re watching this month reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day—shows that explore technology, science, politics, culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.

From prestige dramas to absurd comedies and one truly groundbreaking sci-fi series, these are the TV shows we think are worth making time for this month.

Star Trek: The Original Series

On September 8, 1966, science fiction changed forever with the premiere of the original Star Trek TV series. In the 60 years since, Gene Roddenberry’s ahead-of-its-time tale of the USS Enterprise crew’s journeys into deep space has spawned dozens of films, TV series, and video games, plus hundreds of books and comics—not to mention a number of real-world tech innovations. The legendary series has also shaped pop culture in countless other ways, giving us everything from Vulcan salutes and Klingons to the Prime Directive and the immortal command to “beam me up.”

Whether you’re a lifelong Trekkie or a curious newcomer, there’s never been a better time to see where one of television’s most influential franchises began. Though it ran for just three seasons, Star Trek: The Original Series left an outsized legacy, breaking barriers with one of television’s first interracial kisses, featuring a remarkably diverse cast at the height of the Civil Rights Movement, and inspiring generations of scientists, engineers, and storytellers to imagine a more optimistic future. Sixty years later, its blend of adventure, social commentary, and boundless curiosity remains as compelling as ever. Best of all, Paramount+ is home to nearly every corner of the Star Trek universe, from the beautifully remastered original series to its many spinoffs and feature films. If you’re celebrating the franchise’s 60th anniversary, there’s no better place to boldly go back to where it all began.

Futurama

Following a decade-long hiatus, Futurama made a triumphant comeback in 2023, complete with gags about The Twilight Zone and “Momazon” drone deliveries. Created by Matt Groening and David X. Cohen, the animated sci-fi comedy is set in the 31st century and follows the employees of the Planet Express delivery company as they stumble through bizarre adventures, alien encounters, and laugh-out-loud takes on everything from AI to corporate greed.

Tech.title: Zohran Mamdani’s NYC Tech Team Is What DOGE Should Have Been
Tech.content:
A go-kart track is an odd location to launch a tech initiative in the nation’s biggest city. Yet last month there was New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, zipping around the 900-foot oval at Coney Island’s Luna Park before stepping up to a podium to unveil a program called Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crews. Thus the go-kart theme.

PIT will consist of five “game-changing” teams that, Mamdani promised, will “raise the bar for what New Yorkers can expect from City Hall.” Working closely with city agencies, these small groups of engineers and designers will strive to change the hidebound and confusing tenor of current city services by using state-of-art skills to rapidly whip up specialized apps that solve real problems. “We want to transform how New Yorkers interact with the government,” said the mayor. “We want to raise expectations on what government can deliver, because we really can deliver.”

Do those words sound familiar? If you follow government tech, they might. Because Mamdani’s message could have fit quite comfortably in the pitch that Barack Obama’s chief technology officer, Todd Park, delivered in 2014 while recruiting tech talent for what would become the United States Digital Service. The USDS was an idealistic effort to bring top Silicon Valley talent into the executive branch to bypass the logjams caused by outdated and inefficient IT, by building great, user-centric software.

The agency somehow survived the first Trump administration and kept going through the Biden term. But in 2025, Elon Musk and his DOGE wrecking crew infiltrated the agency and pulled the plug on much of the useful stuff. (Now, with the National Design Service, the Trump administration is ostensibly trying to revive some of what it destroyed.)

Mamdani’s PIT crew initiative adopts much of the original USDS ethos, with a timely twist: It embraces Silicon Valley expertise while taking a skeptical, almost adversarial, stance toward Big Tech itself. The combination of mayoral charisma and a chance to make software that doesn’t serve advertisers, the military, or the pocketbooks of centibillionaires makes the Mamdani team an attractive, high-status, mid-career change of pace for some techies. Suddenly, one of the sexiest places in geekdom is the Brooklyn headquarters of New York City’s Office of Technology and Innovation.

Mamdani’s transition team set the stage for an urban, democratic-socialist-adjacent, USDS-style tech squad when it tapped Lisa Gelobter for the city’s chief technology officer job. Gelobter’s résumé includes stints at big companies and startups, but the standout item was her post at the United States Digital Service, where she was embedded in the Department of Education. She led the effort to create a College Scorecard that focused on nuts-and-bolts criteria like costs and graduation rates. To this day, she gets misty when recalling her Washington experience; she even remembers what she was wearing when the USDS team took a group picture with Obama just before he left office.

“I’m really excited about trying to recapture that essence, that energy here,” she says. Her budget for the program is $5.24 million, with an additional $2 million grant from the Rockefeller Foundation, which will fund one of the crews.

Gelobter says she brings an engineering mindset to New York City government. “I know how to build software,” she says. “I know how to run a technology organization from a technology perspective.” It’s also a cultural thing for her. “I’m wearing jeans to work—not because I don’t look great in a suit, but it’s a statement, right?” she says. (The same norm-breaking happened in the USDS, which had to overcome objections from bureaucrats who didn’t want to meet with anyone wearing a hoodie.) Naturally, the two people Gelobter hired to run the PIT crew program are also USDS veterans, Luke Farrell and Maya Israni.

Tech.title: Scientists Used AI to Create 16 New Viruses
Tech.content:
For the first time, an artificial intelligence system has created a series of previously unknown viruses capable of infecting and eliminating certain types of bacteria. This breakthrough opens up new possibilities for combating bacterial resistance. However, it also raises concerns about the potential misuse of this technology to design biological weapons.

For several years now, scientists have been able to synthesize viruses from scratch; these are typically used to develop and evaluate antiviral drugs and vaccines, as well as to expand our understanding of how these microorganisms behave. However, the production of these viral genomes has primarily relied on replicating previously known pathogens or variants.

In contrast, a new study conducted by scientists at Stanford University and the Arc Institute succeeded in having an AI design simple, functional, and previously unseen viruses based on information contained in the genetic sequences of millions of animals, plants, microbes, bacteria, and viruses found in nature

The researchers worked with bacteriophages—microorganisms characterized by relatively small genomes, which are relatively easy to synthesize and manipulate under controlled conditions. These viruses infect only bacteria, making them a tool with enormous biotechnological potential and a promising alternative to antibiotics for combating resistant bacterial infections.

The creation of these entirely new viruses was based on Evo 1 and Evo 2, foundational AI models developed for computational biology applications. Both algorithms were trained on millions of genomes from all domains of life, with the goal of identifying and learning complex evolutionary patterns, including how genes are typically organized, which sequences are conserved, and the biological constraints that allow an organism to remain functional.

The experimental design used the bacteriophage Phi X-174—which is capable of infecting the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli)—as a reference. The goal was not to reproduce this virus, but rather to use it solely as a guide for the algorithms to generate thousands of completely new genomes with a genetic architecture compatible with infecting E. coli.

In other words, the viruses derived from the genomes created by the AI retained the functional organization essential for recognizing the bacterium, inserting their DNA, replicating it, producing new viral particles, and assembling them correctly. However, the specific DNA sequences differed considerably from those observed in naturally occurring bacteriophages.

16 New Viruses Created Using AI

The scientists then evaluated the AI-generated genomes to select those most likely to be functional, taking into account factors such as gene organization, the presence of regulatory elements, and other criteria inspired by the biology of the Phi X-174 bacteriophage.

This selection resulted in a sample of 300 genomes, which were artificially synthesized, molecule by molecule, in the laboratory. They were then introduced into E. coli bacteria to test whether they were capable of producing functional viruses.

Of the 300 synthesized genomes, only 16 gave rise to fully functional bacteriophages, featuring previously unpublished sequences, different genes, new regulatory elements, and even varying genome sizes. The behavior of these viruses also varied: While some infected the bacteria more quickly, others exhibited different abilities to replicate.

The research, published this week in the journal Science, also evaluated the ability of AI-generated bacteriophages to combat resistant bacteria. The experiment involved exposing a mixture of AI-designed phages and a mixture of natural phages similar to Phi X-174 to strains of E. coli that had already developed resistance to that virus.

The results showed that the AI-generated viruses were able to rapidly overcome bacterial resistance and establish infection. According to the authors, this finding demonstrates “a path toward artificial intelligence–generated phage therapies against rapidly evolving bacterial pathogens.”

The Two Sides of the Milestone

The discovery opens up new possibilities for tackling the growing problem of bacterial resistance. According to the researchers, this approach could facilitate the development of personalized treatments capable of evolving at nearly the same rate as the pathogens themselves.

Although this milestone represents a significant advance for molecular biomedicine, it also raises concerns about the potential malicious use of this technology to develop, for example, new diseases, highly toxic substances, or pathogens capable of triggering a new pandemic.

Tech.title: Best Webcams (2026): My Honest Take After Testing the Best
Tech.content:
It's not perfect—no webcam is. Sometimes there's a bit too much processing and smoothing for my taste, especially in some of the details around the face. And out of the box, the colors skew a bit cool. The easy-to-use software makes adjusting these issues easy, but it's something to be aware of nonetheless. Hopefully, by now, you'll be convinced that there's little reason to buy the Logitech MX Brio over the Insta360 2C Pro. Logitech has a lot of brand equity in the world of webcams, but considering both models retail for $200, Insta360 definitely has the superior product.

The standard Insta360 Link 2C ($150) is also a strong option. It's $50 cheaper, with a slightly smaller sensor and narrower aperture, resulting in worse low-light performance. I noticed that it introduced more noise, especially in areas of high contrast, such as along my hairline. But let's be real: Though you can hunt down the differences between these two webcams, the standard Link 2C still punches above its weight for the price.

One of the biggest disadvantages of the non-Pro model, though, is in microphone quality. The Insta360 2C is more in line with other webcams I tested. It uses just a single microphone and lacks the ability to pick up the deeper frequencies in my voice, whereas the 2C Pro uses a dual-microphone beam-forming system that does a far better job capturing the fuller spectrum. I still think that the Insta360 Link 2C is one of the best options at around $150, though, handily beating out models like the Razer Kiyo V2 and Logitech Brio 4K.

Cheap Webcams That Get the Job Done

Proceed very carefully with the following recommendations. That's especially true if you are working from a laptop with a built-in camera or already have a decent webcam. In general, I suggest dishing out some extra cash for one of the more premium options listed above, or buying a light to help your existing camera work better. Even a simple lighting accessory, like the $70 Logitech Litra Glow, will dramatically improve the quality of your video calls more effectively than buying a budget webcam.

That said, if you're using an external monitor and need a budget-friendly webcam to pair with it, there are a couple of decent options to consider. The Anker PowerConf C200 ($66) is the best of the bunch that I've tested. It has issues, such as the built-in mount, which can't swivel left or right. It also doesn't grip the monitor as effectively as I'd want. While the 5-megapixel camera can't compare with the larger sensors in the more premium webcams, the image quality is decent enough, especially if your room has nice light and you don't mind tweaking the picture quality in the software.

I'd also hesitantly recommend the Logitech Brio 300 ($60). Like the C200, it has a number of deficiencies. On this model, those drawbacks include an unappealing sticky pad built into the integrated mount and the built-in cable. The microphone also won't be much of an upgrade over the ones built into MacBooks, though it's still better than built-in mics on many of the Windows laptops I've tested. I also don't like that the Brio 300 has a fixed 70-degree field-of-view, which gives it a smaller framing than all the other webcams I’ve tried.

Tech.title: The 5 Best Laptop Power Banks I've Personally Tested (2026)
Tech.content:
Toss the right laptop power bank in your bag, and you'll never need to do that panicked run to the nearest outlet again. A hefty portable charger frees you to sit anywhere with your laptop and keep it running. Power banks with USB-C ports can charge phones and headphones as well, and I’ve tested more than 100 of them over the past few years. These powerful, high-capacity portable batteries are the best ones when laptop charging is a priority. For this guide, I considered power banks that are 20,000 mAh and up, enough to charge most laptops twice.

If you want some smaller portable chargers, check out my guide to the Best Power Banks or Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks, or for more power, the Best Portable Power Stations.

Updated August 2026: I added power banks from ReelCharge and Pisen, removed some older devices, and updated prices.

Best Laptop Power Bank

Power bank manufacturers have made strides in pushing up potential charging rates in their high-capacity portable chargers. EcoFlow’s Rapid Pro X is a prime example, just edging out Anker’s Prime series below. Capable of delivering 300 watts, this power bank is close to the maximum capacity allowed on flights, and can charge a couple of laptops and phones at the same time via the three USB-C ports (140W, 65W, 65W) and a retractable USB-C cable (140W). It has a wee display showing remaining power as a percentage and the charging rate for each connected device. You can also check temperature and battery health, tweak the brightness and screen timeout, and even connect to your phone via the Ecoflow app (though most folks won’t need to).

The Rapid Pro offers a laundry list of charging capabilities (PD3.1, PPS, QC3.0, AFC, Apple2.4A, BC1.2, SCP, FCP, UFCS), but its greatest feature could be its super speedy recharge rate. Charge from a single USB-C input at 140 watts, and it takes an hour or so to fill, but you can plug in both at once to hit 80 percent from dead in under half an hour. Even better, Ecoflow’s dock can charge via the pogo pins on the bottom at 320 watts, enabling you to go from zero to 80 percent in just 20 minutes. You can fully charge it while you pack a bag. The Rapid Pro X comes with the 27,650 mAh model and the charging dock. Ecoflow also offers a 20,000-mAh, 230W Rapid Pro model ($140).

Specs Ports: USB-C x 3, retractable USB-C cable Capacity: 27,650 mAh Charges: Most laptops one to two times Wattage: 300 watts Warranty: 2 years

Best Laptop Power Bank With a Dock

Anker introduced an innovative, high-wattage, high-capacity Prime Power Bank series a few years ago with an optional docking station for faster recharging via pogo pins on the bottom. This model is more compact and powerful than ever, offering 26,250 mAh at 300 watts across two USB-C ports and one USB-A, making it suitable for charging a couple of MacBooks and a smartphone at once. It also boasts a smart display and app control, and it comes with a 3.3-foot USB-C cable. Plug in both USB-C ports, and you can recharge at 250 watts to 80 percent from zero in 20 minutes.
